Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in my area could be much improved if we prioritise growing the workforce with a clear plan to recruit, retain and support staff. I’ve seen my local surgery frequently advertising GP vacancies for months, and mental health slots often fill up weeks in advance, which pushes people into urgent care or online triage. To fix this, I would push for targeted recruitment campaigns in regions with GP shortages and open to international hiring, with robust, fast-track registration and local induction to ensure safe practice. Pair this with pay improvements and practical incentives—salary uplifts, housing allowances in high-cost areas, and student loan forgiveness—to make NHS posts competitive with the private sector.

Flexibility is essential: more job-share and part-time roles for GPs and nurses, extended hours, and remote triage options to reduce unnecessary clinic visits. Wellbeing support and realistic workloads must go hand in hand with recruitment; protected admin time, dedicated wellbeing champions, and calmer rostering can curb burnout. Finally, empower multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, therapists, and social care coordinators—to handle routine issues so GPs can focus on complex cases. With these changes, timely access could improve without sacrificing safety or staff morale.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in my area remains uneven, but I believe we can make real progress by treating NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation as the backbone of urgent care. The aim should be to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication, and simplify patient flow so people don’t have to explain their history multiple times to different teams.

First, NHS111 needs to be a reliable front door. It should offer not just a phone number but a rapid clinician-led triage, with clear outcomes and direct next steps. In urgent situations, callers should be offered same-day slots or rapid assessment with the appropriate team—GP, urgent care, mental health crisis support or a community nurse—without endless redirects. In my experience, a more decisive triage outcome would have cut down on multiple phone calls and hours spent trying to secure the right appointment for someone with a worrying symptom.

Second, clinical triage should be consistent across services. A unified triage process, with specialists who can recognise red flags and escalate to urgent care where necessary, would ensure the patient is seen quickly by the most appropriate clinician. This would also prevent patients from bouncing between NHS111, out-of-hours and in-hours GP lines, each asking for the same information again. I’ve seen how even small delays compound when the wrong service is initialised; faster, better-informed triage could cut through that maze.

Third, booking systems must work together. A single, real-time digital platform linking GP practices, community health teams, and mental health services would remove the need to log into several portals and repeat personal details. If you could check for same-day GP slots, a nurse-led urgent care slot, and a psychology or talking therapy opening in one place, it would be much easier to secure timely help. In rural areas, where capacity is tighter, this could be the difference between a patient getting an appointment within 24 hours or waiting a week.

Fourth, care navigation should be embedded locally. Trained navigators who know the range of services—GPs, district nurses, physiotherapists, community mental health teams, social prescribers—can guide patients to the right option quickly. They can also help with referral pathways, explain what to expect, and chase follow-ups if a problem isn’t resolved after a first contact. This would be particularly valuable for older residents and those with multiple conditions, who can feel overwhelmed by the system.

Fifth, reduce duplication and streamline patient flow. Shared electronic records accessible to NHS111, GPs and mental health teams would stop people having to re-tell their symptoms every time they switch service. Clear consent and privacy controls would be essential, but the payoff would be fewer repeated assessments, more accurate triage, and faster access to the right care.

Sixth, ensure mental health pathways match the urgency of the need. For someone in distress or with escalating symptoms, there should be a direct route from NHS111 into immediate mental health support, with options for same-day or rapid access to talking therapies and crisis teams where required. This should include straightforward signposting to emergency services if safety concerns arise.

Finally, I know there are real constraints on workforce and budgets. Any changes must be rolled out with capacity planning, training and clear metrics: wait times for urgent versus non-urgent care, conversion rates from triage to appointment, patient satisfaction, and overall system efficiency. Pilot programmes in a few areas with transparent data would help refine the model before wider adoption.

Overall, I support a coordinated package that strengthens NHS111 triage, unifies booking, and deploys effective care navigation. If done well, it could make urgent GP, community and mental health services noticeably faster and easier to navigate for patients like me and my neighbours.

I welcome proposals to speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services. In our area the queue for a GP appointment can stretch for weeks, and mental health referrals seem to take even longer. Expanding community mental health teams, with early intervention and robust crisis response, would stop problems from building into emergencies and help people stay well at home. More talking therapies and easier access to same-day assessment would be particularly valuable for older residents dealing with loneliness, anxiety or bereavement.

It’s also crucial to target resources to those who face the greatest barriers. Interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus proactive outreach to deprived and ethnic minority communities, migrants and marginalised groups, would close gaps we see in practice. I’ve seen how a simple language service makes all the difference when a neighbour needed help with a mental health referral, and how outreach clinics in community centres can reach people who wouldn’t attend a traditional surgery.

If we invest in these areas and ensure parity with physical health services, waits will shorten and care will be more humane and local.

it's outrageous that from my experience in a town in England, getting a GP appointment often depends on the day you call. I tried to get a same-day appointment last month for a chest infection for my partner; the call came in at 7:15am; there were no morning slots; I was offered a slot two weeks later. A nurse triage call suggested monitoring symptoms rather than an urgent appointment; we ended up going to urgent care. For mental health, my niece waited weeks for an initial talking therapy appointment after a stressful period. The community physio and district nursing support sometimes arrive late or are canceled because of staff shortages. I’m not sure what would work best, but I think the system could change in a few practical ways.

Here are some possibilities, though I’m not sure what mix would be best in practice:

- Make same-day/urgent access easier: more reserved slots for urgent needs, plus quick triage that prioritizes those at risk. But ensure staff aren’t overwhelmed and that reception staff can explain what counts as urgent.

- Expand access outside traditional hours: some GP practices operate only 9-5; I’d welcome early mornings or evenings and perhaps a Saturday morning slot, with protections to staff rest to avoid burnout.

- Strengthen local multi-disciplinary teams: closer cooperation between GPs, nurses, district nurses, physio and mental health professionals to avoid patients bouncing between services. A 'one front door' approach at local clinics would help.

- Improve mental health access: increase number of counsellors and therapists available in or near primary care; establish faster initial assessments and clearer crisis pathways; better referral routes for longer-term care.

- Use technology and train more support staff: online booking should be accessible to older users too; use pharmacists for minor ailments and nurse practitioners for routine checks; digital triage could help but not leave those less comfortable with tech behind.

- Provide clear information and local data: practices should publish waiting times and realistic expectations in plain language; enable patients to see when slots open and where to go for urgent care.

- Target support for carers and rural residents: those caring for others or living far away need simpler access options, perhaps mobile clinics or home visits.

I don’t claim to have all the answers. A mix of better triage, extended hours, stronger community teams and clearer information might help, but I’d want to see pilots with local measurements so people know there’s real improvement, not just promises. And crucially, any changes must avoid increasing burnout among already stretched staff or making the system harder to navigate for older or vulnerable residents!
Expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care, freeing GPs for complex cases; simultaneously invest in training, return-to-practice and CPD to sustainably grow the workforce.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I would prioritise investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health teams and mental health services with social care and Voluntary, Community and Social Enterprise (VCSE) partners for seamless local care. A single, accessible hub in each locality would cut duplication and shorten waits by enabling triage and same-day appointments across disciplines. 

Concrete steps: establish multi-disciplinary hubs within existing GP practices or nearby community facilities with shared reception and a unified patient record so a person can be seen by a GP, a nurse, a mental health clinician or a social worker in a coordinated sequence. implement a single booking and triage system, with extended hours and same-day referrals, plus care coordinators to organise home visits and fast links to voluntary support and social care. 

Invest in an integrated digital platform for consented shared records, secure messaging and remote monitoring to speed up decision making while protecting privacy. Ensure robust governance and patient choice, with staff trained across disciplines so capacity isn’t trapped in silos. Train and fund VCSE partners to participate meaningfully in design and delivery. 

There is evidence from pilots in several areas that true co-location and coordinated care can improve wait times and satisfaction; the key is sustainable funding, clear governance and strong local involvement.

it's outrageous that access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in our area is variable, with queues and long waits for non-urgent issues. I would support expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to treat routine cases and free GPs to focus on complex care. In practice, this could mean a pharmacist handling minor med questions and simple infections, a physio triaging musculoskeletal issues, and a paramedic or PA doing home visits for fall risks or post‑injury checks. This has the potential to cut pointless GP referrals and speed up help for many people like me who just need early advice. 

However, I have concerns about how this would be implemented. Clear training, supervision, and delegation rules are essential, along with secure IT links so notes are shared with GPs. Funding must align with workforce planning; otherwise, we’ll risk fragmentation or inconsistent care. Additionally, patient navigation must be straightforward so people know who to contact and when; a mix of self-booking and triage could reduce duplication if NHS111, booking systems, and care navigation are well integrated. 

Overall, conditional support: if scaled with strong governance, funding, and integrated IT, this could improve timely access while preserving continuity of care!

Agree. To improve timely access, we need a steady growth of the primary care and mental health workforce, which includes targeted recruitment and international hiring. Flexible working and wellbeing support will help keep skilled staff long term. Practical steps: fast-track recruitment campaigns in high-demand areas; use overseas recruitment with language and adaptation support; offer relocation grants and sign-on bonuses; ensure pay reflects workload and rising costs so clinicians choose to stay. Expand training routes and return-to-practice schemes to bring more people into GP, district nursing and allied health roles.

Offer flexible working: more part‑time or job‑share roles, better‑structured rotas, and protected time for training and wellbeing. This reduces burnout and keeps practices open for evenings and weekends where needed. Invest in community health teams—more district nurses, chronic disease specialists, pharmacists and mental health practitioners embedded in GP clinics—and ensure faster same-day triage by phone or video where appropriate to cut unnecessary visits.

From my experience, when a GP or nurse is off, demand balloons quickly; with more staff recruited and retained, older residents like me would get earlier appointments and avoid unnecessary hospital trips. I’ve also seen neighbours with anxiety benefit when mental health support is readily available in the community rather than waiting months for specialist care.

I think the most immediate improvements would come from smarter triage and booking, alongside longer-term workforce planning. In my area, NHS111 and telephone triage often feel like a bottleneck; urgent cases can be shuffled between services and same-day GP slots are scarce. I would support modernising NHS111 with clinical triage that can accurately prioritise urgent needs and route patients quickly to the right clinician, plus a clearer booking flow that reduces duplication and asks patients to repeat details. For longer-term capacity, increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus return-to-practice support and CPD, would help grow the workforce sustainably. Also, targeted outreach to deprived and migrant communities, with interpreters and culturally competent staff, is essential to avoid delays and miscommunication. Concrete ideas: expand apprenticeship pathways for practice nurses; fund local mental health workers to offer same-day slots; and embed care navigators in practices to guide patients to the right service, including community health teams. In the short term, more flexible hours and weekend GP access could relieve urgent demand for working people. As someone who has faced language barriers trying to book care for a family member, these changes would make access fairer and faster.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a critical everyday concern for many families, including mine. My view is that the most meaningful long‑term improvements will come from a coherent, well-funded workforce strategy that focuses on sustainable growth of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Specifically, we should:

- Expand training places and pathways: increase the number of medical school places and GP specialty training places in a way that reflects demand across regions, with targeted support for practice‑based teaching and early exposure to primary care. Pair this with more training posts for district nurses, physiotherapists and mental health professionals so communities see a broader range of skilled staff locally, not just on a rota from elsewhere.

- Strengthen return‑to‑practice routes: make it easier for GPs, nurses and therapists who paused their careers (for caring responsibilities or other reasons) to rejoin with shorter, funded bridging courses, supervised practice and flexible re‑entry timelines. A practical example would be a 6–12 month return‑to‑practice programme in local NHS trusts with protected time for supervision and gradual patient load.

- Expand apprenticeships and career ladders: offer apprenticeships that start with health and care support workers and progress into registered roles (nurses, allied health professionals, mental health practitioners) where practical. Apprenticeships should be designed with clear competency milestones, academic credit and guaranteed progression opportunities so people in local communities can train and stay in the area.

- Invest in continuing professional development and retention: provide protected time and adequate funding for CPD so staff keep up‑to‑date with best practice, new treatments and digital tools. Strong CPD should be linked to local workforce planning and career progression so staff feel there is a tangible path forward rather than a revolving door.

- Accelerate multi‑disciplinary, community‑based care: build integrated care hubs where GPs, district nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, social workers and mental health professionals work side by side, with shared records and clear referral routes. This would reduce unnecessary work for GPs and help patients get timely assessments and treatment in a familiar local setting.

- Improve access in the short term with sensible triage and capacity: while training pipelines take time to grow, we should bolster capacity now by expanding same‑day slots, enabling more nurse‑led and pharmacist‑led triage, and extending hours in busy practices where possible. We must guard against digital exclusion and ensure older or less tech‑comfortable patients can still book and access care easily.

- Ensure equitable distribution and resilience: plan workforce growth not just for urban centres but with explicit attention to rural and underserved areas where access is often worse. This requires stable, long‑term funding, predictable training pipelines and local partnerships with universities and employers.

In my area, there have been pockets where a new multi‑disciplinary hub helped shorten some waits by bringing together GPs with district nurses and a mental health practitioner. But there are still long waits for talking therapies and gaps in community nurse capacity, especially outside of peak times. Training expansion and better return‑to‑practice routes would start to address the root cause rather than just patching the surface. If we invest now in the people who deliver care, we’ll reap better access, more consistent care, and, importantly, safer and more sustainable services for the long term.

Overall, I’m supportive of the principle: grow the workforce through training, re‑entry routes, apprenticeships and CPD. The caveat is that it must be paired with robust funding, clear career structures, and local implementation that prioritises patients who currently struggle most to access timely care.

I welcome the focus on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely and easier to access. As someone who works full-time and tries to juggle family commitments, the ability to get a same-day urgent slot and to attend an evening or weekend clinic would make a real difference. I’ve experienced how waiting for a daytime appointment can disrupt work and add unnecessary stress, and I know others in my community face the same pattern. Here are the changes I think would have the biggest impact:

- Evening and weekend clinics across GP practices, with predictable hours tailored to working people. For example, two weekday evenings until 7pm and a regular Saturday morning slot per practice would mean people can book without taking time off or using sick days. If a practice isn’t able to run its own extended hours every week, a regional network of sorely needed weekend or after-hours urgent care hubs could provide a reliable alternative.

- Guaranteed same-day urgent slots for non-emergency health concerns. A policy that ensures someone is available for urgent symptoms or pressing health issues on the same day—whether that’s a GP, a practice nurse, or a dedicated urgent care clinician—would prevent issues from spiralling and reduce pressure on A&E. In practice, this could mean an initial triage call or digital check-in first thing in the morning, followed by a booked slot the same day if needed.

- Stronger triage and routing to the right service. Urgent requests should be quickly assessed and directed to the most appropriate team—GP, nurse-led acute care, mental health crisis line, or a community health clinician—so people aren’t bounced between services. A simple online or phone pre-assessment that feeds into a same-day appointment would help people avoid repeated calls and wasted journeys.

- Integrated mental health access with rapid entry points. For people with escalating anxiety, depression, or other conditions, rapid access to talking therapies (IAPT) and, when required, urgent mental health assessments should be available the same day. A dedicated mental health urgent line or same-day slot, linked to GP triage, would prevent crises from forming and allow earlier intervention.

- Expanded and co-located community health services. Local hubs that bring together district nursing, physio and rehabilitation services, social prescribing, and minor illness care in one accessible place would cut down on unnecessary referrals and back-and-forth. When someone isn’t well enough to travel, having community services delivered in a nearby clinic or home visits where appropriate would keep people supported and out of hospital.

- Staffing, workload and quality. To sustain longer hours and more appointment slots, we need clear investment in workforce: more GPs, nurses, mental health professionals, and admin support. Adequate time per appointment is essential so clinicians can properly assess and treat, rather than rushing through a backlog. Retention and fair caseloads are crucial to prevent turnover that would undermine access improvements.

- Transparent information and local monitoring. People should easily know what access options are available in their area—times, locations, and how to book urgently. Local wait-time dashboards, performance reporting, and feedback loops should be public so communities can see improvements and hold services to account.

A concrete example from my own experience: last winter my partner developed a sudden, painful back issue. We phoned for an appointment at 9am, expecting a same-day slot, but the earliest available was two weeks away. If there had been an evening clinic or a guaranteed same-day urgent slot, we could have seen someone sooner and started treatment sooner, possibly avoiding escalation to more invasive care. Another example is a family member who struggled to access timely mental health support; a rapid same-day entry point linked to GP triage would have reduced anxiety and prevented a crisis.

If these changes were implemented, I believe people would stay healthier, miss fewer days at work, and feel more supported in managing non-emergency health needs. It would also ease pressure on urgent care services and create a more equitable system for those with caring responsibilities or irregular work patterns. I’m encouraged by the direction of proposals, and I’d strongly support practical steps to deliver evening/weekend access and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, alongside integrated community and mental health provision.

Expand community mental health teams and early intervention, with robust crisis response and talking therapies, to cut waits and improve parity with physical health. But ensure sustainable funding, staffing, and fair access in rural areas; maintain GP continuity and personalised care.

From my 60s vantage point in England, timely access to GP and mental health services matters more than glossy reports. In practice, though, what helps me avoid risk is not just appointment slots but the whole network around it. Last winter I needed a quick chat with my GP after a scare; the earliest slot was two weeks away, and planning a call with a mental health counsellor took months. What often makes a difference in our street is transport and nearby support networks. The local bus is unreliable, and travelling to the surgery with an elderly relative can be a day-long affair. Digital-first approaches can help some, but not everyone is comfortable online or has stable broadband. I’ve seen neighbours miss sessions because of poor reminders or because a carer’s sick day left gaps in cover. I would value stronger links between GP practices, social care, and community groups, so people don’t fall through the cracks when life gets busy. If the aim is better access, we need to make the whole system easier to navigate, not just create more clinics.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in our area has become more hit-and-miss, and that affects people who work, care for others, or have limited mobility. I think a combination of long-term workforce development and smarter local access arrangements would be the most effective way forward. In practice, we need both sustainable staffing and practical ways to reach people where they are.

Ways to improve the workforce in a durable way
- Expand training places, return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD. Our area has repeatedly faced gaps because there aren’t enough GPs, nurses or therapists moving into, or staying in, primary care. Increasing training places and funding for return-to-practice would help people who trained here, or who started a career elsewhere and could be brought back with proper support. Apprenticeships for allied health professionals and nurses could attract people who want to train locally while contributing to the local NHS needs.
- Invest in long-term retention and morale. It isn’t only about new staff; it’s about stabilising teams with manageable workloads, protected training time, and career progression. Local clinics could benefit from a structured CPD calendar, more joint positions across GP and mental health teams, and clearly defined pathways for advancement.
- Align staffing with demand signals. We need proactive workforce planning that anticipates spikes—flu season, school- holiday periods, or surges in mental health referrals—and uses bank staff or flexible rotas to keep appointment slots available without burning out existing teams.

Making access practical for rural and mobility-limited residents
- Bring care closer through mobile clinics and outreach. A regular mobile clinic schedule that visits villages and stops at community hubs would cut travel and waiting times for many residents who can’t easily reach a surgery. If a monthly clinic could screen chronic conditions, update medications, and run simple mental health check-ins, it would reduce unnecessary trips to town.
- Establish telehealth hubs and co-located services. A telehealth hub in a convenient community space (library, community centre, or GP reception) with trained staff could offer urgent triage, minor physical checks via connected devices, and access to counsellors or therapists where in-person slots are limited. Co-locating with other services—pharmacy, social care, or a youth advisory centre—would create a one-stop access point and reduce fragmented care.
- Improve transport and parking, with incentives for rural postings. Addressing parking deficits and unreliable transport, plus offering incentives for clinicians to work in rural or town fringe areas, would help. Clear information about bus routes or subsidised travel could make it easier for more people to attend appointments when needed.
- Invest in Premises and digital access. Some clinics operate out of outdated or cramped premises, which limits how many patients can be seen daily. Modernised, flexible spaces and well-publicised online booking and triage systems would help manage demand more effectively.

Increasing capacity and smarter scheduling
- Expand slots with staffing and smarter scheduling. Lengthening clinic hours, adding weekend sessions, and increasing routine appointment slots would immediately drop wait times. This needs hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, plus flexible rosters so staff aren’t stretched across multiple sites.
- Use triage and stepped-care approaches. A robust telephone or online triage process can direct patients to the right level of care (self-management resources, short-term therapy, or an urgent face-to-face slot) and help free up clinicians to see those who need a physical assessment. For mental health, more brief, evidence-based interventions and group sessions could relieve pressure on individual therapists while still delivering timely support.
- Prioritise efficient practice workflows and digital integration. Integrated care records, shared calendars, and a uniform approach to referrals would reduce duplication and shorten waits. A few pilot sites could test scheduling optimisations—e.g., reserve a portion of slots for same-day or next-day requests—then roll out what works area-wide with proper monitoring.

A phased approach with clear accountability
In the first year, I’d want to see: (1) a targeted program to boost training and return-to-practice numbers; (2) several mobile clinics and telehealth hubs launched in key rural pockets; (3) a proof-of-concept for extended hours and triage-based scheduling in several practices, with measurable indicators for wait times and patient satisfaction.
Over 2–3 years, extend successful pilots, expand workforce capacity, and stabilise premises and transport arrangements. By 3–5 years, the aim should be a consistently shorter wait for GP and mental health slots across the area, better patient experience, and a clear pipeline linking education, recruitment and retention with service delivery.

In short, timely access will come from growing the workforce in a sustainable way and giving people practical, local routes to care—whether that’s a mobile clinic visiting their village, a telehealth hub nearby, or more appointments and better scheduling at their local practice. It will require investment and cross-sector cooperation, but the potential benefits for health outcomes and people’s day-to-day lives are substantial.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. We support a package of changes that would make GP, community health and mental health services more timely and easier to access, especially for people living in rural or mobility‑limited situations, busy workers, and those who would otherwise face barriers related to transport or premises.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are a real barrier to timely care. To address this, we advocate a multi‑faceted approach:
- Mobile clinics and outreach: Deploy GP and nurse‑led mobile clinics to rural villages and hard‑to‑reach housing areas on a regular, predictable rota, visiting each community weekly or fortnightly. These clinics should be co‑ordinated with district nursing and pharmacy teams and staffed to offer quick routine checks, chronic disease reviews, and minor urgent care. Premises challenges in small communities can be mitigated by using suitably equipped community venues (village halls, community centres, or school hubs) with accessible entrances and reserved parking bays for health vehicles. We have seen in practice how a mobile clinic in a nearby village reduced travel time by up to 40 minutes for residents and cut missed appointments when parking and access were easier.
- Outreach and telehealth hubs: Combine outreach work with telehealth hubs in libraries, community centres and town halls. These hubs would provide private spaces, Wi‑Fi and trained staff to support video consultations with GPs, nurses, or mental health professionals. Patients could choose to attend a hub for a video or telephone appointment, or to obtain devices to use at home. This would be especially valuable for older people, carers, or those with transport limitations who still need timely access to clinical advice.
- Incentives to improve rural and mobility‑limited access: Offer capital and revenue incentives to GP practices and community partners to run extended services, including evening and weekend clinics, and to participate in mobile/outreach models. We would support funding for dedicated transport solutions (e.g., patient shuttles) and subsidised parking or drop‑off zones outside clinics to reduce access friction. Acknowledging the workload pressures on staff, incentives should also cover staffing costs for extended hours, clinical supervision, and back‑office co‑ordination so that these services are sustainable.

Evening and weekend access, and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, are essential for working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs:
- Extended hours: Establish predictable, regular evening and weekend clinics in each locality—targeting at least two weekday evenings and one Saturday morning per GP cluster. These sessions should be staffed by GPs, nurses, and allied health professionals and designed to handle routine issues, chronic disease management, mental health triage, and urgent non‑emergency issues. This approach would reduce the need for taking time off work or waiting in busy daytime clinics.
- Same‑day urgent slots: Guarantee same‑day urgent appointments (including mental health triage) through a structured telephone/online triage system that flags urgent cases and directs patients to the most appropriate clinician within the same day. This would prevent escalation of problems and lower avertable emergency attendances. In practice, a robust triage pathway can identify mental health concerns early and connect people with rapid in‑hours or out‑of‑hours support when needed.

Co‑located community hubs integrating primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners will deliver the seamless, person‑centred care that people expect:
- One‑stop hubs: Develop local hubs where primary care, district nursing, physiotherapy, mental health teams, social workers, and VCSE partners (charities, carers groups, housing and employment services) operate from a single site or shared building. A co‑located hub should use a unified care plan and common referral pathways to reduce duplication and confusion for patients.
- Local care coordination: Create multi‑disciplinary “care teams” anchored by a navigator or link worker who can help people move between services, access housing or welfare support, and connect to community services. This would be particularly impactful for older adults, people with multiple long‑term conditions, carers and those with mental health needs who often navigate several organisations.
- Local anchors and transformation: Start with pilots in 3–5 sites to test governance, data sharing, privacy, and performance metrics. Clear information governance and consent processes must underpin any data sharing across primary care, community health teams, social care and VCSE partners.

What success looks like in practical terms:
- Waiting times reduced and patients reporting easier access to care, with fewer journeys to multiple locations.
- Higher vaccination and preventive care uptake due to easier access and more flexible appointment times.
- Better mental health engagement with quicker triage and rapid access to talking therapies or crisis support where needed.
- Stronger local relationships between GP practices, schools, pharmacies, voluntary groups and local authorities, delivering more proactive, holistic care.

Implementation would require careful planning, clear governance, and robust monitoring. We would welcome an evaluation framework that tracks access indicators such as average time to appointment, number of same‑day urgent slots used, transport times saved, and patient satisfaction across services. Overall, we believe these changes would deliver timelier, more integrated care and reduce the strain on A&E by meeting people closer to home, in the ways they prefer to access care.

Thank you for considering these proposals. We stand ready to participate in pilots, provide local insight, and work with commissioners, GP practices and VCSE partners to make timely access a reality across our area.

From my perspective living in Scotland and drawing on what I’ve seen in my own community, the biggest quick wins to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services are twofold: targeted resources to close gaps for those most at risk, and a robust, sustainable plan to grow the workforce with proper training and support, backed up by sensible use of digital tools alongside non-digital options.

First, targeting resources and culturally competent outreach. It’s clear that deprived areas, ethnic minority and migrant communities, and marginalised groups often miss out on timely care because of language barriers, distrust of services, or simply lack of information about what help is available. I’ve personally seen how interpreters and culturally trained staff make a real difference. In our area, a local outreach day run with a charity and volunteers at a church hall and community centre brought in interpreters for Urdu, Polish and Romanian speakers, and staff who understood different cultural approaches to health. Attendance at diabetes and blood pressure checks rose, and people who hadn’t engaged with services for years felt more able to seek help. I’d like to see ongoing funding for these outreach workers, translated materials, and clear routes into services through trusted community partners—grocery stores, churches, mosques, and social clubs—so people know where to turn and trust the system.

Second, expanding training places and workforce support for the longer term. Our GP practices and community teams are stretched. Increasing training places for GPs, nurses, and mental health professionals, along with return-to-practice support and apprenticeships, would help build a resilient workforce that can respond quickly when someone phones or walks in seeking help. I’ve heard colleagues talk about how a few extra trainees or a returned nurse can reduce waiting times considerably, and I believe Scotland would benefit from a sustained programme of CPD and mentoring to keep staff up to date and motivated. It’s not just about numbers; it’s about creating supportive career paths so people stay in the system, which is especially important for rural or coastal communities where staff turnover can be high.

Third, harnessing digital tools without leaving anyone behind. Expanding online booking and e-consults can reduce unnecessary delays, especially for routine follow-ups or triage for mental health concerns. In my experience, online options work well for many, and they can free up phone lines for those who need them most. But we must maintain non-digital routes: reliable telephone triage, walk-in slots, and face-to-face appointments for those who find digital systems confusing or expensive to access. For elderly people, carers, or those with limited internet, community hubs equipped with simple-assist devices and trained staff could offer a digital-friendly, human-supported pathway to care. In practice, this means same-day telephone access, clear information on how to request urgent help, and in-person clinics in local hubs alongside online services.

Finally, integrated care and timely access must be visible in communities. Mental health support needs to be embedded in primary care with rapid access pathways, crisis lines, and proactive outreach to schools and workplaces where early signs often appear. I’m encouraged by stories of improved relationships between GPs and mental health teams when funded staff can share information, coordinate packages of care, and follow up quickly with patients in distress.

In short, I’d like to see a balanced mix of targeted, culturally competent outreach; a scalable workforce plan with training and return-to-practice options; and a thoughtful blend of digital and non-digital access routes. If these elements are funded and monitored for impact, timely access to GP, community health, and mental health services can improve for everyone, including Scotland’s older residents who may rely more on traditional access routes.

I disagree that only shorter-term fixes will help. Real, sustainable improvement in NI requires workforce growth: more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health staff, alongside flexible hours—otherwise access won't be reliable long term.

In my area in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters, but I find the question leads me to tangents. For example, last month I tried to book a GP appointment for a persistent skin issue; the earliest slot was two weeks away, and I ended up at a nurse-led walk-in clinic after work. A friend waiting for CBT for anxiety faced a months-long wait. The digital booking app sometimes crashes; phone lines are busy after 5pm. What would help me day-to-day feels broader than just more appointments: better weekend and evening slots, clearer triage so people aren’t bounced between services, and more community hubs so people don’t have to travel far. I also think staff wellbeing matters; if clinicians are overstretched, access won’t improve no matter how many slots are opened. So while I’d welcome practical tweaks like weekend slots and stronger mental health triage, any policy needs to address funding and staffing to be truly reliable.

I don't believe these proposed changes alone will reliably improve timely access in our area. Co-located community hubs, while well-intentioned, risk creating a two-tier system of 'hubs' and 'everyday GP access.' In practice, the current town centre hub is poorly located for families without cars, with limited parking and inconsistent bus links; more of these hubs could leave rural or peri-urban residents with even longer journeys. And without guaranteed long-term funding and governance, hubs could drift apart from existing GP practices, fragmenting care. 

Expanding multidisciplinary teams can help with routine cases, but it could erode GP continuity and increase confusion for patients who don't know who is in charge of their care. If pharmacists and physiotherapists handle triage without robust supervision, important red flags may be missed, and the costs of training and oversight may simply shift rather than reduce demand on doctors. 

NHS111 and care navigation improvements could streamline urgent routes, but they often fail in practice: call-centre capacity is variable, digital tools exclude those with limited tech access or literacy, and triage errors can delay critical care. 

Better solutions would be to fund flexible, locally driven appointment systems, extend GP hours or urgent care slots, and ensure clear, patient-centred triage within primary care, with strict evaluation at scale.

Timely access to GP, community and mental health services would improve most if we prioritise growing the workforce and making local services genuinely integrated. Increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is essential for a sustainable, long‑term uplift. In my area, staffing gaps often mean multi‑week waits; when a clinician returns or a trainee joins, the queues shrink and patients get seen sooner.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners under one roof would cut unnecessary travel and speed up care. Shared digital records and same‑day triage in these hubs would help people access the right service quickly without repeating their story.

Finally, expanding community mental health teams, enhancing early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies would reduce waits and improve parity with physical health. With stable funding and clear workforce planning, these changes could deliver timely, local care for families in our area and ease pressure on A&E and hospitals.

Timely access in our area is hampered by transport gaps, limited parking at busy GP sites, and cramped premises. My own schedule makess after-hours availability essential, and too often I end up waiting days for a routine appointment or squeezing telehealth into a poor signal. I would support a mixed package of changes. - Mobile clinics visiting residential estatrs and rural village halls on a rotating timetable; they could handle routine checks, vaccination, and triage to primary care. - Outreach teams to workplaces, schools and community centres to offer quick checks and signpost to GP or mental health services; reduces travel. - Telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres with staff on site to assist or connect to GP care, plus digita appointment booking. - Incentives for practices to extend hours or run weekend clinics, and subsidised transport or parking improvements near clinics in busy towns. From a working-person perspective,, evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would be transformative for urgent non-emergency needs. In a recent case, a friend waited a week for a GP appointment; a same-day triage line with an urgen slot would have prevented that delay. Mental health access would similarly benefit from a fast-track urgrnt slot with integrated same-day support, reducing crisis risk. In short, a pragmatic mix of mobile/outreach, telehealth hubs, and flexible hours appears to offer timely access without overwhelming existing premises.

Access to timely GP, nurse and mental health care in our area remains inconsistent. I’m often forced to wait too long for a GP appointment for a routine issue, and after-hours or urgent symptoms can leave me juggling urgent care options. Access to talking therapies is even tighter; a recent referral moved me to a queue of several weeks. For working parents like me, evenings and weekend slots would make a real difference.

I would support changes that increase appointment slots and session capacity through three levers: hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists; expanding session formats (more shorter appointments and group/community sessions where appropriate); and smarter scheduling to reduce gaps (same-day triage, reserved urgent blocks, and extended hours). Digitally, a robust online booking system with clear wait-time estimates and reliable reminders would help families plan around work and childcare.

However, any expansion must be sustainable: we need sufficient staffing with steady funding, strong supervision for new clinicians, and careful coordination to maintain continuity of care. It’s essential we avoid overloading staff or fragmenting care as capacity grows.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area is inconsistent. Some weeks you can get a same- or next-day appointment; other times you’re left on hold for ages or told to try again later. I think the most effective changes would combine targeted resource allocation with practical access points that recognise language barriers, cultural differences and the realities of work and family commitments.

First, I would like to see more language support and culturally competent staff across primary care and mental health services. In my experience, language barriers rarely cause a single, simple problem; they cascade into longer talks, miscommunications about symptoms and treatment plans, and more follow‑ups. A partner who speaks limited English has repeatedly struggled to book an appointment online because the portal isn’t always available in their language and the phone line is hard to navigate after work. Interpreters are sometimes offered, but not reliably, and that inconsistency can lead to rushed consultations and mistakes. I’d rather see guaranteed interpreter booking capacity, plus ongoing training for reception and clinical staff on cultural humility, mental health stigma, and how to ask about sensitive topics without making patients feel judged. It would also help to have multilingual information about symptom checkers, urgent care pathways and how to access crisis support.

Second, proactive outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups is essential. I’ve seen community-driven models work well, like pop‑up clinics in local community centres or faith venues that offer basic health checks, blood pressure, vaccine status and signposting to mental health work. These sessions not only meet people where they are but build trust, which is often the barrier to accessing care. Hiring and training bilingual community health workers as navigators who can accompany people through the appointment process, explain what to expect from a GP visit or a mental health intake, and help with transport or carer support would reduce avoidable delays and improve adherence to treatment plans.

Third, extended and flexible access, including evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would make a real difference for working people and those with urgent, non‑emergency needs. In my borough there are a few Saturday slots, but they fill up quickly, and if you work full time, you often can’t attend. I’d like to see a model where every practice holds a guaranteed same‑day urgent appointment window and offers a selection of after‑hours slots, with a simple, transparent triage route for mental health concerns so people aren’t waiting weeks for help. Digital booking should be supplemented with phone triage and in‑person options for those without reliable internet access, so no one is excluded.

Fourth, better integration at local level would help. A single, mapped hub where GP, community health, mental health teams, pharmacy and social care coordinate around a patient’s needs would reduce duplicate trips and confusion, especially for families managing chronic conditions or caring responsibilities. Data sharing and privacy safeguards would need to be strong, with patient consent front and centre.

I recognise these changes require upfront investment and careful workforce planning. The risk is over-optimistic targets without sustainable staffing or the means to support interpreters and outreach workers. It is therefore vital that any expansion is co‑designed with communities and includes concrete milestones, independent evaluation and flexibility to adapt if targets aren’t being met. Overall I’d support a measured programme of targeted resources, language access, outreach, and extended access hours, provided there is clear accountability, rigorous monitoring and a plan to protect staff welfare and service quality alongside demand.

As a local organisation representing residents across rural England, we believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains hampered by transport gaps, scarce parking and fragile premises. Even where appointments exist, getting there by bus or car is often not practical, and clinics sit on cramped sites with limited spaces. In my area, elderly neighbours delay seeking help because a quick visit isn’t feasible and online systems fail where mobile reception is patchy. 

What would really improve access is a package of changes that goes beyond digital expansion alone. First, deploy mobile clinics and targeted outreach teams that visit villages on predictable timetables, sharing space with village halls or libraries and coordinating with district nurses. Second, establish telehealth hubs in community venues with private rooms and reliable broadband, staffed to assist users. Third, provide incentives for GP and mental health services to extend hours, include weekend slots and actively recruit in rural areas. Fourth, broaden digital access while preserving non-digital routes: robust telephone triage, in-person clinics, drop-in slots, and substantial support for those who are digitally excluded including devices and training. Fifth, invest in premises and parking near clinics or co-locate services to reduce travel for patients. Finally, collect outcome data to prove these approaches reduce delays. This balanced mix would improve access without leaving vulnerable groups behind.

I read the consultation with interest. Living in England and in my late fifties, I’ve seen how even a small shortage of appointment slots can quickly lead to stress and delays for families. I strongly support steps to improve timely access by increasing capacity across GP services, community health and mental health services. The goal should be to have more predictable, easier-to-book slots so people get help when they need it, not weeks later.

First, expanding GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots is essential. This means recruiting more GPs and expanding the roles of practice nurses and other trained clinicians so that routine and medium‑complex conditions don’t clog up doctor time. Longer, more flexible opening hours—early mornings, evenings and some weekend slots—would help people who work or have care commitments. It would also be sensible to use trained nurse practitioners and physiotherapists to run routine check-ups and follow-ups for chronic conditions, with GPs focusing on more complex cases. A robust, transparent booking system is critical: online triage that immediately flags urgent cases, same‑day urgent appointments, and protected slots for vulnerable patients (older adults, those with multiple conditions) would all reduce avoidable waits.

Alongside more slots, better scheduling and care coordination can make a real difference. For example, a modern, user‑friendly booking platform that confirms appointments promptly, sends reminders, and offers short follow‑ups if symptoms persist would stop people from slipping through the cracks. Group clinics for chronic disease management or prevention checkups could free up GP time for those who need more intensive care. And a dedicated care coordinator or patient navigator in each practice could help patients move smoothly between services, ensuring that when mental health support is needed, people aren’t left waiting while other issues are addressed first.

On the community health and mental health front, expanding community mental health teams is crucial. More therapists, psychologists, social workers and link staff in every locality would enable earlier intervention and more proactive care for people at risk of deterioration. It’s particularly important to extend crisis response capabilities so people experiencing mental health crises can access timely help without resorting to emergency departments. The ambition should be to offer robust talking therapies, including cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness and other evidence‑based approaches, with options for individual and group formats. A stepped‑care model that quickly guides people to the right level of support—whether short‑term counselling, early intervention teams or more intensive community support—would promote quicker relief and better long‑term outcomes.

Parity with physical health must underpin all of this. Mental health services deserve the same level of funding, staffing and planning as physical health. Stable, predictable funding for recruitment, training and retention will help the workforce grow and stay. I would also welcome better data sharing across NHS services so capacity can be planned to meet real demand, including predictable surge responses during winter or flu seasons when pressures rise.

From personal experience, when there is a stretch of days with accessible GP slots and a clear pathway to mental health support, the impact is immediate: shorter anxiety, less time off work, and fewer crises that escalate to urgent care. When wait times stretch, even minor concerns become stressful, and people delay seeking help, which can worsen outcomes. If these proposed changes are rolled out consistently—more slots, smarter booking, stronger community teams, and timely talking therapies—the overall experience of care will improve and the system will feel more reassuring and fair for everyone.

In short, I back expanding appointment capacity and smarter scheduling in primary care, and I back expanding community mental health teams and early intervention. The combined effect will be shorter waits, better health outcomes and a fairer balance between mental and physical health services. Implemented with clear funding, workforce planning and robust IT support, this would make a real difference to families in our communities.

it's outrageous that i fully support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. For patients with complex, chronic needs, continuity of care matters most. Longer appointment times would let clinicians review multiple conditions in one visit, coordinate meds, and build a plan that actually sticks, reducing needless follow-ups. In my own family, a single longer appointment with the same clinician would have avoided several unnecessary trips and conflicting advice.

Transport and access are real obstacles. In rural pockets near my town, parking is a nightmare and bus links are unreliable. Mobile clinics, outreach teams, and telehealth hubs could bring care nearer to people, while flexible incentives encourage practices to run satellite clinics and longer evening slots. Parking vouchers and safe drop-off points would also help.

Sustainability depends on growing the workforce. Increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD would build a steady stream of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Local mentorship, funded placements for medical students in primary care, and paid CPD time would keep staff motivated and here for the long term.

If these changes were supported together—with patient‑centred appointment lengths, smarter access points, and a stronger workforce—we’d see better outcomes and fewer avoidable crises!

I live in Wales and want to see real, practical changes that make accessing GP, community health and mental health services faster and simpler, especially when the situation feels urgent. I’m supportive of improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation that prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and smooth patient flow. In my experience, the journey from a first concern to a face-to-face appointment is too often frustrating and repetitive, with multiple steps and little clarity about where to go next.

First, strengthen NHS111 with genuine clinical triage. I’m not against automation, but a triage process driven by qualified clinicians—nurses or GPs who can assess risk and severity—can save time and prevent escalation of problems. When I’ve had a potential urgent issue, a clinician-led triage that could book an immediate same-day slot or direct me to the most appropriate service would have made a huge difference. For example, a recent family health concern could have been handled quickly if the triage could arrange a same-day GP or urgent care slot instead of sending me through a cycle of phone calls and redirection. A robust clinical triage would also ensure mental health concerns are treated with appropriate urgency, rather than waiting for a longer non-urgent pathway.

Second, overhaul booking systems so there’s one real-time, patient-friendly platform across GP practices, community services and mental health. At the moment, it often feels like you’re parrying different systems: you call GP reception, you’re told there are no slots, you try NHS111, you get sent elsewhere, and you end up duplicating the same information to multiple teams. A single, integrated booking portal that shows real-time availability, including same-day urgent appointments, would cut down on phone queues and wasted trips. Extending online booking to urgent care, community nurse clinics, and mental health crisis teams would help people access the right service promptly. Even better would be a feature that allows a care navigator to reserve a slot across services when the triage flags urgent need, so the patient is not bounced from pillar to post.

Third, deploy dedicated care navigators who help guide people through the system. Navigators could be located in GP practices, within NHS111, and in community hubs. Their job would be to assess the patient’s needs, select the most appropriate service on the day, and coordinate care to avoid duplication. For instance, after calling 111, a navigator could arrange a same-day appointment with a GP if necessary, or direct someone with a simple infection to a pharmacist-led minor ailments clinic for antibiotics where appropriate. For mental health, navigators could fast-track individuals to urgent community mental health teams or crisis lines, ensuring quicker access to talking therapies or psychiatric input when needed. This would also reduce the burden of repeating stories during different appointments.

Fourth, prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication by improving data sharing and appointment etiquette. Shared, consenting access to essential health records between GP practices, community services, and mental health teams would prevent patients from recounting symptoms or medical histories multiple times. A clear escalation framework and defined maximum wait times for urgent referrals would help families feel they are not left waiting in limbo. During peak periods, such as winter, it becomes even more important to flag urgent cases early and route them into the right service immediately, rather than layering delays on top of delays.

Fifth, simplify patient flow with more integrated, flexible care pathways. This could include same-day “one-stop” urgent care hubs where appropriate, and the option of video or phone consultations when physical attendance isn’t essential. A smoother flow—from NHS111 triage to booking, to the right clinician (GP, nurse, physiotherapist, or mental health professional)—would cut out unnecessary steps and reduce the sense that people must continually chase an appointment.

Lastly, invest in training and oversight so these changes are consistently delivered. Staff should be confident in the new booking and triage processes, and there should be routine patient feedback loops to monitor how well the changes are working in practice. Local pilots with transparent evaluation, involving patients and carers, could help refine the system before wider rollout.

In summary, I support a reset of NHS111, clinical triage, and booking systems to prioritise urgent needs, coupled with dedicated care navigators and better data sharing. If implemented thoughtfully, these changes would make access to GP, community health and mental health services in Wales faster, less duplicative and easier to navigate for families like mine. This would reduce stress, prevent avoidable complications, and help people get the right care when they need it most.

Agree. To improve timely access, the most effective changes would be to expand training places for GPs, nurses and mental health workers; strengthen return-to-practice support; expand apprenticeships and CPD to grow the workforce sustainably. Increased training slots mean we won’t face years of shortages; a robust return-to-practice fund with mentoring would quickly restore capacity as people move back from career breaks. Apprenticeships create local career paths, attracting people to serve in our communities; CPD funded across the board keeps staff confident with new treatments and digital tools, reducing wait times for referrals and follow-ups.

In my area, GP appointment slots and community nurse cover have become stretched; local mental health teams have long waits. If more staff are available through these routes, patients would access care sooner, fewer unnecessary referrals, and better continuity of care. I would welcome a national framework to align these routes with local services and ensure training and re-entry support are consistently funded.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area would be greatly improved by practical changes that address transport, parking and premises deficits, plus flexible options for busy and mobility-limited people. I would support mobile clinics that visit village halls and rural clusters on a rotating timetable, with outreach teams to identify those who struggle to reach town centres. Mobile units could offer blood pressure checks, mental-health triage, and prescription reviews, reducing travel time for many.

Telehealth hubs in community venues, with trained staff to help those who are not comfortable with tech, would speed up triage and enable remote monitoring. Incentives for GP practices to extend hours or deliver weekend clinics in rural hubs, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would help those in work or with urgent non-emergency needs.

Expanding online booking and e-consults should go hand in hand with non-digital routes: a dedicated phone line, in-person walk-in slots, and support from volunteers or carers to assist with bookings. In my experience, a mix of online and face-to-face appointments has worked: telehealth for quick checks, followed by timely in-person follow-ups when needed. This balanced approach would make a real difference.

i really think timely access in our area is hampered by a mix of aging premises, limited parking, and buses that run only sporadically. For older residents and those with mobility problems, the journey to an appointment can take several hours. I would welcome mobile clinics visiting village halls and care homes on fixed days, plus outreach nursing and mental-health link workers in community settings. Telehealth hubs in local community centres or libraries could cut unnecessary trips, provided there is support for digital literacy and affordable data.

Critically, I think expanding multidisciplinary teams could free GPs to focus on complex cases. Allowing trained pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine ailments would speed access and improve continuity, but it must come with clear scopes of practice, supervision and safe prescribing.

Investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care with mental health, social care and VCSE partners could streamline referrals and follow-up. In my experience, where local services sit under one roof with good IT links, patients report better navigation and quicker support. Any rollout should be piloted, evaluated and funded with patient involvement to avoid widening inequalities!

I support funding co-located community hubs that integrate GP, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners; plus more training, return-to-practice support and interpreters to reach deprived and minority communities.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area is too often limited by staffing gaps. As someone in my early 20s, I’ve felt the waiting times for GP appointments and the struggle to get timely mental health support. To fix this, I think the most effective changes are: expanding training places, strengthening return-to-practice support, widening apprenticeships and boosting CPD for all frontline staff. If funded properly, more GP training posts within primary care networks, nurse and mental health professional trainee slots and incentives for rural clinics would gradually grow the workforce we rely on, reducing delays.

But it has to be done carefully: training must not create longer wait times for patients while people are learning. Implement robust supervision, realistic timelines and protected patient load for trainees. Apprenticeships could create clearer routes for care assistants to become nurses or therapists, helping local recruitment pipelines. Return-to-practice schemes should be accessible, affordable and tailored to those who paused due to family or burnout, with mentoring and reduced revalidation barriers.

In addition, CPD should be accessible online and in-work, with practical rotations that reflect community needs. A regional plan with committed funding, better retention incentives, and transparent governance will prevent gaps when reforms end. Local pilots could test which models deliver faster access without compromising safety.
I disagree that piecemeal fixes help; invest in co-located hubs uniting GP, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners for quicker local access.

As an organisation representing residents across our town in England, we find that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is shaped by factors beyond the clinic doors. For many older residents, getting a same-week GP slot is inconsistent; delays ripple into nursing visits and home-care support. Mental health services often feel distant, with long waits for talking therapies and limited out-of-hours cover leaving people anxious in crises. Our volunteers repeatedly see transport and digital barriers creating extra hurdles: someone may miss a GP appointment because the only feasible route requires two buses late in the day; others cannot book online because they lack a smartphone or reliable broadband. We also hear that navigation between GP, hospital, community teams and social care isn’t as seamless as it could be, which makes access feel slow even when capacity exists. What would help, in our view, is easier cross-service co-ordination, with clearer information about pathways and more locally accessible points in community hubs. While funding and staffing pressures are part of the problem, addressing transport and digital exclusion would make a practical difference for people in our area.

absolutely i’m a pensioner living in England and I’m responding as an individual. I do not think the changes proposed would do enough, quickly enough, to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area. In my view, the priority should be to recruit and retain more GPs and practical staff, not to assume that shuffling resources into interpreters or rolling out broader multidisciplinary teams will automatically speed things up.

First, addressing access gaps through outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups is a worthy aim in principle. But I’ve seen how it plays out in real life: even when interpreters are available, appointments are scarce and often take a long time to secure. In our local practice, the day we finally managed to arrange a same-day appointment after hours of phone calls, it turned out the interpreter would only be free a couple of days later. Interpreters are essential, yet if the underlying problem is shortage of clinicians and tight appointment books, interpreters alone won’t fix timely access. More predictable GP availability must come first, with resources directed at recruiting, training and retaining GPs, plus reliable locums to cover gaps without leaving patients waiting weeks for a slot.

Second, while culturally competent staff and targeted outreach can improve patient experience, they do not automatically shorten waiting times. In fact, if clinics over-emphasise outreach while not expanding the core GP base, the net effect can be longer queues for everyone. My neighbours and I would welcome language support and culturally aware care, but we cannot wait weeks for an appointment while those services are being built around the edges. The focus should be on practical access: same-day or next-day appointments, better telephone triage that doesn’t squander hours, and extended hours that fit older people’s routines and mobility limits.

Third, expanding multidisciplinary teams including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates could help in some cases, but I’m wary of how this affects continuity of care for complex, long-standing problems. For many of us with chronic conditions, seeing the same GP who understands our history is important. In my experience, when a routine case is handed off to a different professional, it creates duplicated tests, repeating questions, and delays in decisions about medications or referrals. If MDTs are to be part of the solution, there must be strong coordination, clear roles, and an easy way to revert to/consult the GP when the case is not straightforward. We need a system that preserves continuity for the patient while still relieving pressure on doctors with manageable handoffs and robust record-sharing.

Fourth, many older residents struggle with digital-first approaches. I worry that relying heavily on online triage or video consultations will worsen inequalities for those who aren’t comfortable with technology, or who have unreliable internet access or hearing difficulties. Any plan to widen MDTs should include non-digital pathways, with the option of a real-life appointment the same day, and home visits where appropriate. We should also think about practical support to get people to appointments, such as transport assistance or community outreach teams that can check on people who miss appointments rather than just emailing reminders.

What would actually improve timely access in a tangible way? Several concrete steps come to mind:
- Recruits and retention of GPs, supported by fair pay and manageable workloads, plus reliable locums to cover sudden gaps so patients aren’t bounced from pillar to pillar or left waiting.
- More same-day slots, easier telephone access, and predictable out-of-hours care so urgent needs are addressed promptly.
- Practical transport and home-visit options for housebound or mobility-impaired patients.
- Thoughtful integration of MDTs with the GP role, ensuring patients retain continuity with a primary clinician who coordinates the team, rather than layering new providers without clear accountability.
- Language and cultural support that is timely and well-funded but is implemented in a way that actually speeds up access rather than becoming a bottleneck in itself.

I want to see a system that is person-centred, with real capacity to see patients quickly when needed, and with care that remains coherent and continuous for those with complex health histories. Interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential, but they must work alongside a stronger GP workforce and robust, well-coordinated teams if timely access is ever going to improve in practice.

If the government wants to improve access now, the emphasis should be on funding and staffing, not solely on reorganising teams or broadening outreach. Timely care depends on enough doctors and practical mechanisms to book and deliver appointments, with flexible, accessible options for older people and those with limited digital literacy. Deputy funding and targeted schemes that deliver real GP capacity, fast triage, and dependable transport and home-visit options would be my priority.

I think the biggest win for timely access would be practical, on-the-ground changes that fit the realities of daily life, not just tinkering with online systems. In my area in England, working people and parents often have to juggle work, school runs, and appointments, so evening and weekend clinics should be standard rather than rare exceptions. If a GP practice is only open 9-to-5, someone on a 9-to-5 job can’t realistically step out for a 20-minute consultation without taking unpaid time off. I’ve seen neighbours switch their working patterns around to catch a morning slot, and still end up waiting two weeks. It would be far more useful to have extended hours a few evenings per week and a weekend clinic that rotates between practices, so people aren’t stuck with the choice between work and care. A guaranteed same-day urgent slot policy for non-emergency but urgent problems would also make a tangible difference. If I wake up with a sudden twinge that could be treated or a sudden mental health concern, I don’t want to be told to wait two weeks while the clock ticks on worsening symptoms.

I’m also wary of moves to push everything online. Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care has clear benefits for those with reliable internet, flexible jobs, and the confidence to use digital tools. But it also risks excluding the most vulnerable: older people, those with limited data capacity, and households without a private device or stable broadband. In my community, a decent proportion of pensioners rely on family or public libraries for access, and some simply prefer a face-to-face chat. There have been times when I tried to book for a parent online; the system timed out, or the page wouldn’t load properly on their tablet. Other friends report that while online booking is promoted, there’s little real-time support if something goes wrong, and phone lines are often busy with automated menus that repeat you back to the start. A non-digital pathway must stay robust and well-funded.

Practically, that means you keep a staffed phone line with sensible peak-time capacity, and don’t fold it into an outdated, merely toll-free option. It means practices must invest in a hybrid model: online booking and electronic triage where it genuinely speeds things up, plus walk-in slots or same-day triage at local hubs for those who can’t or won’t use digital tools. In my town, a developing model involving an extended-hours “health hub” that aggregates GP, nurse, and mental health staff under one roof would cut down multiple visits and reduce delays. People could be directed to the most appropriate professional quickly, rather than being bounced between departments or forced to wait for a specialist appointment months away.

On mental health specifically, timely access is critical but often neglected. If urgent slots are guaranteed for primary care, there should also be a clear, rapid triage pathway to community mental health teams, with same-day or next-day access where issues arise—especially for crises and for those transitioning from crisis care back into routine support. The current patchwork means people sometimes deteriorate while waiting for a service to open a slot. The policy should fund real-time triage via a dedicated mental health rapid access line or appointment window that feeds directly into local community teams, with a clear handover to ongoing care when needed.

All of this needs proper staffing and funding. Evening and weekend clinics can only work if there are enough GPs, nurses, and support staff to cover them without burning people out. Likewise, digital tools should be designed with input from older patients and low-income households to ensure they’re usable and not an extra barrier. I’d like to see flexible funding models that reward practices for delivering accessible, same-day urgent care and for maintaining inclusive service options—rather than rewarding only the fastest digital ticketing systems.

In short, timely access will improve if we combine: extended hours with guaranteed same-day urgent slots; a true hybrid service that blends online convenience with reliable non-digital access; and robust mental health pathways that ensure urgent support is available quickly and smoothly. If we push digital-first care without addressing the digital divide, we’ll simply move the barrier from the reception desk to the screen.
