I’m in favour of smarter, more flexible access, but only if every patient has a real and easy choice about how they receive help.

In my area in England, the most impactful changes to improve timely access would be to boost GP access and crisis response first, rather than relying mainly on expanding community mental health teams. While I understand the aim of better parity with physical health, recruitment for new teams will take time and won't cut waits in the near term. Practically, that means: more same-day and after-hours GP appointments through longer hours, additional staff, and improved triage to direct urgent cases quickly; rapid access to talking therapies through direct, fast-track referral and clearer pathways—my local wait for CBT was around 6-8 weeks, and referrals often got stuck in the system; a standard within 4 weeks would be a real improvement. A 24/7 crisis line and a mobile crisis team that can attend if needed would prevent unnecessary A&E visits; digital triage with guaranteed response within 24 hours; better sharing of records between GPs and mental health services so no repeating forms. In short, faster GP access, reliable crisis support, and streamlined therapy referrals would have the quickest, most tangible effect on waits now, with community mental health expansion targeted to areas with the worst need in the medium term.

I’m 22 and live in England. To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I’d push for a mix of long‑term workforce growth and smarter access channels. First, increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus robust return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD. In my area, waiting times and staff shortages feel real, and more trainee posts would help create a stable workforce for the coming years. Second, targeted recruitment and international hiring, with incentives, pay progression and flexible working, would help attract and retain frontline staff. I’ve seen peers struggle to get timely appointments; flexible hours and wellbeing support would make roles more sustainable. Third, expand online booking and e‑consultations, but keep non‑digital options such as phone triage and home visits to avoid leaving older or disadvantaged people behind. Finally, invest in integrated urgent‑care hubs and multi‑disciplinary teams so care is quicker and more coordinated, including pharmacist and mental health support in communities. This combination would meaningfully shorten wait times and improve continuity of care.

In my area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services can feel a bit like a lottery. I strongly support expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, but it must be possible to use non‑digital routes as well so no one is left behind—especially the older or digitally-excluded. For example, my elderly neighbour relies on a straightforward phone line and in‑person triage when urgent advice is needed; a digital‑only system would leave her stuck and waiting longer.

Equally important is continuity of care and longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Keeping a named GP and offering longer, coordinated multi‑disciplinary slots would reduce repeat visits, improve medicines management and outcomes, and ease the burden on carers who juggle work and family commitments.

Thirdly, expanding community mental health teams with robust early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies would shorten waits and bring mental health care closer to parity with physical health. In practice, earlier access for people with anxiety or depression would prevent crises and reduce hospital admissions.

Taken together, these changes would make services more timely, more equitable and easier to navigate for families like mine.

From my perspective as a student in England, the changes that would most improve timely access aren’t just about “more appointments” but about smarter systems and better staffing. NHS111 and the current booking process often slow things down: NHS111 triage can push mental health issues down the list when urgent support is actually needed, and online booking can repeat questions or lose slots mid-session. A friend with a viral illness waited two weeks for a GP appointment, and someone else struggled to get timely mental health support. We need a single, patient-centred care navigation that quickly directs urgent cases to urgent care, while non-urgent problems stay with a familiar GP or small team to build continuity.

Recruitment is essential: targeted recruitment, flexible hours, and wellbeing support to attract and retain primary care staff, plus international recruitment where appropriate with proper induction. Longer appointments for complex or chronic needs would improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits, freeing up urgent slots overall. In short: fix triage, streamline care navigation, invest in staffing and continuity, and ensure mental health and community services can act promptly when people reach out.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if resources were targeted to the groups who face the greatest barriers: additional interpreters, cultural competence training for front-line staff, and outreach in deprived neighbourhoods. In my area, languages like Bengali and Polish are common among patients who miss appointments because interpreters aren’t available in urgent slots, and information in plain English is not always accessible. A local scheme employing bilingual community health workers and drop-in clinics in faith centres or residents associations has helped; I’d like to see that expanded with stable funding and data to identify gaps.

I would also support improvements to NHS111, triage and booking systems to prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. Clear pathways and care navigators can stop patients bouncing between GP, urgent care and mental health services.

At the same time, expanding online booking and e-consults could help many, but non-digital options must remain: telephone lines with trained operators, in-person booking at community hubs, and home visits for those who cannot travel. This ensures older and disadvantaged residents aren’t left behind while reaping the benefits of digitalisation.

As an organisation representing frontline health services in England, we are compelled to be frank: simply tinkering with appointment systems, digital triage or opening more same-day slots will not deliver timely access while the core problem remains underfunded and overstretched staffing. We disagree with approaches that rely mainly on process changes or short-term fixes. The most substantial and lasting improvements will come from growing and retaining the primary care workforce through targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, meaningful incentives and pay reforms, flexible working, and strong wellbeing support.

What would make the biggest difference in our area is a cohesive, long-term workforce strategy that targets shortages where they bite hardest and removes barriers to recruitment and retention. To that end, we propose the following priorities:

- Targeted recruitment and development: Implement area-by-area recruitment plans that actively attract clinicians to high-need localities. This should include expanding GP training placements in underserved practices, improving return-to-practice programmes, and offering graduate-entry routes for nurses, physios and pharmacists who can take on extended roles in the practice team. We have seen in our own networks that when a dedicated recruitment push is coupled with career progression incentives, patient access improves within months rather than years.

- International hiring with robust integration: Create a clear, efficient pathway for international GPs and qualified nurses, with streamlined visa processes, fast-track professional registrations, and funded induction programmes. We need to pair international hires with structured supervision, language and cultural integration support, and protected time to settle in practice. This must go hand in hand with retention planning; otherwise the gains will be short-lived and staff may move on to other systems or sectors.

- Incentives and pay improvements: Recalibrate pay and reward structures to reflect workload, living costs, and the value of primary care to the wider health system. This includes meaningful base pay uplifts, competitive sessional rates, relocation allowances, and targeted sign-on bonuses in hard-to-fill areas. Financial incentives should be paired with clear career pathways and reduced non-clinical admin burdens so clinicians can spend more time with patients and less time chasing paperwork.

- Flexible working and workforce design: Expand flexible and part-time working options, including job-sharing and cross-site rotations, to widen the pool of available staff and improve retention. Enable multi-disciplinary, team-based models where practice-based pharmacists, mental health practitioners, and physiotherapists share responsibilities with GPs, so access to care isn’t constrained by an individual clinician’s hours.

- Wellbeing and workload support: Increase funding for workload redistribution, admin support, and protected time for clinicians to plan care, consult with colleagues, and pursue professional development. Establish accessible occupational health and mental health services for staff, with proactive measures to prevent burnout. Practices must not be asked to carry on with unsustainable workloads in the name of “efficiency.” Patient safety and access depend on the wellbeing of the people delivering care.

In our networks, where a deliberate policy mix around recruitment and retention has been attempted—combining international recruitment with flexible hours and administrative support—patients have seen shorter waits for routine GP appointments, and staff report greater job satisfaction and lower burnout. Conversely, where staffing remains tight and reliance on agency locums grows, continuity of care suffers, and access deteriorates.

We therefore urge the government to commit to a long-term, adequately funded workforce plan that prioritises recruitment, training, and retention as the driver of better access. That plan should include clear milestones, robust evaluation, and a willingness to adapt based on evidence from pilot areas. If we want timely GP, community and mental health services, we must first ensure there are enough people with the time and support to deliver them.

We are ready to work with policymakers to design and implement this approach, but without a decisive focus on growing the workforce, any other changes will only yield temporary improvements at best and will not address the fundamental bottleneck in access to care.

I strongly welcome moves to overhaul how people access GP, community health and mental health services. In practice we need better NHS111 and clinical triage to steer urgent cases quickly to a clinician, reduce multiple calls and duplication, and streamline patient flow so people aren’t bounced between services. A centralised booking system with transparent same-day slots would cut out delays and confusion. Expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care is essential, but must come with clear non-digital options (phone line, local hub, home visits for those who need them) to avoid leaving older or less tech‑savvy residents behind.

Specifically, local expansion of community mental health teams, with early intervention and crisis response, would help reduce waits and ensure parity with physical health. More accessible talking therapies and quicker access to crisis support—ideally within hours when needed—would make a real difference. In my area, simpler triage and cross‑team referrals would avoid duplicating assessments and cut waiting times. Providing clinicians with better digital tools and data sharing would help coordinate care.

Wait times to see a GP or a mental health clinician in my area are simply not acceptable. I disagree with plans that focus mainly on adding a few more evening slots or calling in more private providers without tackling core staffing and outreach issues. The biggest fixes are consistent, well-paid staff and a smarter system for booking.

First, expand capacity: hire more GPs, practice nurses and therapists and keep them; offer longer appointment blocks for complex cases; invest in robust rostering and same-day triage to reduce backlog.

Second, recruitment and retention: targeted recruitment campaigns, international hires where needed, improved pay, flexible hours, and wellbeing support to stop attrition.

Third, bridge access gaps: more interpreters and culturally competent staff; proactive outreach in deprived and ethnic minority communities; partnerships with community groups, faith centres and pharmacies to signpost services; mobile clinics and pop-up sessions in areas with poor access.

In practice, locally we see 2–3 week waits for routine GP slots and mental health wait times of 6–8 weeks; interpreters are sporadic; online booking is clunky. If these changes aren’t implemented, waits will worsen and health inequalities will widen.

Our organisation welcomes clear steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients is essential. When patients can see the same clinician for longer, medication regimes stay coherent, care plans are followed and avoidable crises are reduced. In practice, longer, focused reviews for people with long-term conditions also support carers and families, helping people stay independent at home. 

We also strongly support investment in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners. A single hub where a GP, nurse, mental health practitioner, social worker and voluntary sector colleagues work side by side makes care more seamless, cuts wasted journeys and speeds up decision‑making. In our area, a pilot hub bringing these teams together shortened waits, improved follow‑up and reduced repeat referrals for hundreds of residents.

To deliver real improvements, reliable long‑term funding, robust digital information sharing, and proactive workforce planning are needed, alongside ongoing patient voice involvement. We urge rapid progress on these changes to create safer, kinder and more effective local care.”

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a daily concern for many households, including mine. I don’t think there’s a single silver bullet; what helps most is a bundled approach that increases capacity where it’s most needed, makes booking smarter, and keeps the patient journey simple and predictable. In practice, that means more appointment slots, more flexible staffing, smarter triage, and better care navigation to steer people to the right service promptly rather than bouncing between systems.

First, expanding capacity and streamlining scheduling for primary and community care would make a real difference. When I’ve tried to book a routine GP appointment, it’s often two to three weeks out, with longer waits for nurse or therapy slots. The most effective signal we’ve seen locally is when practices hire additional GPs, nurse prescribers and physiotherapists, and then extend hours into evenings or Saturdays. Not every patient needs a standard 10-minute GP slot, so offering longer appointments for chronic conditions, and group or walk-in slots for common issues, can free up time for new or urgent cases without overburdening clinicians. It would help if several practices within a cluster shared a common roster so patients could book across sites if their own practice is full. Digital booking that shows real-time availability, with a simple option for same-day slots, would reduce the frustrating cycle of phone calls and re-checking.

Second, improving NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation is essential to prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. NHS111 is invaluable when it routes people quickly to the right service, but the experience is inconsistent. A clinician-led triage pathway that prioritises red-flag symptoms and triggers urgent GP or mental health slots when appropriate would prevent delays for those in real distress. This requires reliable staffing levels for triage lines and a robust handoff to primary or community services—so a caller isn’t bounced from one number to another or asked for information already captured elsewhere. In parallel, a modern booking system should learn from patterns: if someone is trying to book mental health support after a crisis, the system should offer the most direct route, not passive “book later” prompts.

Care navigation roles, where trained staff help patients understand their options and coordinate referrals, have the potential to cut duplication and confusion. For instance, a navigator could confirm eligibility for community therapies, allocate a likely first-available slot, and then monitor progress, so people don’t slip through the cracks while waiting for a referral to a specialist. In situations where I’ve navigated multiple services for a family member, the absence of a coordinating point often meant repeated explanations and wasted time. A navigator who can stay with a patient through the care pathway—from GP or NHS111 triage through to therapy or community support—would save hours and reduce anxiety.

Local examples illustrate both the gains and the gaps. A weekend walk-in clinic connected to a group of practices helped during a period when weekday slots were scarce, and it drastically cut the time to see someone for a non-urgent issue. Conversely, when mental health referrals take eight to twelve weeks, even a well-booked GP appointment doesn’t compensate for the delay in getting appropriate support. It’s this mismatch—expanded slots in some areas, but persistent delays in mental health pathways—that underscores the need for an integrated plan rather than piecemeal fixes.

One practical path forward would be a regional programme that:
- funds targeted workforce expansion (GPs, nurse prescribers, therapists) with protected training and supervision time to prevent burnout.
- deploys a shared, patient-facing digital booking platform with real-time slots across all local practices, plus clear markers for urgent and crisis referrals.
- establishes care navigation teams to guide patients through the system, triage effectively, and monitor progression.
- pilots extended-hours clinics and flexible appointment formats (short, medium, and longer sessions) tailored to the complexity of the condition.
- collects transparent data on wait times, appointment type, and outcomes, disaggregated by demographics to identify and address inequities in access.

Concerns remain about implementation: we must guard against overpromising capacity without sustainable funding, ensure new processes don’t add to clinician workload, and protect patient data across multiple sites. Any reform should be co-designed with frontline staff and patients, tested in stages, and adjusted quickly if it leads to unintended bottlenecks.

In summary, the changes that would most improve timely access are: expanding capacity and flexible scheduling in GP and community services; smarter, triage-driven booking systems; and robust care navigation that guides patients through the system efficiently. When these pieces work together, we’re far more likely to see shorter waits, fewer duplicated contacts, and a smoother experience for people trying to get the help they need, when they need it.

I strongly support the proposal to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by investing in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health teams, and mental health services, with social care and VCSE partners. In our area in England, people often fall through gaps when they have to navigate multiple separate services, especially when work and caring responsibilities limit their ability to travel and book multiple appointments. A local model that houses these services under one roof would make a real difference to everyday life and to health outcomes.

Co‑located hubs would mean a patient can see a GP, speak with a clinician from community health or mental health teams, and access social care or housing advice all in one place. That continuity is crucial. People don’t just need a medical diagnosis; they need timely social support, help with welfare benefits, and connections to community resources. When professionals from different services can share information (with consent) and agree on a care plan, the result is faster, safer, and more person‑centred care. In practical terms, this could reduce the number of separate trips someone has to make, cut waiting times for referrals, and decrease unnecessary crises that lead to hospital admissions.

I’ve seen the benefits of a local hub in our town. A community centre now hosts a GP clinic, a district nursing team, a mental health practitioner, and a VCSE‑run advice service. Since it opened, the uptake of flu and other vaccines has improved, appointments are booked more efficiently, and people who were hesitant about mental health support have been more willing to engage when they can access counselling or psychological support alongside their general care. Staff can triage quickly and arrange appropriate follow‑ups—sometimes same‑week appointments—without the patient having to navigate a maze of phone lines and different buildings.

Targeted outreach and resources are essential to ensure everyone can benefit, especially deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In diverse communities, language barriers and cultural expectations can create real obstacles to timely care. I support targeted investment in interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to build trust and familiarity with local services. Practical steps could include extended interpreter cover (evenings and weekends), on‑site bilingual navigators who can help people understand treatment options and follow‑up plans, and culturally tailored health information available in multiple languages.

Beyond language, services should be geographically and culturally accessible. Co‑located hubs should be placed in or near high‑need neighbourhoods and offer flexible hours, including evenings and some weekend slots, to fit work patterns. VCSE partners can play a vital role in proactive outreach—running drop‑in sessions, accompanying people to appointments, and helping families address social determinants of health such as housing, Debt/benefits advice, and food security. I’ve found that peer support workers and community champions from local organisations can bridge gaps in trust and understanding, making people more likely to seek help early rather than waiting for problems to escalate.

To make this work over the long term, I’d like to see clear funding and governance so hubs can plan services across primary care, mental health, and social care with a stable workforce. Joint targets and shared data (with robust privacy safeguards and consent) should track access times, referral flow, and patient outcomes, and most importantly, patient feedback must shape ongoing service design. Training for all staff on cultural humility and trauma‑informed approaches should be mandatory, not optional.

If these hubs are well supported, we’ll see fewer delays, better health and wellbeing, and a more confident, connected community. Please invest in the co‑located model and the targeted outreach needed to close access gaps for marginalised groups. Thank you for considering these changes and for prioritising timely, integrated care that treats people holistically and with dignity.

From my perspective, the question asks what changes would improve timely access, but I don’t think quick tweaks will fix the core problem. In my view, the biggest improvements will come from long‑term workforce growth and retention.

First, increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, backed by robust return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. This would create a stable pipeline and reduce repeated shortfalls as staff move on or burn out. In our area we’ve seen GP vacancies linger for months; without new entrants and ongoing training, access won’t improve.

Second, expand community mental health teams with stronger early‑intervention, crisis response and more talking therapies. Referrals sit in queues far too long, and crisis slots vanish quickly. A more comprehensive, well‑staffed network would stop people turning to emergency services.

Third, broaden digital access while protecting non‑digital routes. Online booking and e‑consultations are helpful, but they must come with maintained phone lines, same‑day in‑person slots and outreach for those who are digitally excluded or uncomfortable with tech.

Taken together, these steps would shrink waits, align mental and physical health access, and build resilience for future pressure in Wales.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area is hindered by language and transport barriers, limited local presence and fragmented services. I strongly support changes that target those gaps:

- Resources for interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. This includes on-site interpreters in clinics, multilingual appointment reminders, and training for frontline staff in culturally sensitive care.

- Co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners. A single hub attached to a GP practice with on-site district nursing, mental health workers and social care coordination would reduce referrals and speed up support.

- Practical fixes for transport, parking and premises deficits: mobile clinics, outreach teams visiting estates and rural villages, telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, and incentives to extend hours and attract staff.

In my experience, when hubs exist nearby it’s easier for people to attend urgent appointments, and appointments are kept rather than delayed. These changes would make services more accessible and reduce unnecessary hospital visits.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care would significantly improve timely access. In my area, routine issues like medication reviews, minor injuries, asthma checks, or back pain often clog GP appointments and create delays. If a pharmacist were embedded in the practice, they could handle repeat prescriptions and minor symptom queries within days, freeing GPs to focus on complex care. A physiotherapist for musculoskeletal problems could assess and deliver treatment plans quickly, reducing unnecessary referrals and waiting times. Paramedics or physician associates could run Saturday clinics or triage calls, capturing more same-week slots and taking pressure off the usual weekday queue. I’ve seen a family member benefit from physiotherapy triage instead of waiting weeks for a GP appointment, which sped up recovery. Pilots in similar schemes show shorter waiting times and higher patient satisfaction when teams share records and coordinate care. My main caveat is ensuring robust IT systems, clear role boundaries, and adequate funding so rural practices aren’t left behind and data sharing is seamless.

I live in England and, as a 65+ resident, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters deeply to me. In my area, GP slots are often booked weeks ahead and timely mental health support can feel out of reach. The changes that would help most fall into two linked strands. First, we need to grow and stabilise the primary care workforce: targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, better pay and incentives, flexible working, and strong wellbeing support so staff stay longer. If the workforce is supported and fairly rewarded, it reduces reliance on temporary locums and improves appointment availability, which I’ve observed in neighbouring practices that introduced protected admin time and wellbeing initiatives. Second, invest in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community teams, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners. A single hub with clear care pathways would speed up referrals, improve coordination and keep people out of hospital. That said, these hubs must be funded for the long term, with robust governance, data sharing that respects privacy, and attention to transport and patient choice. In short, gentle expansion of workforce plus local integrated hubs could meaningfully improve access in our communities.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. In Scotland, timely access to GP services, community health, and mental health support is a key determinant of people’s ability to stay well and avoid escalating problems. Our organisation sees real potential in two practical changes that could improve access for working people and those with urgent but non-emergency needs, while still protecting and strengthening core services on weekdays. Any implementation must be carefully planned to avoid overburdening staff or fragmenting care, and it should be underpinned by robust workforce planning and consistent funding.

First, extending access through evening and weekend clinics is worth pursuing, with a clear, regional network rather than a patchwork of isolated pilot sites. This would help parents, carers, shift workers, and small business owners who cannot take time off during the day. A sensible model could be rotational or hub-based clinics offering GP appointments alongside nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacist-led consultations. In our experience, patients often delay seeking care until a problem becomes more serious because weekday daytime slots clash with work and school commitments. A structured evening/weekend offer would help them get timely advice, prescribing, or prompt referral when needed, reducing unnecessary emergency attendances. A key caveat is to ensure that extended hours are supported by adequate staffing, training, and predictable rotas, so clinicians are not stretched and the quality of care remains high.

Second, guaranteeing same-day urgent slots for non-emergency issues within primary care would be a meaningful improvement. A validated triage process—whether by telephone, digital pre-assessment, or in-practice triage—should determine if a same-day slot is required, with careful allocation to clinicians who can address the concern promptly or escalate to a mental health or community health specialist as appropriate. For example, a parent dealing with a rapidly deteriorating child’s symptoms, or an adult presenting with a sudden worsening of anxiety or depressive symptoms, would benefit from a same-day assessment rather than waiting several days. This approach can reduce anxiety for patients, prevent deterioration, and help keep people out of urgent care settings unless necessary.

Alignment with mental health services is essential. We need rapid access pathways integrated with primary care, including same-day or next-day mental health triage slots, short wait times for talking therapies, and efficient referral routes to CAMHS or IAPT-type services. In our experience, delays in mental health access often feed demand in GP practices and can contribute to crises that require hospital-based care. Co-locating counsellors or trained mental health professionals within primary care practices or community hubs, with clear handovers to tertiary services when required, would streamline care and provide reassurance to patients who may otherwise disengage.

Equally important is expanding and strengthening community health capacity. Timely access to district nursing, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and social care support can prevent deterioration and support independent living, particularly for older adults and people with chronic conditions. This could include mobile clinics for rural areas, temporary expansion of community teams during peak periods, and better scheduling systems so patients know when to expect visits or follow-up reviews. We should also ensure that these services are fully integrated with primary care so care plans are coordinated and patients do not have to repeat information repeatedly.

A pragmatic approach is to couple these access improvements with robust digital tools, including online booking with visible slots, secure video or telephone consultations where appropriate, and a streamlined triage workflow that respects patient choice and digital inclusion. Any digital expansion must address the digital divide, ensuring those without reliable broadband or devices can still access services and receive timely care.

We recognise the resource implications. Extending hours, guaranteeing same-day slots, and staffing additional community and mental health teams will require stable, long‑term funding and a clear workforce plan (training, recruitment, retention, and appropriate remuneration). It will also demand careful data monitoring—tracking wait times, uptake by area (urban vs rural), patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes—to ensure that access improves without compromising safety or equity.

From our ongoing engagement with communities, our strongest preference is for a carefully staged expansion that prioritises high-need areas and includes a strong evaluation framework. If we can couple extended hours and same-day urgent slots with integrated mental health pathways and expanded community support, we have a real opportunity to make timely care more available to the people who need it most, while building a more resilient and person-centred health system.

Overall, we support the direction if designed with safeguards: predictable staffing, funding, rural equity, robust triage, and transparent outcomes reporting. Implementation should be co-produced with patients and frontline staff to avoid unintended consequences and to ensure the changes truly deliver faster, safer, and more convenient access for everyone in Scotland.

it's outrageous that i welcome the focus on improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, and I strongly support policies that protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for patients with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. From my own experience in our area, short appointments often feel like a hurdle for people who require comprehensive assessment and long-term support, and this can lead to avoidable repeat visits when a problem isn’t fully understood or managed.

I’ve seen how continuity makes a real difference. A friend managing both diabetes and anxiety recently faced back-to-back short GP slots, which made it hard to address how the two conditions influence each other. The result was frequent follow-ups and avoidable escalation. Conversely, when a named clinician followed their case and offered a longer slot, the clinician could review medication interactions, check mental health symptoms alongside physical health, and agree a plan that reduced crises and subsequent visits. For my neighbour with chronic back pain and weeks of sleep disturbance linked to depression, longer appointments with a multidisciplinary team meant a single appointment could adjust the pain plan, address sleep and mood, and set up a home exercise and support plan—reducing the need for urgent care or repeated tests.

What would help most are practical changes that put continuity and time at the centre of care:

- Guaranteed named clinicians and continuity of care for people with long-term or complex needs. If patients know who is coordinating their care, and that this clinician will see them across GP, community nurses and mental health services, it reduces confusion and miscommunication and builds trust.
- Longer appointment times for complex cases. A standard 10-minute slot is rarely enough for someone with multiple chronic conditions, medication reviews, and mental health considerations. I’d back longer GP appointments (for example 20–30 minutes) and longer mental health slots (30–60 minutes as needed) so clinicians can properly assess, adjust plans and check for interactions or barriers to adherence.
- Multidisciplinary care plans and integrated teams. Patients with complex needs should have a personal care plan that follows them across services. A small team—GP, nurse, physiotherapist or social prescriber, pharmacist, and, where needed, a mental health professional—could meet regularly (even virtually) to review progress. Shared, secure records would enable real-time updates so everyone can see what’s already been tried and what’s next.
- Proactive scheduling and responsive triage. A strong triage system that flags high-need patients and ensures timely access to longer slots when a problem could otherwise escalate would prevent avoidable crises. Offering same-day or next-day slots for urgent issues, alongside reliable routine reviews, would balance accessibility with quality.
- Flexible access that respects people’s lives. Evening or weekend clinics, more drop-in community health slots, and safe options for video calls where appropriate can make a real difference for people who work or have caregiving responsibilities. Importantly, digital access must be inclusive and not create new barriers for those less comfortable with technology.
- Investment in workforce and training. Expanding the capacity of GPs, nurses, mental health professionals and allied health workers, and training them in coordinated care and risk stratification, will support longer consults without compromising access for others.
- Transparent measurement. Clear metrics on continuity of care, appointment length, wait times and patient satisfaction will help us see improvements and adjust policies if gaps emerge.

If these changes are implemented thoughtfully, we’ll likely see better control of chronic conditions, earlier mental health support, and fewer repeat visits or crises. Patients will feel heard and supported, and the system will work more efficiently by preventing small problems from becoming bigger emergencies.

Thank you for considering these priorities. I hope they inform a practical plan that makes timely access possible while preserving the quality and continuity of care that patients rely on!

From my experience living in England and juggling work with family health needs, I think the biggest gains in timely access would come from three practical changes. First, protect continuity of care by lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When a family member with diabetes and arthritis sees the same GP, a 10-minute slot rarely feels long enough to review medications, blood test results, and the impact on mental health after a stressful week. Longer appointments—20 to 30 minutes for those with multiple conditions—would let clinicians take a holistic view, catch potential drug interactions, and coordinate better with community supports. That kind of consistency reduces repeat visits, prevents avoidable crises, and ultimately saves time and stress for patients and families alike.

Second, improve NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and streamline patient flow. There have been occasions where a concern over a weekend needed urgent attention, but the path between NHS111, a triage nurse, and a booking system felt slow or inefficient. A more reliable triage process that flags urgent needs for same‑day GP or urgent care slots, supported by a care navigator within the booking platform, would cut duplication and confusion. A single, user‑friendly portal showing available appointments across GP, community health, and mental health services—with clear next steps and reminders—would make it much easier to pull together tests, prescriptions and follow-ups without multiple phone calls.

Third, provide evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. For many working people, daytime appointments simply aren’t possible, which leads to delayed care or skipped check-ups. An evening clinic once a week and a Saturday morning slot would be a real help for routine reviews, chronic disease management and timely mental health support, without requiring unpaid leave. Equally important is a guaranteed same‑day urgent slot for non‑emergency concerns: when someone has a worrying symptom or a mental health crisis, there should be a clear, fast route to a clinician rather than a multi‑day wait.

In my area, these changes would work best if primary care, community services and mental health teams were better integrated. A shared, secure record that travels with the patient and a trained care navigator who can arrange tests, transport and social support would reduce miscommunication and gaps in care. In summary: longer appointment times for complex cases, smarter triage and booking with effective care navigation, and flexible access through evening/weekend slots and guaranteed urgent care would markedly improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area. This isn’t just about convenience; it’s about delivering safer care, reducing avoidable harm and support needs, and helping people maintain their independence and well-being.

Expand GP, nurse and therapist slots by hiring and smarter scheduling; recruit locally and internationally with better pay and flexible shifts; add evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots to help working people.

From where I sit in rural England, I’m not convinced that pouring money into large, co‑located hubs will automatically deliver timelier access to GP, community health and mental health services. In practice, the biggest barriers I see are distance, transport, and staffing gaps, not the absence of a shiny new building on the map.

First, the cost and the time to deliver a truly integrated hub would be substantial. Planning, acquiring premises, fitting out spaces for general practice, mental health teams, social care, and VCSE partners, plus the IT and data sharing systems—all of that would take years and divert money from frontline care that is already stretched. In the meantime, people in small towns and villages will continue to wait for appointments or have to travel long distances to reach a single centre. The danger is that these hubs become run by bureaucratic processes rather than front-line care, and rural residents are left behind while plans are rolled out elsewhere.

Second, staffing remains the bottleneck. You can’t magically conjure doctors, nurses and therapists by building a larger building. If we end up pulling staff into a central hub, we risk weakening local practices that already struggle to recruit. In my area the GP practice has had to shorten hours and cancel nurse clinics because staff are overstretched. A grand new hub could feel efficient on paper, but without a reliable workforce it won’t translate into quicker access for patients who need timely consultations, blood tests, or simple mental‑health check‑ins.

Third, accessibility for older and mobility‑impaired people is not solved by geography alone. A hub miles away, even with a better car park, is no better if someone cannot drive, cannot afford the bus fare, or cannot get a lift. Our village has limited bus services and poor links to the town. Parking at existing surgeries is often tight or charged, which deters people from turning up for appointments they really need. A hub that doesn’t address local transport and parking won’t improve timeliness; it may even increase it for some while leaving others out altogether.

Digital and telehealth fixes also need a reality check. Telehealth can be a real help for those who can access it, but many older people struggle with digital literacy or suffer from unreliable broadband in rural areas. I’ve seen relatives have to cancel video calls because the connection drops or the screen won’t work, while a phone call isn’t always enough for a proper assessment. A telehealth hub sounds efficient, but unless there is staff on site to help people use the equipment and to triage correctly, it risks becoming a barrier rather than a route to timely care.

Finally, the idea of co‑located hubs raises governance questions. Who coordinates which services, who makes quick decisions when a patient needs urgent mental health support, and how is data shared securely across primary care, social care and VCSE partners? Without robust, simple governance and fast decision‑making, we risk more fragmentation, not less, and longer waits while people navigate the system.

What I would support instead—what would really improve timely access in the near term—are targeted, practical measures that fit our communities better:
- Expand mobile clinics and outreach to villages, towns, and care homes on predictable schedules. A nurse or GP visit in the village hall or a local church hall, with a simple blood test or a mental health triage, would cut travel time dramatically for many older residents.
- Create and fund small telehealth hubs in existing community spaces with trained staff to assist patients. Ensure reliable broadband and simple processes, but keep a strong option for face‑to‑face appointments when needed.
- Improve local transport and parking: more flexible bus routes, subsidised or volunteer driver schemes for medical appointments, and free or affordable parking near clinics so people are not deterred by cost or convenience.
- Offer clear staffing incentives targeted at rural and inner‑city areas where shortages are worst: flexible hours, housing allowances, and retention payments to keep experienced clinicians delivering care locally.
- Strengthen collaboration with local VCSE and social care groups, but with simple, transparent governance and direct funding streams to deliver immediate improvements in access rather than creating another layer of administration.
- Ensure that any digital solutions are inclusive: training, user‑friendly interfaces, and immediate access to human support to help people navigate the system.

In short, I would not prioritise building big co‑located hubs as the fastest route to better access. The quicker wins come from bringing care closer to people through mobile, flexible, and digitally supported services that acknowledge the realities of rural transport, parking, and digital inclusion—while still maintaining strong in-person options for those who need them most. Please keep the patient voice at the centre of these plans and fund proven, locally responsive approaches that can be rolled out quickly rather than waiting years for a single hub to come on stream. Thank you.

In my area in England, I’ve felt the pressure on GP, community health and mental health services more than once. Booking a same-day GP appointment can feel hit-or-miss, and when a friend tried to get CAMHS support for their child, the wait stretched into months. I’m not against improving care in the short term, but I’m trying to think long haul—how we actually grow the workforce in a sustainable way so people aren’t left waiting years for help. My instinct is to back a careful, staged approach: expand training places and support pathways, but couple that with practical, on-the-ground fixes that work now and don’t overload teams later. 

What changes seem most promising to me:

- Increase training places and targeted pipelines, especially in primary care and mental health. England could commit to expanding medical school places and GP specialty training slots, plus dedicated places for nursing, allied health professionals and CAMHS routes in or near communities that experience the longest waits. The idea would be to grow a steady pipeline rather than chasing short-term fixes. Providing more clinical placements in GP practices, with protected time for supervision, could help new graduates build confidence and stay in primary care after qualification. For my area, that could mean more student placements at our local practices and university-affiliated community clinics, so students learn to work in teams and understand local health needs.

- Return‑to‑practice support and flexible routes into the profession. I’ve spoken to people who paused their careers for family reasons or due to burnout during the pandemic. A structured return‑to‑practice pathway with tailored refresher modules, supervised shifts and flexible hours would make it easier for qualified professionals to rejoin the workforce. This isn’t just about recruiting fresh graduates; it’s about re-integrating skilled people who already know how to care for patients but need a bridge to rebuild confidence and update skills. In mental health, shorter, modular CPD that focusses on current best practice and digital therapy tools would help practitioners regain pace without taking them away from patients for months.

- Apprenticeships and CPD as a long-term growth lever. Apprenticeships offer a practical route into roles like nursing associates, healthcare assistants moving into registered roles, or mental health support workers who then specialise. If funded well, they can deliver hands-on experience while people earn and learn, which is important in communities where the cost of living pressures can deter traditional student routes. A robust CPD system—recognised qualifications, funded time away from base duties, and clear progression ladders—would keep people up to date with new therapies, new digital tools, and team-based care models. I’d like to see employers, training providers and local NHS trusts co-design programmes that align with local needs, not just national targets.

- Embed multidisciplinary, community-based teams to improve access. For timely care, patients benefit from teams that include GPs, nurses, mental health professionals, pharmacists and social care workers collaborating in one hub. If training pipelines seed these teams, new graduates will be socialised into this model from day one. In practice, this could mean co-locating a CAMHS clinician with a GP practice for joint assessments, or having a nurse practitioner run same-day clinics in the community to triage and manage non-urgent cases, freeing GPs to handle more complex needs.

- Immediate steps that don’t wait for a full pipeline. While expanding training takes time, there are quicker wins: more protected time for GP partners to supervise trainees, better use of digital triage and remote consultations to manage demand, and additional funding for urgent mental health crisis teams in the community. In my experience, a small boost in immediate access—like same-day slots reserved for mental health triage or a dedicated phone line for urgent concerns—can prevent crises from spiralling and ease downstream pressure.

A few caveats I’d want to see addressed: training expansions must be matched with adequate supervision and realistic patient loads so trainees aren’t overwhelmed and service quality doesn’t slip. We also need a fair, sustainable pay and progression system to keep graduates in the NHS long term, otherwise the “pipeline” may leak as soon as people qualify. And while we push for more training, we must ensure rural and underserved urban areas aren’t left behind—geography should guide where new training and posts are created so wait times shrink across the board, not just in cities.

Overall, I’m cautiously supportive of the long-term plan to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals through training, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. The key is to pair ambitious workforce development with concrete, time‑bound improvements to access now and with safeguards that maintain patient safety and staff wellbeing. If done thoughtfully, this could reduce wait times in a way that feels fair and sustainable for communities like mine.

I’ve read the ideas about improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, and I don’t think the most effective fix is to simply expand certain teams or create more hubs without protecting what actually helps people stay well: continuity of care and honest appointment lengths for complex cases.

First, continuity matters. For patients with long-term, multi-system problems—like diabetes plus heart disease, or chronic pain with mental health overlay—the best outcomes come when you know the clinician you’ve trusted over time. Short, rushed 10-minute slots often mean important details get missed and plans need re-doing, which leads to more calls, more visits and more anxiety. In our practice, when appointments were extended to 20–30 minutes for people with complex needs (even if only a couple of days each week), there was a clear drop in repeat calls within the following fortnight and fewer urgent escalations. Yet the default in many areas remains a 10-minute slot. If we’re serious about reducing waits, we should invest in longer appointments for complex and vulnerable patients and ensure patients can see the same clinician where possible. That alone would shave off many repeat visits and hospital admissions later on, and it would be fairer for people who need consistent, ongoing support.

Second, expanding community mental health teams and increasing early intervention and crisis response can be helpful in principle, but only if they’re tightly anchored to primary care and patient records. Otherwise you risk fragmenting care and creating new scheduling bottlenecks. In practice, when mental health teams operate as separate strands from a patient’s GP, information isn’t always transferred quickly, and the patient ends up telling their story again and again to different people. This slows everything down and undermines trust. I’m not opposed to more CMHT capacity or quicker access to talking therapies, but I want it integrated with the person’s clinical pathway, with shared records and a named point of contact in primary care who follows the patient across services. If a crisis team is ready to help but cannot hand over care smoothly to a GP, the patient may bounce between services and the benefit is lost.

Third, co-located community hubs have potential to improve access by bringing services together, but they are not a magic wand. They can, in theory, reduce travel and friction, but only if they deliver a genuinely single point of access, same-day triage, and a guaranteed ability to see a clinician who knows the patient’s history. Without that, hubs can become busy “one-stop shops” that still force people to wait for referrals between teams or to repeat information. In rural or outer-city areas where transport is a barrier, simply relocating services into a hub doesn’t automatically speed things up. If hubs are pursued, they must be built around a universal record, a clear care plan, and an option to see a familiar clinician in a timely way—ideally the clinician who has managed the patient’s conditions for years.

What would actually improve timeliness in my view is a combination of these elements, but with the emphasis squarely on continuity and capacity in primary care:

- Extend appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients (the same clinician wherever possible) to 20–30 minutes, with a named/continuing clinician where feasible, so issues aren’t repeatedly left unresolved and hospital visits are reduced.
- Strengthen primary care capacity through more GPs, practice nurses, and allied health professionals, plus streamlined administrative support so clinicians spend more time with patients and less time on paperwork.
- Build integrated pathways between primary care and mental health services, with shared records and a single care plan, so early intervention and crisis response feed directly into ongoing care rather than creating new silos.
- If hubs are to play a role, ensure they offer genuine one-stop access, same-day triage, and a clear route back into ongoing primary care with continuity. Patient flow must be designed to avoid extra waiting and extra handoffs.
- Invest in flexible access (after-hours slots, walk-in slots for urgent problems, and validated digital triage with rapid human follow-up) so people aren’t forced to wait days for non-life-threatening concerns.

Personally, I’m not convinced the headline promises of “more teams” or “new hubs” will automatically reduce waiting times unless they’re paired with a strong commitment to continuity, longer consults for complex patients, and tight integration with primary care records and follow-up. If these conditions aren’t met, the changes risk trading one set of problems for another—fragmented care, confusion for patients, and even longer waits in the back offices of individual services. What matters most to me is that people with chronic conditions and mental health needs can see the same clinician, get a proper appointment length, and have a clear, coordinated plan that prevents crises and unnecessary hospital visits.

I would welcome investment in co-located hubs that bring GP, community and mental health care together with social care and VCSE partners, but insist on robust funding, sustainable staffing, and accessible transport to ensure timely access across my area.

Multidisciplinary teams can help, but only if IT, supervision, and funding accompany them, otherwise patients bounce between services. In short, scale up flexible access (same-day slots, extended hours) and invest in retention, with concrete timelines for apprenticeships and CPD to feed the pipeline.

From where I’m standing as a young person in England, I don’t think simply extending daytime hours is enough to sort out timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The real problem isn’t just when doctors are available; it’s about whether there are actually reliable slots, enough staff, and ways to reach services when you’re busy with work, studies or caring responsibilities. So I would push for a multi‑layer approach that goes beyond “more hours” to a mix of flexible access points and logistics that match how young people actually live.

What I’d push for instead of just longer opening hours
- Guaranteed same‑day urgent slots and evening/weekend clinics: It’s not enough to promise more appointments if urgent non‑emergency needs still get bumped or pushed online to weeks away. I’d want a system where urgent slots are reserved and guaranteed on the day, with enough after‑hours availability (evenings, Saturdays) to fit students and part‑time workers. In practice, this means a national/combined booking pool that can funnel urgent cases to the next available slot across local networks, with proper triage so people aren’t stuck waiting for days for a non‑emergency issue.
- Transport, parking and premises addressed with mobile and hub options: Rural and mobility‑limited areas are often left out. Mobile clinics that visit villages and town centres on a regular schedule can bring GP and mental health support closer to where people live. For those in towns with patchy bus routes, telehealth hubs placed in libraries or community centres—with staff to help people use the tech—could reduce digital barriers. On-site parking and subsidised transport options for those with restricted mobility would make a real difference.
- Telehealth hubs and outreach as standard practice: Not everyone can queue in a waiting room or has fast, private internet at home. Establish staffed telehealth hubs where you can talk to a clinician in private, with the option for video or secure audio, and a nurse or counsellor on site to assist. Outreach teams could visit schools, universities and workplaces to offer drop‑in mental health checks and quick GP assessments, cutting down the time people lose in getting help.
- Mobile and outreach mental health services: Mental health access is particularly slow for young adults. A rolling schedule of mental health clinicians visiting smaller communities, colleges and workplaces would cut out the two‑three month waiting times that many report. This would pair with rapid outreach for urgent concerns and an easy pathway to longer‑term care if needed.
- Practical improvements to premises and capacity: Even when clinics exist, cramped waiting rooms, old facilities and limited parking or poor accessibility push people away. Upgrades funded with clear delivery targets and patient input (including young people) would help. More importantly, we need assurance that adding clinics doesn’t simply shift bottlenecks elsewhere; staff recruitment, supervision, and workload balances must keep up.

Personal context and why this matters
- I’m 20‑something, juggling part‑time work and study. An after‑hours GP slot would be a lifeline if I’m dealing with a sudden back‑to‑university stress spike or a worsening mental health issue. If I can book something for 6–9pm or Saturday morning rather than missing a shift or a lecture, that makes the service usable rather than a theoretical option.
- I know friends who can’t access the NHS properly because the nearest GP is a long bus ride away, or because the car park is always full and the reception is chaotic. A mobile clinic rotating through our town two evenings a week, plus a connected telehealth hub for quick checks, would mean people don’t give up after one failed appointment or a missed bus.
- For mental health, long waits are common and young people often first reach for informal support or online forums. A network that offers quick in‑person or telehealth contact, with short, clear pathways to longer‑term care, could prevent crises and support early help‑seeking.

What I’d want to see measured and held to account
- Short, transparent wait times for urgent slots; published weekly data on availability across GP, community health and mental health services.
- A funded 12–24 month pilot across diverse areas (urban, rural, coastal towns) with mobile clinics, telehealth hubs and after‑hours services, with independent evaluation and clear roll‑out criteria if targets are met.
- Safeguards for digital inclusion and data privacy, so that telehealth doesn’t leave anyone behind or compromise sensitive information.

In short, the goal should be timely access through a balanced mix of extended hours, guaranteed urgent slots, local mobility solutions, and accessible telehealth options. If the plan remains focused only on “more appointments” without tackling staffing, transport, and the real-world convenience of access, then it won’t work for people like me who need flexible, reliable care outside standard office hours. The changes I’ve outlined would better match how young people live and work today, and could genuinely improve timely access without simply piling more pressure onto already stretched surgeries.

I strongly support changes that will grow the health workforce over the long term, so people can get timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services. The most effective steps are: 1) increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals; 2) robust return-to-practice support so skilled clinicians can rejoin quickly after a break; 3) expanding apprenticeships into registered roles to create clear career paths; 4) strong CPD and flexible study routes that fit family life and current work commitments. 

In practice, this means regional training hubs that host GP and district nurse placements with good supervision, funded return-to-practice programs with mentoring, and apprenticeship routes from care roles to registered positions (for example from nursing associate to registered nurse or from support workers into mental health practitioner roles). I’ve seen how vacancies and long waits for non-urgent referrals can affect families in our area, and I know that building capacity now will reduce those waits in a few years, delivering safer, more local care. Investing in training and upskilling is essential to ensure timely access to the care people rely on when they need it most.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains uneven. To improve, I would prioritise expanding and funding community mental health teams, with clear rapid access pathways and stronger integration with GP practices. This should include more psychologists, therapists, nurses and social workers who are co-located in local hubs, so someone can be seen quickly rather than waiting weeks. Early intervention services for psychosis and mood disorders must be expanded, with a guarantee of slots within two weeks of referral and smoother transitions from hospital to home.

Crisis response must be reliable: a 24/7 crisis line, mobile crisis teams able to respond within hours, and a designated crisis hub near town centres. Talking therapies should be increased through IAPT with shorter waits and broader modalities (CBT, ACT, EMDR where appropriate), including flexible delivery in-person and remotely from community settings. These should be accessible to people with long-term physical health conditions as part of truly integrated care, achieving parity with physical health in both access and outcomes.

From personal experience, a family member waited months for CBT after referral, while help for a physical condition arrived much sooner. Local, transparent wait-time reporting would help families understand and plan, and prevent deterioration that leads to hospital care.

While I welcome the idea of more online booking and e-consultations to speed things up, I’m worried about leaving behind those of us in Wales who rely on phone calls or face-to-face help. In villages with patchy broadband, online portals can be a barrier rather than a shortcut. If there’s no clear non-digital route, people will delay care and end up needing more urgent treatment later.

To improve timely access, keep a simple telephone line and in-person options for GP, community health and mental health services, with clear guidance on how to access them. NHS111 needs stronger clinical triage, quicker routing to urgent care, and a single, easy-to-use booking system to reduce duplication and confusion between services. We’ve seen referrals duplicated or lost when different teams use separate systems; a unified care-navigation hub could guide people to the right service first time and ease patient flow.

Provide real non-digital support: trained staff to help with booking, local community hubs offering assistance, and paper-based or home-visit options when needed. Remote care should augment, not replace, local access.

I’d like to know how targets will reflect elderly and rural experiences, and what protections will be in place to prevent digital exclusion while improving timeliness.

I welcome the proposals to improve timely access to GP, nurse and therapist appointments and to expand community mental health services. In my experience, waits for a GP can stretch into two weeks for a routine check, and when a quick review is needed, that wait can be stressful, especially for someone with chronic conditions. Increasing appointment slots by hiring more practice nurses and therapists and offering extended hours would help. Better scheduling tools and load management could reduce bottlenecks. I also support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to bring mental health care on par with physical health. Early support can prevent crises and hospital admissions, which is better for patients and costs. Transport and access remain a barrier in many rural areas. I have seen mobile clinics visit villages, and telehealth hubs in community centres work well, especially for follow-ups. Providing transport assistance, better parking and more local premises would encourage people like me to seek timely help rather than wait until it becomes urgent. These changes would make a real difference to my community.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a frontline issue for young adults trying to juggle study, work and life balance in England today. When urgent care is needed, delays aren’t just frustrating – they can become real health risks. I think the changes proposed would, if implemented well, move us in the right direction, but they need to be supported by long‑term workforce planning and smarter patient flow systems that actually meet people where they are.

Long-term workforce development is essential. To sustainably grow the numbers of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, we should expand training places and create robust return-to-practice routes. That means more GP registrar posts in every region, more nurse and allied health professional pathways, and dedicated CPD and apprenticeship options so people can train or retrain while working. In my area, there’s a growing demand but only a handful of training posts, which means after qualification there’s a bottleneck before you can practice independently. A structured return-to-practice programme would also help: people who paused clinical work for parenting or other reasons could rejoin with updated skills rather than leaving gaps in frontline care.

Flexibility will matter too. We should incentivise training in underserved areas and support multidisciplinary teams that spread the workload more evenly across GPs, nurses, therapists and pharmacists. I’d like to see more community-based hubs where NHS staff rotate between primary care, mental health, and social care so young people can receive coordinated care without endless handoffs. The aim is not quick fixes, but a stable pipeline that grows the workforce year after year, so we aren’t back in this same place in five years.

On the service side, improving NHS111, triage, booking systems and care navigation could deliver real gains in the near term and reduce duplication. Often, people end up repeating information to multiple services, or get routed to the wrong place and waste a lot of time before they’re seen.

Specific changes I’d prioritise include:
- Better triage and clinician-led NHS111: Quick access to a trained clinician who can assess urgency, including mental health crises, and direct people to the right service first time. For example, someone with escalating anxiety or depression should be fast-tracked to a mental health professional or community team rather than bouncing between urgent care and GP reception.
- Real-time, user-friendly booking: A national or regional booking system that shows real-time GP and clinic slots, with same-day or next-day availability for urgent concerns. Linked to a simple app, it would reduce the fog around “when can I be seen?” and cut down on repeated calls.
- Integrated care navigation: A dedicated navigator or care-coordinator in each locality to help patients move smoothly between GP, nurse-led clinics, physio, mental health services and social care. This would cut duplication of forms, prevent multiple referrals for the same issue, and ensure people aren’t lost between services when symptoms cross boundaries (for example, a person with musculoskeletal pain who also experiences anxiety).
- Better routing for mental health: Ensure crisis lines and urgent mental health pathways are clearly signposted through NHS111 and the app, with direct referrals to crisis teams where needed, rather than defaulting to general clinics that may have long waits.
- Digital integration with local services: When possible, keep patient records and history in a single, secure system so clinicians can see past notes, recent tests, and medicines without recounting everything from scratch. That alone would save time and reduce the stress of medical encounters for younger patients who may switch between universities and hometowns.

In practice, these changes would require investment now in people and systems, but the payoff is more timely access, less wasted time in queues, and care that matches the urgency of the situation. When people can get an appointment quickly, receive appropriate advice, and be guided through the right service with minimal repetition, it greatly improves confidence in the NHS and reduces the pressure on urgent care in peak times.

I’m supportive of the direction this policy signals, as long as it’s backed by concrete steps to grow the workforce and modernise the way patients are triaged and booked. Without that dual approach, the gains from better systems could be undone by insufficient frontline capacity. In short: invest in people, invest in smarter systems, and make care navigation genuinely structured to prioritise urgent needs and clear patient flow.

i really think i live in England and I’ve seen how waits for GP appointments and mental health support can affect everyday life, from trying to book a same-week GP slot around exams to worrying when a friend can’t get timely mental health help before a crisis hits. I think there’s a clear case for action now, but I also know that longer-term reform has to sit beside immediate capacity fixes so people don’t have to wait months while the workforce is being built up.

In the short term, increasing appointment slots and session capacity feels like the most urgent need. Practices could expand hours with safer, more sustainable staffing plans—more GP and nurse appointment slots, and more time for longer or more flexible consultations for complex cases. It would help if practices could pilot same-day triage and smarter scheduling so people who need urgent help aren’t bounced to later slots when the system is already busy. For students and younger adults like me, evening or weekend GP slots, student health clinics on campus, and nurse-led clinics for chronic conditions could make a real difference. I’ve seen some local clinics run weekend “quick clinics” for common issues, but they’re not universally available, and where they exist the slots fill up fast.

We also need to improve access to mental health services, which are often the bottleneck. Expanding a broader suite of community therapies and ensuring quicker triage to a therapist or counsellor could prevent problems from escalating. In my area, wait times for counselling can stretch into several months, which is just not acceptable when someone is struggling with anxiety, exams pressure or housing stress. If general practice could provide more integrated pathways with mental health professionals—for example, nurse prescribing support or stepped-care options in primary care—it would reduce delays and offer timely help before things become unmanageable.

On the longer horizon, I’m supportive of boosting the pipeline so we don’t just patch over the gap. Increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals matters a lot. That should go hand in hand with more return-to-practice support so people who paused their careers aren’t lost to the system entirely. Flexible retraining routes, apprenticeships in clinical settings, and continuous professional development funded and valued by the NHS would help grow the workforce sustainably. I’ve talked to a few people who are considering returning to practice after a break but fear the bottlenecks in re-licensing or getting up to date on new guidelines; clearer pathways and funding would make a real difference.

There are practical concerns to manage. Expansion has to be matched with quality control and patient safety. Hiring more clinicians is essential, but they need proper supervision, mentorship and integrated care teams so patient care remains coherent. And expansion must be equitable: the largest gains won’t help if they’re concentrated in a single city, leaving rural or coastal areas with slower progress. Digital access can also help, but we must ensure online booking and remote consultations don’t exclude people who rely on phone or in-person support, or those with limited connectivity.

Ultimately, I’d like to see a plan that pairs immediate capacity improvements with a credible, well-funded long-term strategy to train and retain the workforce. If local health authorities publish a transparent timetable—showing when extra GP and nurse slots will appear, where training places will be added, and how return-to-practice schemes will be rolled out—communities like mine can feel confident that improvements aren’t just promises but practical steps happening now.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services often hinges on how well the system organises triage, booking and navigation. I would welcome stronger clinical triage within NHS111 and a streamlined booking system that prioritises urgent cases and reduces duplication. A single, patient-centred care navigator who can see a person’s history across GP, hospital and community services would help avoid the back-and-forth I’ve seen and shorten waiting times. 

At the same time, we must address gaps for deprived and minority communities. Language barriers and limited interpreters leave some people at risk of delayed mental health support. Targeted funding for professional interpreters, culturally competent staff and proactive outreach would help people know what is available and feel confident to access it. 

Finally, transport and premises matter. Rural and mobility‑limited residents struggle with travel to clinics and parking. Mobile clinics, telehealth hubs and outreach to community venues, plus incentives for clinics to offer extended hours and better access to accessible premises, could make a real difference. If these changes are delivered with equity in mind, timely, appropriate care should become more achievable for everyone in my area.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains uneven.. Waiting times for routine GP appointments and stretched community teams lead to condition deterioration and pressure on urgent care. Any changes should focus on growing and sustaining the primary care workforce, with robust implementation to protect patient safety and continuity of care. Practical steps we could support: - Targeted recruitment in the area, including expanded training placements and clear progression routes to attract local entrants into general practice and community teams. - Thoughtful international recruitment, backed by rigorous induction, language support and mentoring to ensure newcomers integrate quickly andd safely. - Better pay and structured incentives, including progression within pay bands and retention allowancrs for practices that reduce waits or extend hours. - Flexible working and staffing models, such as job-sharing, longe daytime slots, and protected time for wellbeing and supervision. - Strong wellbeing support, including access to mental health resources for staff and manageable workloads to reduce burnout. - Digital triage and closer integration across GP, community services and CAMHS to shortrn pathways and avoid unnecessary hand-offs. Pilot these measures in a few practices with robust patient feedback and clear evaluation before broader rollout. A strategy that grows the workforce while supporting thosee delivering care has the best chance of improving timely access without compromising quality.
