THAT MEANS TARGETED RECRUITMENT, INCLUDING INTERNATIONAL HIRING WHERE APPROPRIATE, PLUS STRONG INCENTIVES TO JOIN AND STAY: COMPETITIVE PAY, CLEARLY DEFINED PROGRESSION, AND RELOCATION OR SIGN-ON ALLOWANCES FOR CLINICIANS WILLING TO MOVE TO UNDERSERVICED AREAS. i really think from living in Scotland, I’d welcome changes that make NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation work together to prioritise urgent needs and smooth patient flow. For example, when a family member felt unwell, NHS111 triaged quickly but follow-up appointments were not available the same day, and we had to chase multiple practices. A unified system showing same-day options and intermediate slots would have reduced delay and anxiety.

A dedicated care navigator at the local health centre could coordinate across GP practice, district nursing, physiotherapy and CAMHS, so we’re not repeating the same information to different teams and patients aren’t bounced between services. Strengthening NHS111’s clinical triage with clearer escalation paths for urgent mental health and community care needs would also help; crisis slots or rapid access projects should be funded and protected so they don’t get rolled into waiting lists.

Data-sharing with consent, transparent referral tracking, and staff training are essential so triage improves things rather than adding bureaucracy. Overall, targeted investment in these integrated pathways would deliver timely, person-centred care across GP, community and mental health services!

I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Protecting continuity of care is vital, especially for people with complex or chronic needs. Longer appointment times and a priority on seeing the same clinician when possible help people manage ongoing issues and reduce rrpeat visits, which saves time for patients and staff alike. In practice, this could mean longer initial assessments and clear follow-ups, with better triage so urgent concerns are dealt with quickly but less urgent cases aren’t left waiting weeks. I also back investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners together. A single site where you can see a GP, get mental health support, and access housing or benefits advice would save journeys, cut no‑shows and support early intervention. In my area, a university town hub or town centre hub would make it easier for students and young workers to get holistic help in one visit. Proper funding, flexible hours and strong links to local charities are essential to make this work.

Technology can help reduce waiting times and bring care closer, but it must be designed with fairness in mind. I welcome expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote monitoring for GP and mental health services, as they can cut delays when traditional slots are full and help working families. In my area, having a same‑day online booking option could have helped when I had a minor infection, with a quick video check‑in avoiding a long wait. For colleagues with mobility issues or unreliable phone signal, digital options are a lifeline. However, there must be robust non‑digital routes and support: a clear phone line, walk‑in slots, and reception staff to assist with booking, plus translators and easy‑to‑use interfaces. We also need to protect continuity of care; for those with chronic conditions, longer appointments and a named clinician should be standard, not a series of 10‑minute slots. Where digital tools are used, they should integrate with patient records and allow clinicians to review history easily to prevent repeat visits and miscommunication. Overall, a blended approach would boost timely access without leaving vulnerable patients behind.

Honestly, I think there isn’t one magic fix for getting GP, community health and mental health services to people on time. It feels like a mix of things would help more than any single change, and a lot of it depends on where you live and what time you try to access it. In my area there are days when a simple GP appointment is almost impossible to grab quickly, and you end up waiting weeks even for a routine check-up. I tried dialing at 8am last month and was on hold for ages; when I got through, the earliest slot was two weeks away and the online system didn’t show any same‑day availability. That makes it hard to know whether you should push through with self-care or push for a proper check, which isn’t great when you’re dealing with something that could escalate if left untreated. I’ve got friends who ended up going to walk‑in clinics simply because they couldn’t get a timely GP slot, which isn’t ideal for continuity of care.

For community health and mental health, I’d like to see more visible outreach and easier access. A lot of people don’t know what support is actually available or how to navigate it quickly. A relative with a chronic condition had to chase routine blood tests because the local community clinics are booked up for weeks. If there were more flexible outreach slots—like nurses visiting homes or pop-up clinics around campus areas in the evenings—that would cut down on hospital visits and reduce the stress of long waits. In mental health, a friend waited many months to access talking therapies after being referred. That wait makes it easy to disengage or try to cope on your own, which isn’t healthy in the long run.

What might help most, in practice, would be a combination of things. First, more staff and longer hours in GP practices, plus more real-time online booking that actually shows what slots are available today, not just generic “soon.” If you can grab a same‑day or next‑day appointment for minor illnesses, it saves time and keeps people out of urgent care centers. Second, stronger community health teams—district nurses, mental health professionals and social prescribers—working alongside local pharmacies and urgent care hubs to share information and coordinate care. Third, clearer, faster pathways for mental health, with university or school outreach and better-funded campus services that can bridge people to NHS therapies quickly. Fourth, better data sharing across GP, hospital and community services so people don’t have to repeat the same information every time they’re seen or referred. Finally, some weekend or evening access points, especially near student hubs, would help those who work or study during the day.

I know some of this will require more funding and workforce planning, but without visible, practical options that work for people who aren’t free during standard hours, delays will keep piling up. If changes are made with real-time appointment access, better local hubs, and clearer mental health pathways, it would feel a lot more doable for people like me and my peers who don’t rely on NHS services every day but still need timely help when something comes up.

I live in England and, in my area, timely access to GP, community and mental health services often hinges on how NHS111 and clinical triage work in practice. A more consistent and rapid triage pathway that accurately directs urgent cases to same‑day slots would cut duplication and anxiety for families. The current spread of booking systems is confusing: I’ve encountered multiple portals for GP, 111 and urgent care, with misaligned slots and re‑entries. A single linked booking platform, with triage notes visible across services, would simplify patient flow and help people get timely advice before needing a clinic visit.

Co‑located community hubs could be a real game‑changer. If primary care, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners are based in one accessible hub, patients can navigate referrals quickly, carers can coordinate support, and we’d see fewer avoidable visits to urgent care. In my neighbourhood a parent had to visit three locations for a single issue, delaying care and support.

Longer‑term, expanding training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD would sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff to meet demand. That workforce renewal is essential to deliver reliable access.

From our local patient representative group across England, we support measures to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. For older residents managing multiple chronic conditions, continuity of care is essential. Allowing longer appointments for complex cases (for example 30–40 minutes for people with diabetes and heart disease) helps clinicians spot problems early, reduces hospital visits, and builds trust. Ensuring patients see the same GP when possible improves outcomes and reduces repeat visits. We also support targeted outreach to remove barriers for deprived and minority communities. Providing interpreters, training staff in cultural competence, and using community health workers to reach isolated migrants or marginalised groups can close gaps in access. Information in multiple languages and flexible appointment times, including after-hours clinics, would help many grandparent carers. Finally, to grow and retain staff, we back targeted recruitment, international hires, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support. If staff feel valued and supported, services will be more available locally and consistently. In our area, this would translate to fewer missed appointments and better management of chronic conditions.

I support investing in mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs to reach rural and mobility-limited residents, plus incentives to attract staff. Expand community mental healthh teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to cut waits. Offer evening/weekend clinics andd guaranteed same-day urgent slots.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in Scotland could be improved most by growing the workforce in a sustainable way. That means increasing training places for GPs and nurses, expanding return-to-practice support, and widening apprenticeships and CPD so people can enter and progress in the system without losing years to long pathways. Specifically, more GP training posts and placements across urban and rural areas would help reduce bottlenecks and keep patients in their own communities. A robust return-to-practice scheme with funded refresher periods and supervised clinics would help clinicians re-enter after a break. Expanding nurse associate roles and mental health practitioner apprenticeships would bring skilled staff into community teams, improving triage and timely access, including digital and same-day consultation options.

Personally, I’ve seen local delays when a GP vacancy opened; after a nurse joined via an apprenticeship and a colleague used a return-to-practice route, appointment slots improved and people in our area could be seen more quickly (as if that will ever happen). It’s a model that could work across Scotland, but it needs sustainable funding, clear career pathways, and strong supervision to protect quality. The focus must also be on rural and deprived areas to avoid widening gaps.

absolutely expanding online booking and e-consultations alone won’t reliably improve timely access, and risks leaving the most vulnerable behind. In my area the online system often crashes or is slow, and phone lines can be jammed, so people wait days for routine GP slots or mental health referrals. I’ve seen a neighbour miss a timely check because the digital triage suggested self-management she couldn’t safely follow. We need a genuine multichannel approach that includes non‑digital options.

What would help most is a mix of measures: guaranteed same‑day triage slots, reliable non‑digital channels (a well‑staffed phone line, clear call‑centre information, and some walk‑in clinics), plus transparent information on appointment types and current wait times. Digital tools can help, but they must complement, not replace, face‑to‑face care and home visits for those who can’t access online services.

On staffing, I support targeted recruitment, incentives and flexible working, but only with real funding increases, reduced admin burden, and sustained wellbeing support to retain clinicians. In my experience, burnout and admin overload drive turnover. Practical steps include more practice nurses and physician associates, better pay and progression, international recruitment with solid local supervision, and mentoring. Also expand rapid community teams and home visits for hard-to-reach patients.

I’m not convinced that the answer lies in one silver bullet, like more training places alone. In our area, GP and mental health access is already inconsistent while we wait weeks for routine appointments and months for some CAMHS referrals. Yes, expanding training, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential for the long term, but that won’t fix today’s bottlenecks or the risk to people who need timely help.

What would help now, while those workforce aims are being built up, includes practical capacity boosts and smarter workflows. For GPs, fund more same‑day triage slots with nurse practitioners and practice staff, extend hours, and use digital booking and triage to prioritise urgent cases. Porting some routine chronic care to well-supported nurse or pharmacist teams could free GP time for those needing urgent attention. For community health, invest in district nursing, physio, and community mental health teams so they can visit people at home and reduce unnecessary hospital trips (as if that will ever happen). In mental health, embed more practitioners in primary care and speed up access through clearer digital pathways and robust crisis support.

On the ground, I’ve seen waits grow and people slip through the cracks. We need both the long-term plan and immediate, concrete steps to see real improvements in timely access.

I strongly support the changes proposed to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. Transport, parking and premises shortages are real barriers, especially in rural and mobility‑challenged communities. Mobile clinics and outreach, paired with telehealth hubs and incentives to improve rural access, would make a tangible difference. For example, a weekly mobile GP/nurse clinic could visit village halls or market days, with essential services available on the doorstep and referrals to local mental health support where needed. Improving parking at existing centres and offering community transport vouchers would also remove practical hurdles.

I also welcome increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots by hiring more staff, expanding session lengths where appropriate, and using smarter scheduling so people can book promptly, including same‑day or late‑evening slots for working families. In my experience, even modestly longer slots and better triage can cut avoidable waits significantly.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners would create seamless local care. When services share facilities and information, referrals are quicker, follow‑ups are easier, and preventative care is more consistent for residents who would otherwise fall through the cracks.

Thank you for the chance to respond. I wholeheartedly support changes that improve timely access by investing in co-located community hubs, where GP services, community health teams, mental health support, social care, and voluntary sector partners work alongside each other. When all the right professionals are in one place, people don’t have to tell the same story again and again, and urgent concerns can be picked up and acted on quickly.

In our area, I’ve seen neighbours struggle to navigate multiple appointments at different sites—often with long waits and repeated information. A local hub would mean a same-day triage in a single building, with a nurse, a GP, or a mental health worker coordinating care, plus on-site access to social support. Carers would benefit too, as one appointment could address medication reviews, housing or home-help needs, and community services.

I also welcome improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation that prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. A single, well‑led care navigator who can book across GP, community teams and mental health would simplify patient flow, cut wasted journeys and speed up access to treatment and medicines. With stable funding and sensible data sharing, this would bring real, practical relief to older people and their families.

I welcome these proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. Expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care is a sensible step, but I know from experience that not everyone can use digital channels. My neighbours who are older or have limited broadband often struggle with apps or online forms. It’s important to keep non‑digital options—telephone triage, in‑person bookings and paper forms—with sensible help in the surgeries to support those users. Providing staff to assist with setting up video calls or digital access at the practice could help, without leaving anyone behind.

Targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential. Our town has diverse communities and sometimes vital information doesn’t reach deprived, ethnic minority, migrant or marginalised groups. Interpreters at appointments and outreach through community hubs would improve access and reduce delays, particularly for those with limited English or unfamiliar with the NHS system.

Longer‑term, increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals and cut waiting times over time. In summary, I support these changes and believe they would help me and many others secure timely care when we need it most.

I welcome the proposals to make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services more reliable. In our area the bottleneck is not patients but staff. Targeted recruitment and international hiring, plus clearer career progression and pay improvements, are essential to grow and retain GPs, nurses and therapists. Flexible working patterns—job-sharing, extended hours, and protected wellbeing time—would help staff stay in the profession and deliver consistent access. I’ve seen practice colleagues burn out after vacancies linger, and patients wait weeks for a GP appointment and longer for mental health referrals.

Expanding community mental health teams, with early intervention and crisis response, would prevent crises and keep people out of A&E. More talking therapies and rapid access to psychology staff would restore parity with physical health services. Local examples include a recent delay in mental health referrals that could have been avoided with a broader team; with stronger investment we could see quicker assessments and support. Please prioritise recruitment, wellbeing, flexible working, and expanded mental health capacity.

i strongly believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve if NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation were redesigned to prioritise urgent cases and simplify patient flow. In my experience, too much time is spent repeating information across services and online slots disappear before many older patients can respond.

Key changes I’d welcome:
- NHS111/triage: a clinician-led callback within a defined window for urgent symptoms (ideally within 30 minutes) and a consistent urgency scale that guides patients to the right service, not to unnecessary A&E.
- Booking systems: a single, interoperable system that follows the patient across GP, NHS111, community teams and mental health services; auto-fills history and reduces repeated form filling.
- Care navigation: funded navigators in local hubs or by phone who help older people choose the right service and track progress, preventing needless back-and-forth.
- Community and mental health: fast-track pathways within local teams for escalating concerns; quicker access to talking therapies or crisis support, with clear expectations on timelines.
- Practical steps: more flexible GP appointments (evenings/weekends), better social-care links, and home-visit options when appropriate.

This would require investment and governance, but it could cut duplication and make services genuinely easier to use for people like me!

I live in England and I welcome moves to target resources and build a more inclusive system. In my area, getting a GP appointment is often slow; same‑day slots are rare, and for non‑English speakers interpreters aren’t always on site. Multilingual information and culturally competent staff would help reduce gaps for deprived, ethnic minority and migrant communities (as if that will ever happen). Transport and parking problems at surgeries create real barriers; people without private transport struggle to attend. I support mobile clinics that visit housing estates, outreach teams in libraries or community centres, and more telehealth hubs so people can access care without long journeys. Offering incentives for rural and mobility‑limited areas to attract GPs, nurses and therapists, and boosting return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD would grow the workforce sustainably. In my town, a weekly mobile health van and a telehealth room in the library made it easier for families to access mental health advice and GP triage without long waits. If we couple targeted outreach with flexible access points, timely care will truly improve.

I understand the aim of cutting waiting times and getting people timely help, but I’m uneasy about the proposed changes unless they come with careful safeguards. Expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and pushing for bigger community mental health departments sounds sensible in theory, yet in practice it risks fragmenting care and dodgy handovers if the basics aren’t right first.

On routine care, the idea that pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, and physician associates could take on more of the load for everyday ailments worries me as an older patient with several chronic conditions. Pharmacists are excellent for minor, straightforward issues and some medication advice, but many of us rely on a GP to review new symptoms in the context of all our medications and history. A chest discomfort, new fatigue, or a fall could be dismissed as something simple if a clinician isn’t weighing it against heart disease, diabetes, or a previous stroke. If routine problems are diverted away from the GP without robust, integrated records and clear escalation paths, we risk delays in identifying warning signs or making the right referrals.

In our local practice, I’ve seen cases where notes don’t always travel smoothly between services. If an exercise prescription from a physiotherapist isn’t linked to the GP record, or if a pharmacist’s note doesn’t show up in the medical history, someone might be prescribed duplicates or miss a critical interaction. For many older patients, continuity matters: knowing there is a named clinician who follows your case over time gives reassurance and safety. If these new teams operate too independently, even with the best intentions, the safety net frays. And there’s the practical point: in some towns the health economy is already stretched thin. Expanding teams without a corresponding expansion in trained staff, IT systems, and administrative capacity could simply shift bottlenecks rather than remove them. Rural residents would also face transport and access issues if care is spread across more locations without reliable transport or flexible hours.

Regarding mental health, expanding community teams, early intervention, crisis response, and talking therapies is undoubtedly important, and parity with physical health should be the goal. My concern is more about how quickly recruitment and retention can deliver real change and how well services are actually integrated with medical care. Waiting times for talking therapies in many areas remain long, and crisis response services are not always available 24/7 or close to home. When a family member faced a mental health crisis, the immediate support was hard to access, and there were months of waiting for therapy once the crisis had passed. We need a reliable, well-funded system that can respond promptly in a crisis and provide ongoing support, not just an inflated number of teams on paper.

If these reforms are to work, they must be underpinned by a clear, funded plan that keeps the GP as the central clinician for complex cases. I’d want to see:
- Strong, interoperable IT so every clinician can see a patient’s full history, tests, medications, and plans without delay.
- Guardrails to maintain continuity of care, including a named clinician responsible for the patient’s overall well-being and explicit escalation channels when something feels urgent.
- Genuine workforce planning: sufficient numbers of pharmacists, physiotherapists, and mental health professionals, with clear supervision and pathways to involve GPs where red flags appear.
- Equitable access across urban and rural areas, with options for home visits or local hubs and flexible hours for those who can’t travel easily.
- Independent evaluation of outcomes, safety, and patient satisfaction, not just throughput numbers.

In short, while I wouldn’t wholly oppose the idea of broader teams, I’d insist on a staged, well-funded rollout with solid connection to GP-led care, robust information sharing, and real, measurable improvements in safety and timeliness for the people who rely on the NHS most—older patients like myself and those living with multiple conditions. Without that, the reforms could look good on a plan but fail to deliver better, quicker help when it’s actually needed.

As an organisation representing communities across Scotland, we oppose policy ideas that merely push for more rapid access by squeezing appointment times further. The most effective way to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, to improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. Where patients see a different clinician at every visit, information is repeated, and small deteriorations in mental health or chronic disease go unnoticed until crisis. In practice, many patients with diabetes, COPD, or severe mental ill-health need longer, 20-30 minute slots and a named clinician who follows their trajectory. Locum coverage and bolt-on triage have created gaps that lead to repeated referrals, unnecessary A&E attendances, and worse outcomes. We recommend: guaranteed named-GP continuity for high-need patients; longer standard consultations for complex cases; protected slots in GP rosters for ongoing mental health reviews; better integration with community nursing, social support and pharmacy teams; and reliable same-day triage that does not convert into rushed short appointments for vulnerable groups. In our area, patients who have a stable, long-term relationship with their clinician recover faster and need fewer urgent consultations. We urge policymakers to prioritise relationship-based care over throughput targets.

i really think i live in England and I strongly support changes that will improve timely access to GP, nurse and therapist appointments by increasing capacity through recruitment, expanded sessions and smarter scheduling. Waiting two weeks for a GP appointment is still common in my area, and evenings or Saturday slots are too scarce. By hiring more GPs and practice nurses and extending clinic hours, we can offer same-day triage and longer, more effective consultations. Flexible scheduling, better online booking, and protected appointment slots for those with chronic or urgent needs would reduce avoidable crises and follow-up delays.

For mental health, expanding community mental health teams, prioritising early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies will bring parity with physical health. More frontline staff, clearer pathways, and rapid access to CBT or other talking therapies would help people manage issues before they escalate. A dedicated crisis line or rapid outreach in villages would prevent avoidable emergency presentations. Overall, these changes would cut waiting times and restore confidence in local services!

I welcome the proposal to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In rural Wales, transport, parking and premises gaps are the biggest barriers. I support mobile clinics visiting villages on a regular rota, with clear parking and accessible entrances, plus outreach staff visiting schools and workplaces. Telehealth hubs in community venues (libraries, parish halls) would cut needless travel for many, while targeted incentives—rural practice allowances, retention payments, and flexible contracts—would attract GPs and nurses to the area.

I also back investment in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. A shared hub can offer same-day GP or nurse appointments alongside a counsellor and a social worker, reducing missed referrals and duplication. In my town, a pilot with a GP, district nurse and mental health worker in one building has improved signposting and follow-up rates.

Finally, increasing training places, return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD will grow the workforce. More medical school places in Wales, funded retraining routes, and supported CPD would help us keep pace with demand rather than chasing shortages.

To improve timely access, push targeted recruitment including international hires, offer pay improvements, incentives, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain GP, community health and mental health staff.

I strongly support steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in England. From my own family’s experience and what I see in our neighbourhood, the bottleneck is more about people than paperwork: not enough clinicians, inconsistent hours, and too much admin crushing already stretched teams. The way to unlock quicker, more reliable access is to grow and keep a larger, happier workforce, with clear routes for recruitment, fair pay, flexible working and strong wellbeing support.

First, targeted recruitment should be a central pillar. We need to expand GP training capacity in under-doctored areas and create regional recruitment drives that link local schools, universities and employers. Grow-your-own pipelines, with bursaries and guarantees of training places for those who commit to practice in their community, would help. I’ve heard from friends at our local practice that apprenticeships and nurse-led clinics could relieve GP load if there were more trainees and job-ready staff joining each year. A visible, long-term plan—backed by funding—would reassure communities and help young people see a future in primary care here.

Second, international hiring, with sensible, well-structured support, could plug gaps quickly. A dedicated NHS Global Health Recruitment Unit, faster recognition of overseas qualifications, streamlined visa routes and robust induction support would be game-changers. I know capable nurses and GPs who would relocate with a clear path to registration, supervisor support, and mentoring. It’s important, though, that integration is strong—cultural competency training for teams and protected time for onboarding so new colleagues feel valued rather than overwhelmed.

Third, incentives and pay certainly matter. We need fair, consistent pay progression that reflects workload and the complexity of primary care. That includes covering indemnity costs for GPs, meaningful sign-on bonuses for hard-to-staff practices, and improved pay for weekend or extended hours. When the numbers on the payroll look better, clinicians are more likely to stay in NHS roles instead of moving to less-demanding settings. In addition, administrative relief—such as funded clinical software improvements and practice-based scribes—would let clinicians spend more time with patients and less time on buzzwordy forms.

Fourth, flexible working arrangements are essential for retention and timely access. More extended hours in a safe, well-staffed way—early evenings, one-shhift weekend clinics, and robust job-sharing—would help busy families, carers and key workers. Let practices tailor rotas to local needs rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all model. Flexible scheduling, combined with on-site or nearby childcare options, can reduce burnout and keep talented clinicians in post.

Fifth, wellbeing and a supportive culture must be embedded in every practice. Protected admin time, accessible mental health and wellbeing services for staff, and strong line-management support reduce turnover. Practical measures—streamlined IT, digital triage systems, and a well-being lead in larger practices—signal that staff welfare is a priority. I’ve seen colleagues burn out when admin tasks swell; easing that burden directly improves patient-facing time and patient satisfaction.

For mental health and community health specifically, we should embed more multidisciplinary teams in GP practices: psychologists, social workers, pharmacists and physiotherapists co-located to offer same-day or rapid-access support. Integrated care pathways and shared digital records would prevent delays and ensure each patient gets timely help, whether it’s a mental health concern or a long-term condition needing coordinated inputs from several professionals.

Finally, these changes must be tested and scaled with solid funding and clear milestones. Pilots in varied parts of the country, with transparent metrics on waiting times, same-day access rates and patient experience, will show what works and what needs tweaking. If we get this right, timely access to GP, community and mental health services won’t feel like luck or a postcode lottery; it will be the norm across England. In my area, I’d welcome a joined-up plan that makes recruitment faster, supports international colleagues, offers flexible working, and puts staff wellbeing at the heart of every patient interaction.

Here in Wales I strongly welcome proposals to improve timely access by strengthening NHS111 and clinical triage, and by making booking systems and care navigation clearer so urgent cases are prioritised. In practice this could reduce duplication and confusion. I’ve experienced how details get repeated across reception, triage, and out‑of‑hours services, and how a fragmented flow can waste precious time when symptoms feel urgent. A single, reliable triage path would quickly identify those needing urgent review and direct them to the right clinician, rather than bouncing between services. An improved online and phone booking system with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would also cut delays for people who work or who have non‑emergency needs that can’t be left unresolved. Evening and weekend clinics would make a real difference for working people and carers. A care navigator to guide patients to the right service—pharmacist for minor issues, district nurse for ongoing care, or mental health support when needed—would simplify the journey and reduce unnecessary trips to hospital. I believe these changes would keep people healthier at home and ease pressure on the system overall.

I’m responding as a resident of England in my early 20s, and I’ve seen firsthand how changes aimed at making access seem quicker can end up making care feel fragmented. For me and for people I know, the real improvements come from protecting continuity of care and giving longer appointment times for complex or vulnerable needs. If we’re serious about timely access, we should not trade quality for speed.

- Protect continuity of care: For people with long-term conditions or multiple health issues, having a named GP who knows their history makes a huge difference. It reduces repeated explanations and the risk of conflicting advice. I’ve seen friends who live with both asthma and anxiety struggle when they’re bounced between clinicians or when every appointment ends up with a new person who has to re-check the patient’s story from scratch. Those handoffs almost always lead to delays in adjusting treatment or escalating mental health concerns. A system that guarantees a named clinician or a small set of trusted clinicians would cut out a lot of avoidable churn and reduce repeat visits later, which is a form of better “timeliness” in practice.

- Longer appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients: Ten-minute slots rarely suit chronic conditions or mental health concerns. When I’ve tried to talk through persistent fatigue, sleep problems, and rising anxiety in a single visit, the time simply isn’t enough to cover all the angles: history, current meds, sleep hygiene, stressors, and a plan. The result is a rushed discussion, a rushed prescription change, and a need to book another appointment—sometimes weeks later. Longer appointments would not only improve the quality of the initial assessment but also reduce the number of follow-ups required for the same issue, which is a net win for timely access in the long run.

- Integrated care and better care coordination: I’d welcome a model where GP, community nurses, and mental health services share a single care plan and notes (with appropriate privacy protections). When someone has both physical and mental health needs, a coordinated approach prevents conflicting advice and gaps in treatment. A central hub that can quickly pull together the right professionals—rather than making the patient navigate multiple referral steps—would bring genuine timeliness by preventing avoidable delays.

- Mind the workforce and the process design: It’s hard to improve access if there aren’t enough clinicians. In my area, wait times for mental health support can stretch for weeks, which then pushes people to rely on urgent care or drop out of the system altogether. Rowing in more patients through with shorter slots is not solving the core problem; it just creates a backlog of unresolved issues that resurface later. We need better recruitment and retention of GPs, nurses, and mental health professionals, plus stable career pathways so clinics don’t cycling through temporary staff. Alongside this, any digital or triage-based changes must preserve the option to see the same clinician and maintain continuity wherever possible.

- Practical delivery with safeguards: If screening tools or online booking are expanded, they should accompany guarantees that a patient can move to a longer, in-person appointment with a familiar clinician if needed. Flexible scheduling that preserves block times for complex care, not just “any available slot,” would help a lot. And there should be clear local accountability: clinics should publish waiting-time data, and patients should have a say in how local services are reorganised to avoid compromising continuity for the sake of a few minutes gained in throughput.

In short, timely access improves when patients can rely on consistent care and when clinicians have enough time to deal with complexity. Moving toward more short, noisy triage or rotating clinicians would undermine that. My clear preference is for: protected continuity (named clinicians where possible), longer appointments for those with chronic or mental health needs, integrated care plans across services, and meaningful investment in staff numbers and training. Without those safeguards, any “faster” access would likely translate into more repeats, more anxiety, and worse outcomes for vulnerable patients.

Yes, expanding community mental health teams and early intervention, plus crisis support and talking therapies, will cut waits. Co‑located community hubs with primary, social care and VCSE partners would streamline access, and targeted recruitment and flexible working will grow and retain essential primary care staff.

From a local health services perspective, the changes that would most improve timely access are not simply to queue more quick appointments, but to protect continuity of care for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Short, one-off slots often fail and can drive repeat visits. For example, someone with diabetes and depression needs a consistent GP who knows their history and can adjust treatment over time; when a different clinician sees them each visit, important information is missed and care is fragmented, leading to delays and hospital visits. Longer appointment times (20-30 minutes) for high-need patients and a named clinician or small care team across their routine care would cut delays and reduce repeat cycles. Implement structured care plans, with annual reviews and integrated community health and mental health input, so issues are anticipated rather than escalated. Invest in staffing and flexible scheduling to sustain continuity—while still offering urgent slots for true emergencies. In practice, this would improve outcomes and be more cost-effective by preventing crises rather than merely increasing throughput.

Access to timely GP appointments, community health teams and mental health support is uneven in our area. I would strongly support changes that expand community mental health teams, invest in early intervention, crisis response, and evidence-based talking therapies. These measures would help reduce waits, especially for people with emerging distress who currently wait weeks for help. In my experience, timely mental health support can prevent crises and unnecessary hospital visits, saving time and stress for families. I also welcome targeted resources to bridge gaps for deprived and marginalised groups: more interpreters, culturally competent staff, multilingual information, and outreach to hard-to-reach communities. In my village in Wales, I’ve seen some residents struggle to access services due to language barriers and lack of awareness about what’s available. Practical changes could include embedding mental health practitioners within GP practices, extended hours, same-day appointments, and easier referral pathways to talking therapies. Parity with physical health, with robust community teams, would make healthcare feel more joined-up and trustworthy.

i really think access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is essential, especially for older residents like me who live with multiple health concerns. I strongly support targeted resources to reduce access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups - funding interpreters, employing culturally competent staff, and active outreach in communities most affected. In my area, volunteers and bilingual staff have already helped patients navigate appointments and understand care plans, which cut down missed visits and anxiety tied to language barriers.

I also back increasing capacity: more GP, nurse and therapist slots by hiring, expanding sessions, and using smarter scheduling to spread demand more evenly. This would make it easier to obtain urgent care and routine follow-ups without weeks of waiting. Protecting continuity of care matters too: longer appointment times for complex or chronic conditions, and having the same clinician or care team where possible, reduces confusion and prevents unnecessary trips back to the doctor. With these changes, older people would stay healthier and less stressed!

I’m writing as a local resident in England, and I strongly support moves to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, while making sure non‑digital options and the right level of support remain available for those who need them. In my experience this combination can save time for patients and free up GPs to handle more complex cases.

What would help most in practice
- More online booking and same‑day options for routine needs: Being able to secure a same‑day appointment with a GP or nurse online would cut the current bottlenecks caused by telephone queues. I’ve found that when online booking is available, I can book quick slots for minor consultations (like a minor skin issue or a persistent cold) without waiting on hold for ages. That said, not everyone is comfortable online, so continuing a clear, easy‑to‑use telephone line and a walk‑in option where appropriate is essential.
- E‑consults and remote triage in a safe, user‑friendly way: A short e‑consult form or virtual triage can help practices direct patients to the right clinician first time—pharmacists for repeat prescriptions and minor issues, physiotherapists for musculoskeletal problems, or mental health practitioners when there are early signs of distress. This could drastically reduce waits for routine problems and free GPs to focus on more complex needs.
- A robust non‑digital support system: For older residents or those with limited internet access, the practice should offer assisted digital appointments, drop‑in help at community hubs, and clear signposting to use the phone line or in‑person visits. Training “digital champions” in surgeries or libraries could help people become confident with online booking without pressure.
- Flexible, multidisciplinary teams: Expanding teams to include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine cases would mean patients are seen faster by the most appropriate professional. Pharmacists can review medicines, manage simple side‑effects, and check for interactions; physiotherapists can handle back and neck pain referrals; paramedics can do home visits when appropriate and escalate only if needed; physician associates can manage common infections and minor ailments. This would free GPs to devote more time to complex or high‑risk cases.
- Integrated mental health pathways: Embedding mental health staff within primary care teams—alongside counsellors and clinical psychologists—can shorten waiting times and reduce deterioration. A patient could be first seen by a GP or nurse, with an immediate follow‑up appointment with a mental health professional or access to digital therapies when suitable. In my circle, quicker, integrated access to mental health support would make a real difference and help people avoid escalating distress.
- Clear, transparent pathways and choice: Patients should be told what the quickest, safest route is for their issue and offered options (online, phone, in person). Where a simple issue can be resolved by a pharmacist or physiotherapist, patients should be offered that route up front. For more complex problems or safeguarding concerns, there should be a clear, rapid escalation path back to a GP.
- Safeguarding digital equity and data privacy: Any expansion must include strong protection of patient information and explicit safeguards for vulnerable users. It should also track outcomes and patient satisfaction so we can prove the changes deliver real benefits and identify who might be left behind.

Practical examples from my experience
- A few months ago I used an online booking link to secure a same‑day appointment for a cold that wouldn’t shift. The nurse conducted a quick remote check and the GP followed up with a short prescription and advice on symptom management. The process felt efficient, and I avoided a long phone wait.
- For a musculoskeletal issue, I was referred to a physiotherapist through an e‑consult. The physio provided a structured home‑exercise plan, with a quick video check‑in a couple of weeks later, which helped me progress without repeatedly visiting the clinic.
- In our area, there’s interest in pharmacists reviewing long‑term medication lists for people with multiple prescriptions. If implemented well, this could catch interactions early and reduce unnecessary GP appointments, freeing time for more complex care.

What I’d like to see done next
- A 12–month pilot with regular patient feedback to measure wait times, satisfaction, and health outcomes, with adjustments based on findings.
- A clear commitment to maintaining non‑digital access routes, and resources to support people who need help using online services.
- Training and support for multidisciplinary teams to ensure everyone knows when to refer to another professional and how to coordinate care smoothly.

In short, expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, supported by strong non‑digital access and expanded multidisciplinary teams, would make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services more reliable. It aligns with everyday needs, reduces delays for routine issues, and lets GPs focus on patients who need complex care. I hope the plan includes robust patient support, careful monitoring, and a commitment to digital inclusion so no one is left behind.

From our organisation representing older residents across England, we strongly support the proposed changes to improve timrly access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding multidisciplinary teams is essential. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can manage routine cases—triaging minor illnesses, advising on medications, guiding back or mobilit problems, and carrying out early home visits—we free GPs to devote time to complex or high‑ris patients. In our area, simple ailments often require waiting for a GP appointment; a pharmacist’s same‑day consultation or a physio‑led back‑pain pathway would reduce unnecessary GP referrals and speed relief. We also welcome increased training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals long term. Long‑term stability in the workforce will help ensure older residents get timely care, including mental health support, without long waits. We have seen experienced nurses stepping back due to workload; funded retraining and flexible roles would retain skills locally. Finally, improving NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation is vital. A more efficient flow—clear triage to urgent cases, fewer duplicate calls, and direct booking to the right professional—would dramatically cut delays and improve confidence in the system.

absolutely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if resources were targeted to reduce gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. That means properly funded interpreters, multilingual information, and staff who understand different cultural expectations. In our area, I've seen neighbours from Polish and Somali backgrounds miss appointments because of language barriers and confusion over how to book. A dedicated outreach worker who can explain services in community settings, and a roster of trained interpreters, could make a real difference. Practical steps include translating essential forms, making same-day urgent slots available in general practice, and training reception staff in cultural sensitivity.

I would also welcome extended access through evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, especially for working people and non-emergencies that can spiral if delayed. But this must be paired with robust triage, mental health crisis pathways, and sustainable staffing—not just occasional pilots. Transport links, digital access, and privacy safeguards should not be forgotten. If done thoughtfully, these changes could reduce avoidable visits and improve wellbeing for older residents like me and for our diverse communities!

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is crucial for people like me who juggle work, family and a mental load of everyday health worries. It would mean more rubix-cube moments where the right professional sees the right problem first, and fewer days spent waiting for a GP appointment for routine concerns.

What would help most, in my view:

- Make same-day access a norm through MDT clinics. If a patient presents with a routine issue like a back strain, a cough that won’t shift, or a skin irritation, they should be able to see the most appropriate clinician that day—whether that’s a physiotherapist for musculoskeletal problems, a pharmacist for advice on medicines and minor ailments, or a physician associate for quick triage. This would free GPs to concentrate on complex cases and people with multiple conditions, which is where GP time is truly stretched.

- Embed pharmacists as front-line triage and care partners. Pharmacists can handle many minor conditions, review medicines for interactions, run long-term condition checks, and offer injections or vaccinations where appropriate. In practice, this means fewer trips to the GP for things a pharmacist can manage safely. I’ve found that a pharmacist’s guidance on dose adjustments or a simple management plan for two-week antibiotic courses, when needed, can stop problems escalating and save precious GP slots for more complicated care.

- Strengthen access to community physiotherapy. For common issues like back pain, neck stiffness or shoulder problems, a physiotherapist’s assessment and exercises plan can often resolve issues faster than waiting for a GP appointment. Community physio referral pathways should be clearly signposted and available via online triage so patients aren’t bounced between services.

- Use paramedics and physician associates to widen capacity and triage safely. Community paramedics can assess urgent but non-life-threatening conditions at home, reducing unnecessary calls to A&E and hospital admissions. Physician associates, working under supervision, can conduct consultations, provide treatment plans, and escalate when needed. In areas where pilots exist, I’ve heard from colleagues that this approach has reduced wait times and helped patients feel they were seen by a knowledgeable clinician sooner.

- Integrate mental health more tightly with primary care. Many people experience early anxiety, stress or mood concerns that don’t neatly fit a traditional appointment slot. Embedding mental health practitioners or IAPT staff within GP practices, with clear referral routes and same-day triage, can shorten waiting times and improve continuity of care. It also normalises seeking help before problems become crises.

- Clear pathways, good information and safety nets. For this to work, patients need simple information about who to see for which issue, and strong referral links between MDTs so care isn’t fragmented. Records must be shareable across the team to avoid repeating history or losing crucial information. And there must be robust governance, training and supervision so everyone operates within their safe scope of practice.

What I’d caution about is funding and staffing stability. It will require committed long-term investment to recruit and retain pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, plus ongoing training to keep skills current. There’s a risk of creating a two-tier system if some practices can—and others cannot—expand teams. That would undermine equal access. So any expansion should come with national guidance, ring-fenced funding and a clear plan to roll out consistently across areas, with embedded evaluation so we can learn what works best for different communities.

If done well, expanding multidisciplinary teams could shorten waiting times, improve patient experience, and free GPs to focus on the most complex cases. It would also build resilience in the network by distributing workload more evenly and offering care closer to home. I’d welcome a model that puts the patient at the centre, with clear, direct routes to the right professional on the day of need.

absolutely timely access to GP, community health and mental health services should be achievable within days, not weeks. In my area in England, the main frictions seem to be how we use NHS111 and triage, how booking systems operate, and how information moves between services. I think a combination of smarter triage, streamlined booking, and a stronger focus on staffing and working hours is needed, with practical steps that patients can feel the benefit from quickly.

First, improve NHS111 and clinical triage so urgent needs are clearly identified and directed to appropriate, available slots. In practice, I’ve found that when a relative had chest pains, the call went through NHS111 and the clinician wasn’t always able to access real-time GP slot availability, which led to delays and anxiety. A nationally standardised triage protocol, run by qualified clinicians, should feed directly into live booking systems so urgent cases get immediate access to same-day slots or rapid nurse-led clinics. This would also reduce duplication: fewer referrals bouncing between NHS111, GP reception lines, and out-of-hours services where the same information has to be repeated. A shared, real-time record of symptoms and triage decisions would prevent patients from being routed in circles and would help avoid unnecessary ED visits for non-emergency issues.

Second, modernise booking systems and care navigation. Patients need a single, user-friendly way to see availability across GP practices, community nursing, and mental health services, with clear guidance on the most appropriate entry point for their needs. Online booking should show real-time slots and, where possible, offer practical alternatives if a preferred time isn’t available—such as a same-day urgent nurse appointment, a same-week teleconsultation, or a clinician-led home visit for those with mobility or transport barriers. A dedicated care navigator in primary care settings could act as a single point of contact to coordinate care, explain options, and arrange follow-ups. In my experience, when someone has multiple conditions, a navigator who understands the full picture prevents fragmented care and makes the pathway smoother for the patient.

Third, invest in staffing and flexible working to grow and retain the workforce. Black-and-white headlines about GP numbers miss the point: the problem is vacancies, burnout and uneven distribution of staff. Targeted recruitment, including international hiring where appropriate, incentives for long-term roles, and improved pay, are essential. Flexible working patterns, wellbeing support, and safer staffing levels would help retain practice nurses, GPs, mental health professionals and district nurses. In our community, after-work appointments and robust on-call cover would relieve weekday bottlenecks for working people. If a patient can’t get an appointment until the following week, many will simply delay care until a problem worsens.

Fourth, practical steps to extend access hours and ensure urgent needs are met. Evening and weekend clinics, where feasible, should be introduced across more practices, with guaranteed same-day urgent slots as a baseline expectation. This does not have to mean every patient gets a same-day appointment with their own GP every time, but there should be a safe, predictable path to urgent care within working hours or a short after-hours window. For mental health, this means rapid referral pathways and guaranteed urgent slots for new presentations or worsening symptoms, with a clear care plan and follow-up in place.

Fifth, better integration between services and simpler patient flow. When a patient moves between GP care, community health, and mental health services, information and care plans should travel with them. A person-centred approach—where a named clinician or care coordinator maintains oversight and ensures timely follow-ups—would reduce gaps in treatment and the stress of navigating multiple services.

In short, I’d prioritise: smarter triage that leads to rapid, appropriate access; single, real-time booking and care-navigation across primary and community services; a staffing strategy that values flexibility, wellbeing and international recruitment where it improves access; and guaranteed same-day urgent slots plus evening/weekend options to fit working lives and urgent non-emergency needs. My experience shows that the friction isn’t just “more appointments” but better routing, better information, and a more resilient workforce. When these pieces align, it’s not just faster care—it’s better care.

I don't think simply expanding community mental health teams will automatically improve timely access. The priority should be an integrated, patient-centred path that prioritises urgent needs and delivers parity with physical health access, with explicit targets for same-- or next-day help when distress is highest.

i strongly believe i welcome the plan to speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area, I think expanding multidisciplinary teams would make a real difference. I’m glad to respond to this question because timely access to GP, community health and mental health services affects people across generations and communities here. I strongly support measures to speed up access, but the detail matters. Based on what I’ve seen and heard in my area, the changes that would make the biggest difference fall into a few practical strands: targeted resources, language and cultural accessibility, and better outreach and navigation for marginalised groups.

Targeted resources where they are most needed
- Increase GP and nurse capacity in practices serving deprived areas. More flexible hours, including evenings and Saturdays, with same-day triage slots for urgent problems, would reduce waiting times and avoid keep-sitting on phone lines. Mobile GP clinics or pop-up clinics in community hubs could reach residents who struggle to travel to fixed sites.
- Back up primary care with stronger community health teams (community nurses, physiotherapists, social prescribers) who can see patients quickly for ongoing conditions and prevention, rather than letting issues escalate.
- Invest in mental health teams that mirror the population. Expanding the staff in talking therapies (IAPT) and CAMHS in areas with higher demand would cut long waits and support families at a critical time.

Interpreters, language access and culturally competent care
- Guarantee access to professional interpreters across GP practices and mental health services, including face-to-face, telephone and video interpreting. When language isn’t a barrier, patients attend sooner and understand their care plan, medications and follow-ups better.
- Ensure multilingual frontline staff, translated appointment reminders, and multilingual information about services. Simple, clear guidance in common community languages helps people navigate the system without fear of misunderstandings.
- Train all staff in cultural competence and humility. This isn’t a one-off session; it needs ongoing learning so receptionists, nurses and clinicians recognise different beliefs about health, stigma around mental health, and practical barriers such as transport or childcare.
- When possible, recruit staff from local communities. People tend to trust clinicians who share backgrounds, or at least speak the same language or dialect and understand the local context.

Outreach, engagement and better navigation
- Proactive outreach to deprived and marginalised groups through trusted venues—mosques, churches, community centres, job centres, and refugee/migrant support organisations. Regular information sessions explaining how to access GP services, what to do in urgent situations, and how mental health support works can demystify the system.
- Health champions in communities who can help people book appointments, understand their care plans, and remind them about follow-ups. A simple, reliable point of contact makes a real difference, especially for older residents living alone or carers juggling multiple responsibilities.
- Simplified, multilingual access points for booking and triage. A single-language helpline and clear, translated online portals reduce confusion and delays.

Data, monitoring and accountability
- Collect and publish data on wait times and access by language, ethnicity, disability and deprivation. When funding and progress are transparent, it’s easier to target improvements where they’re needed most.
- Establish local performance dashboards that practices and community partners can use to adjust resources quickly, rather than waiting for quarterly national statistics.

Personal experience and why these changes matter
In my area, there have been stretches where getting a GP appointment felt like a hurdle course—long phone queues, limited same-day slots, and confusion around which service to use for a given problem. When interpreters were available for a specific appointment, my neighbour could participate fully in the discussion, understand the medication, and adhere to the plan. In another instance, a relative living with chronic conditions missed a follow-up because the clinic didn’t have a staff member who spoke their language or understood their cultural context. That omission isn’t just inconvenient; it can lead to deterioration and re-admission later on.

Bringing these changes together would create a more resilient local health system. It would reduce inequalities and ensure people aren’t deterred from seeking help when they need it most. I’d welcome a clear plan that ties increased funding to specific outcomes—shorter waits for GP and mental health appointments, better language support, and more community-based care—so that improvements are visible to patients, families and communities across the area.

Thank you for listening to local people’s experiences. I’m hopeful these practical, people-centred changes can be implemented in a way that recognises the realities many residents face day to day.

In my area in England, timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services is often stopped at the door by transport gaps, scarce parking, and squeezed premises. The changes that would help most are a mix of mobile options, local outreach, smarter use of digital means, and sensible incentives to make rural and mobility‑limited access feasible in the long term.

Mobile clinics, outreach and flexible premises: I’d like to see a schedule of roving GP clinics and nurse/health‑visitor teams that visit villages, parish halls or community centres on a rotating timetable. A weekly or fortnightly 3–4 hour slot in a familiar local space can catch up on routine checks, vaccinations, blood pressure monitoring and simple follow‑ups, reducing the need for long drives to the nearest town. In our village, a monthly clinic in the village hall used to exist but was cut due to funding. Reinstating that with a small multidisciplinary team—GP registrar, nurse practitioner and a pharmacist—could make a real difference for older residents and those without cars. For mental health, a visiting outreach team with drop‑in sessions in community venues could help people access support before crises develop.

Parking, access and premises upgrades are also critical. Where premises are crowded or parking is limited, quick capital improvements to add consulting rooms or reconfigure space can extend capacity. In the meantime, pop‑up clinics in community spaces with accessible entrances and drop‑in hours would ease bottlenecks. Free or clearly marked parking near clinic sites and staff parking that doesn’t steal spaces from patients would remove everyday friction that keeps people away.

Telehealth hubs and digital access: A network of telehealth hubs in community centres and libraries—supported by trained staff who can help people book and use video consultations—could enable same‑day triage and reduce unnecessary travel. However, we must avoid leaving people behind who lack devices or reliable broadband. These hubs should come with funding for data vouchers or device lending, plus simple, user‑friendly interfaces and patient support to navigate the system. In practice, a hybrid model, with built‑in in‑person support for those who need it, would be the most inclusive.

Outreach and sustainable pathways: Better coordination with social care, schools and voluntary organisations could identify people facing barriers to access and offer proactive appointments or transport assistance. A modest care‑transport scheme or subsidised taxi vouchers for post‑work or weekend appointments could be piloted in rural pockets with poor bus links. Clear referral and follow‑up pathways would keep people in care closer to home and reduce avoidable hospital visits.

Incentives to improve workforce access: To grow capacity quickly, practice teams need targeted incentives. Extended hours, weekend slots and higher per‑patient funding for remote or rural sites could help attract and retain clinicians. This needs to be paired with practical supports—travel time compensation, parking subsidies, and safe, supported on‑call rotas—to reduce burnout. I welcome the idea of recruiting more widely, including international hires, but it must be paired with rigorous induction, language and communication training, and robust supervision to maintain care quality. Flexible working and wellbeing support for staff are essential, otherwise recruitment habits will not translate into retained teams in rural areas.

Long‑term pipeline: For sustainable expansion of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, we need more training places, return‑to‑practice routes, apprenticeships and accessible CPD. Locally, expanding GP registrar posts and allied health training placements with clinical supervision in or near rural communities would help people establish long‑term roots locally. Online CPD should be available in the evenings or weekends to reduce work‑life conflicts and support staff retention.

Monitoring and equality: Any plan should be piloted with clear metrics—waiting times, travel burden, appointment availability, patient satisfaction and clinical outcomes—and reviewed regularly. It’s vital these improvements do not widen disparities for digitally excluded groups or those with the least transport options.

In short, a coordinated package—mobile and outreach services, smart use of telehealth with real on‑the‑ground support, practical premises and parking improvements, targeted workforce incentives, and a strong training pipeline—would most meaningfully improve timely access for people like me who juggle work, family and health needs. When implemented with local input and robust funding, these steps could transform access in rural and mobility‑limited areas without compromising care quality.

Yes, increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD will grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff sustainably, reducing wait times and improving access in our communities over the long term.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in my area is too inconsistent and often feels like you’re navigating a maze of different services that don’t talk to each other. The changes that would make the biggest difference aren’t just tinkering at the edges; they require a re-think of how local health care is organised and funded. - Co-located hubs as the default model: When primary care, mental health and community services sit alongside social care and VCSE partners, referrals are faster and information flows better. - Transport, parking and premises deficits addressed with mobile and outreach work: In rural or mobility‑limited areas, getting to a clinic can take hours or be impossible if buses stop early. Mobile clinics that visit villages, housing estates and university halls on a rotating schedule would bring general practice, nursing care and mental health check-ins to people’s doorsteps or nearby venues. Outreach teams in schools, colleges and community centres could run drop-in sessions for quick health checks, vaccinations, contraception advice, or early mental health support, with same-day triage to longer-term care if needed.

- Telehealth hubs as a bridge, not a substitute: Telehealth should complement physical services, not replace them. This would be especially helpful for students and young people who can’t afford frequent travel or who have tight timetables. - Incentives and workforce planning to sustain access: Rural and mobility‑limited communities often lose flexible staff due to workload, long commutes, or limited career development. Clear career pathways and support for cross-disciplinary roles would also help reduce bureaucratic delays when a patient needs input from multiple services.

- Practical constraints and safeguards: Any rollout must include careful planning around data sharing with consent, privacy in telehealth settings, and patient choice. People must be able to opt into integrated care when they want it and opt out if they prefer single-service access. I’d want to see performance dashboards that show wait times, out-of-hours access, and patient satisfaction broken down by area, so we can spot gaps quickly and fix them.

In short, timely access won’t improve just by more appointments in the same old format. It requires creating connected, flexible, local care ecosystems where GP, community health, mental health, social care and the VCSE sector work together with a clear, user-friendly pathway for people in every part of England, including rural and mobility‑restricted communities. I’m convinced these changes would reduce delays, improve outcomes for young people, and make health services feel more responsive and humane. I’d urge the government to fund and pilot this integrated, hub-based model with strong community involvement and transparent evaluation so we can learn what works best and scale it quickly where it’s needed most.
