A PRACTICAL APPROACH WOULD BE TO OFFER A “DIGITAL ACCESS SUPPORT” SERVICE IN LOCAL HUBS OR LIBRARIES, WHERE TRAINED STAFF CAN HELP PATIENTS SET UP ACCOUNTS, BOOK APPOINTMENTS OR USE E‑CONSULTS WITHOUT FEAR OF BEING JUDGED FOR UNFAMILIAR TECH.

EQUITY MUST BE AT THE HEART OF THIS REFORM. THAT MEANS TARGETED RESOURCES, INTERPRETERS AND CULTURALLY COMPETENT STAFF TO CLOSE GAPS FOR DEPRIVED COMMUNITIES, ETHNIC MINORITIES, MIGRANTS AND MARGINALISED GROUPS. IN SOME COMMUNITIES WE RELY ON ENGLISH‑ONLY INFORMATION THAT MISSES PEOPLE WHO COULD BENEFIT MOST FROM TIMELY CARE. I’D LIKE TO SEE INTERPRETERS AVAILABLE ACROSS GP PRACTICES AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES, TRANSLATED APPOINTMENT REMINDERS, AND MATERIALS ABOUT HOW TO ACCESS HELP IN MULTIPLE LANGUAGES. OUTREACH TEAMS SHOULD WORK WITH SCHOOLS, COMMUNITY CENTRES, FAITH GROUPS AND HOUSING ASSOCIATIONS TO RAISE AWARENESS ABOUT AVAILABLE SERVICES AND TO NORMALIZE SEEKING HELP EARLY, BEFORE PROBLEMS ESCALATE. IT WOULD HELP TO HAVE COMMUNITY‑BASED CLINICS OR MOBILE SERVICES IN AREAS WITH HIGH DEPRIVATION OR WHERE TRANSPORT IS A BARRIER, SO PEOPLE DON’T WAIT UNTIL CRISES TO SEEK SUPPORT. STAFF TRAINING IN CULTURAL COMPETENCE AND TRAUMA‑INFORMED CARE SHOULD BE ONGOING, NOT A ONE‑OFF COURSE.

TO SUSTAIN THESE IMPROVEMENTS, WE NEED A LONG‑TERM WORKFORCE STRATEGY. INCREASING TRAINING PLACES, RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE SUPPORTS, APPRENTICESHIPS AND CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT FOR GPS, NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS IS ESSENTIAL. IN NORTHERN IRELAND WE’VE SEEN HOW SHORTAGES BITE WHEN STAFF LEAVE OR BURN OUT. EXPANDING MEDICAL AND NURSING DEGREE PLACES, OFFERING FUNDED RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE SCHEMES FOR THOSE WHO PAUSED THEIR CAREERS, AND CREATING APPRENTICESHIPS FOR HEALTHCARE ASSISTANTS WHO CAN PROGRESS INTO NURSING OR ALLIED HEALTH ROLES WOULD HELP BUILD A STABLE PIPELINE. IT’S ALSO IMPORTANT TO IMPROVE WORKING CONDITIONS AND ADMINISTRATIVE SUPPORT SO CLINICIANS CAN SPEND MORE TIME WITH PATIENTS RATHER THAN CHASING PAPERWORK. ENCOURAGING DUAL‑TRAINING PATHWAYS – FOR EXAMPLE, BRINGING MORE NURSE PRACTITIONERS OR MENTAL HEALTH SPECIALISTS INTO PRIMARY CARE ROLES – COULD DRAMATICALLY IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS.

FROM PERSONAL EXPERIENCE, I’VE FACED DELAYS IN MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT FOR A FAMILY MEMBER AND SEEN HOW EVEN SMALL CHANGES IN BOOKING FLOW CAN MAKE A DIFFERENCE. A SYSTEM THAT TRIAGES EFFECTIVELY, OFFERS PROMPT CONTACT OPTIONS, AND FOLLOWS UP WITH CLEAR INSTRUCTIONS WOULD REDUCE ANXIETY AND PREVENT CRISES. I’VE ALSO OBSERVED THAT WHEN LOCAL PRACTICES COLLABORATE WITH COMMUNITY GROUPS, LANGUAGE SERVICES AND SCHOOLS, FAMILIES FEEL MORE CONFIDENT ABOUT SEEKING HELP EARLY RATHER THAN WAITING UNTIL PROBLEMS BECOME SEVERE.

IN SHORT, THE CHANGES THAT WILL IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS ARE MULTI‑LAYERED: A STRONG DIGITAL PATHWAY WITH GENUINE NON‑DIGITAL BACKUPS, A FOCUS ON EQUITY AND COMMUNITY OUTREACH, AND A LONG‑TERM INVESTMENT IN THE WORKFORCE. IF IMPLEMENTED TOGETHER, THESE STEPS COULD DELIVER FASTER GP AND COMMUNITY HEALTH RESPONSES, BETTER MENTAL HEALTH ACCESS, AND A HEALTHIER, MORE INCLUSIVE NI.

In my area, improved timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will probably hinge on a blended approach that keeps continuity of care for complex or vulnerable patients while freeing up general practice to handle routine needs through multidisciplinary support and more flexible hours. I’m balanced on this because I’ve seen the benefits of longer, person-centred visits for people with chronic illness, but I also recognise the efficiency of well-supported teams taking on routine tasks.

First, protecting continuity of care for complex cases is essential. For patients with multiple chronic conditions or mental health comorbidities, a single named clinician who coordinates the plan reduces confusion and prevents repetitive testing or conflicting advice. In practice this would mean longer appointment times for tracking conditions such as diabetes, COPD, heart disease or severe anxiety, rather than squeezing a lot of information into a 10–15 minute slot. For example, when my neighbour with diabetes and depression saw the same clinician over several months, they could review meds, monitor blood pressure, and adjust mental health support in one go, which helped avoid non-urgent hospital visits. I’d like to see more 20–30 minute slots reserved for complex cases and a system to ensure patients can consistently see their named clinician, with shared access to an up-to-date care plan across general practice, community services and mental health.

Second, expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs for complex care. I’m not against team-based care; I’m concerned about turning GP clinics into hand-offs without good supervision. A pharmacist embedded in primary care, for instance, can routinely review medications, catch interactions, and provide dose adjustments for older patients or those starting new therapies. A physiotherapist-led triage for musculoskeletal issues could sort out back and joint pain without a GP appointment, reducing wait times and giving patients exercise-based care earlier. Paramedics or physician associates could support home visits or urgent triage, freeing GPs to focus on higher-risk patients. In pilot settings elsewhere, this approach tends to lower GP workload while maintaining safety and patient satisfaction, though it must be accompanied by clear supervision, robust training, and strong pathways back to the GP when complexity rises. The key is seamless handovers and patient choice—people must feel they can still see their GP if they want or need to.

Third, extend access through evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. Working people and those with care commitments can struggle to fit appointments into standard hours, so protected late slots and weekend clinics would make a real difference. Likewise, guaranteed same-day urgent slots for non-emergency concerns would prevent escalation and reduce pressure on urgent care services. In my view, triage must be clear: if someone needs a same-day appointment, they should get it, with a rapid path to in-person or video consultation as appropriate. I’ve also found remote and digital options helpful, but they must be paired with real-time access to a clinician when a physical check is needed, particularly for mental health concerns where timing can be critical.

Finally, there needs to be solid implementation and monitoring. Adequate funding, protected training time for new roles, and shared digital records are essential to avoid fragmentation. Local workforce planning should ensure there are enough pharmacists, physios, paramedics and physician associates, with clear career ladders and supervision. I’d also welcome stronger links between GP practices, community services and schools or workplaces to promote early help for mental health and social determinants of health.

In short, timely access will improve if we keep continuity for complex patients, responsibly expand multidisciplinary teams for routine care, and offer extended hours with guaranteed urgent access. A cautious, well-resourced rollout that preserves patient choice and safety would, I believe, deliver better outcomes and fewer repeat visits without overburdening already stretched general practice.

Expansion of online booking and telehealth must not exclude older or rural patients; protect continuity with longer, in-person GP and mental health slots and fund mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs for transport-poor areas.
Long waits are worrying, but I’d value more community support—friendly visits, volunteers, and better transport to town—to help older folk stay healthy at home.

I strongly support changes to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and simplify patient flow. In practice, this would cut duplication and confusion for people trying to access GP, community and mental health srrvices. For example, last winter my family member had a high fever and we found booking a routine GP slot slow. Using NHS111 triage, we were directed to urgent care, and the clinician arranged a same-day appointment.. The triage questions helped asses severity early, which felt safer and quicker. A more integrated online booking system that shares triage notes and appointment availability across NHS111, GP practices and community teams would prevent repeated forms and multiple calls. Trained care navigators could guide patients to the right service—urgent GP slots, same-day mental health access, or community nursing—without jumping between systems. This would particularly help in rural or underserviced areas where gaps are felt most. If we could also track outcomes to confirm urgent cases aren’t delayed, the whole system would feel more reliable and less stressfu for families and individuals alike.
Agree. Implementing evening and weekend GP clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would improve timely access for working people and those with urgent, non-emergency needs.

Support improving NHS111 and triage to prioritise urgent cases, streamline bookings, and reduce duplicate steps; plus targeted outreach and interpreters to close gaps for minority and deprived groups, ensuring culturally competent staff and easier navigation.

Yes, expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care would improve timely access, and I’d ensure non‑digital options and support are available so older or less tech‑savvy patients aren’t left behind.

Agree. In my area in England, getting timely GP appointments can be tough, andd mental health slots are often scarce. To improve access, I’d welcome increasing appointment slots across GP,, nurse and therapist services by hiring more staff, expandin session capacity, and making scheduling more efficient so cancellations and overflow bookings are quickly filled. For example, last month I waitedd two weeks for a routine GP appointment, and the earliest slot after work hours was only available weeks later. A nurse appointment when a minor issue arose helped, but that was a stopgap rather than a systemic change. Targeted recruitment and internationa hiring could plug shortages faster: offering competitive pay, clear progression, flexible hours and wellbeing support would help retain staff. A colleague at a local practice described burnout from long shifts; better rotas and mental health support would matter. Finally, evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help those who work full-time. If clinics offered late sessions a couple of days a week and reserved urgent slots, I’d be more likely to seek help early rather than delay care.

i really think timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential, especially for someone like me who has multiple health concerns and mobility constraints. In our area, GP appointments can be hard to come by within a reasonable time—often two weeks or more—and waiting lists for mental health support can be lengthy. To genuinely improve access, we should increase appointment capacity by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, and extend consultation times for complex or chronic conditions. Rushing through consultations leads to missed symptoms and more trips back to the practice, which is tiring and distressing for older patients.

I support evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. This would help working people and those with non-emergency but urgent needs who can’t easily attend during the week. A few neighbours have missed opportunities after work or school, and weekend or late slots would make a real difference for check-ins, medication reviews, or mental health support without waiting weeks.

Crucially, protect continuity of care. For those of us with long-term conditions, seeing the same clinician whenever possible and having a bit longer appointment time can improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. I also want accessible booking options—phone lines and simple local booking hubs alongside online systems—so older residents who are less comfortable with digital tools aren’t left out.

Finally, any expansion must be monitored with waiting-time targets and patient feedback to ensure real improvements rather than delayed promises!

As a Welsh organisation, I disagree with proposals that rely mainly on targeted resources, interpreters and outreach, and on expanding multidisciplinary teams to fix timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. These measures matter, but without a solid, well-funded workforce plan they’ll only patch symptoms. In our area, language support is inconsistent; families report booking delays for interpreters, causing missed or late appointments and, in turn, deteriorating health. An outreach project in deprived communities showed short-term gains but couldn’t be sustained due to limited hours and funding, so gaps quickly reopen. Expanding teams like pharmacists or physiotherapists can help, but if routines aren’t integrated with clear referral routes and data-sharing, patients endure longer total times to see a clinician for complex needs. We also see that after-hours access remains a barrier for many workers and carers in Wales, which popularised triage by non-GP staff but didn’t resolve core shortages.
The core fix must be: a secure, long-term investment in GP capacity, robust interpreter services with guaranteed availability, and strong, system-wide pathways linking primary care, community services and mental health, so everyone can get timely help from the right professional. This requires sustained funding and governance, not just new roles.

Expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care would significantly improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services in our area. Online booking makes it easier to grab a slot quickly, and short e-consults can triage issues so urgent matters get seen faster without a full clinic visit. I've found online booking and brief video chats with my GP nurse very efficient for repeat prescriptions and minor concerns, often arranging same-day or next-day contact that avoided multiple trips.

For mental health, a quick online form followed by a short video session can reduce waiting times and stigma, and remote care is invaluable for people balancing work or caring responsibilities. In my street, though, I've seen neighbours struggle with digital access, so we must provide non-digital routes: a reliable phone line with extended hours, in-person triage clinics, and staff who can help people sign up for online services at libraries or community centres. Training, simpler interfaces and interpreter support would also help.

With these safeguards, we can improve timeliness without leaving anyone behind.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a real challenge in my area. I would support changes that widen both hours and formats, while ensuring no one is left behind.

Clarity and reliability of evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would make a big difference for working people and for urgent but non‑emergency needs. For example, last year a family member developed a sudden chest‑tightening sensation after work; if there had been a guaranteed same‑day slot at a local practice, we could have avoided a long wait or an unnecessary trip to urgent care. Consistent late slots across practices would also reduce staff absences and help people manage persistent conditions without taking multiple days off.

Second, expand online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, but maintain non‑digital routes and support. Remote options save travel time and can speed up routine triage, yet not everyone has reliable internet or is comfortable with online forms. Providing telephone, in‑person triage and clear help to navigate between channels is essential, especially for older or disadvantaged patients. For mental health, faster access to counselling or drop‑in slots would prevent crises.

Finally, invest in staff and transparent wait‑time data so patients can plan and services can be steadier.

i really think transport, parking and the condition of premises are real obstacles for many older people in rural or mobility‑limited situations. I would favour a mixed approach: mobile clinics and regular outreach to villages, plus telehealth hubs in community spaces, with practical staff support to help those less confident with technology. A weekly village clinic or nurse‑led visits could cut long journeys and missed appointments; telehealth sessions in local libraries or church halls, staffed by someone who can assist patients with devices and set‑ups, would help when travel isn’t possible. Yet we must guard against digital exclusion and ensure there are options for those without reliable internet.

I also see value in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, community and mental health services together with social care and VCSE partners. In our area a pilot hub reduced fragmented referrals and allowed a single point of contact for transport, housing and wellbeing needs, but it needs stable funding and clear governance to avoid patchy availability across towns.

To make this work, offer incentives for rural practice: flexible contracts, housing or relocation allowances, and protected time for outreach. Invest in parking and accessible premises, and provide digital‑skills support so that telehealth truly enhances timely access rather than leaving older residents behind!

From where I live in England, the proposed changes to improve timely access sound sensible in theory, but they won’t deliver reliably without proper funding and workforce planning. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine cases—could free GPs for complex care, but only if there’s consistent supervision, clear pathways, and decent pay so those professionals stay in primary care. In my area, routine physio and medication reviews are already delayed because staff are stretched thin; without strong governance and integrated IT, patients risk variable quality and needless referrals.

Expanding online booking and remote care helps some families, yet it’s not universal. My elderly neighbour and a friend without reliable internet can’t rely on apps or web triage. We must keep non-digital options: phone triage with trained staff, same-day in-person slots, and accessible interpreter services. Digital access must not become the gatekeeper to services.

Targeted resources for deprived and ethnic minority groups are essential, but they must be backed by genuine outreach, culturally competent staff and flexible hours. Token gestures won’t close gaps if clinics are still hard to reach after dark or on weekends. Overall, this needs sustained investment in staffing, training and locally coordinated service delivery, not just new formats.

absolutely i fully support expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people who work and have urgent non‑emergency needs. To improve timeliness, please expand evening and weekend clinics and guarantee a same‑day urgent slot for non‑emergency issues. As a working individual, daytime appointments are often impossible; I’ve had to take a day off or wait weeks for a standard GP visit, which is stressful and unhelpful. In my area, a practice trialling Wednesday evenings until 8pm and Saturday morning slots has made it much easier to get seen without disrupting work, and it has reduced last‑minute calls to urgent care. For urgent mental health concerns, a guaranteed same‑day slot would make a real difference, preventing escalation and hospital visits. Clear online booking that shows available urgent slots and a straightforward triage process would help planning too. If general practices are supported to extend hours and run flexible clinics, it will ease pressures on A&E and community services while ensuring people get timely care when they need it.

I welcome the government’s focus on making access to GP services, community health and mental health support more timely. In England, the delays many of us have faced are not only frustrating, they affect people’s wellbeing and day-to-day lives. I believe a mix of expanded community teams, smarter GP capacity and a stronger primary care workforce is the right way forward. Here are the changes I think would make the biggest difference, with examples from my own area and daily life.

- Expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies
  - Early help reduces the risk of crisis and long-term problems. If we had bigger, well-resourced community mental health teams offering quick access to talking therapies and evidence-based early intervention for anxiety, depression and stress, people wouldn’t wait until things feel unbearable before they get support.
  - A dedicated crisis response service that can visit people at home, 24/7, would prevent avoidable admissions and keep people connected to their families. In my neighbourhood, when a friend hit a mental health crisis, the absence of an immediate community option left them with few alternatives besides a trip to A&E, which isn’t always the best place for complex mental health care.
  - Practical access to talking therapies, including cognitive behavioural therapy and guided self-help, should be available quickly, with small-step, low-intensity options for those who don’t need long-term therapy. This would help restore parity with physical health where people expect timely treatment for conditions like heartburn or back pain.
  - Local co-ordination between mental health teams, social care and voluntary sector services would streamline care plans and avoid fragmented support.

- Increase GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots and session capacity through hiring, expansion and smarter scheduling
  - More appointment slots and longer or more flexible sessions for complex cases would reduce bottlenecks. This could include extending GP practice hours into evenings and Saturdays, more nurse-led clinics for minor illnesses and chronic disease management, and more slots for therapists (counsellors, psychologists, physiotherapists) in the same practice or local hubs.
  - A tiered triage system with trained nurses and physician associates handling initial assessments could free GPs to focus on the more complex cases, while still ensuring patients get a same- or next-day slot when needed.
  - Group and nurse-led appointments for routine issues (medication reviews, wellness checks, vaccination clinics) would free GP time for new or urgent concerns.
  - Increasing flexibility in scheduling, such as same-day bookings, online triage with rapid follow-up slots, and choice between phone/video and in-person visits, would help people get timely help without overwhelming staff.
  - Practical examples: in my area, walk-in or same-day slots are limited, and many people have to wait weeks for a GP appointment. Expanding session capacity and smarter scheduling would close that gap and reduce the pressure on urgent care pathways.

- Targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff
  - To sustain the improvements above, we need a robust plan to grow the workforce. This includes targeted recruitment campaigns, more flexible working patterns, and better pay and workload protections to prevent burnout.
  - International recruitment can help fill vacancies faster, provided there is clear orientation, safeguarding and professional development so new staff can integrate quickly and provide high-quality care.
  - Incentives such as relocation support, sign-on bonuses for hard-to-staff areas, and career development pathways (including practice-based training for nurse associates and physician associates) would attract and retain talent.
  - Flexible working arrangements, wellbeing support, and supervised professional development are essential to keep staff motivated and reduce turnover. A supported workforce translates directly into shorter waits for patients.
  - In addition, better workforce planning at the local level—mapping demand, identifying gaps and coordinating between GP practices, CCGs and Local Authorities—would prevent repeated shortages in the same areas.

- Practical delivery and safeguards
  - Any expansion must be coupled with clear quality standards, robust data sharing and strong safeguarding practices, so rapid access does not compromise patient safety.
  - Investments should be matched by digital improvements: improved online booking, real-time wait-time dashboards, and seamless electronic health records that allow clinicians to see a patient’s full history and current needs across primary and community care.
  - Local hubs that house GPs, nurses, therapists and community teams in close proximity would make it easier for patients to get everything they need in one place, rather than bouncing between services.

If these steps are implemented well, we’ll see shorter waits for GP and therapist appointments, faster access to mental health support, and better early intervention that reduces crises and hospital admissions. Most importantly, people will feel that mental and physical health are treated with equal urgency and respect, not as an afterthought. I want to see a health system where I can book a same-day GP slot when I’m unwell, access timely talking therapy if I’m struggling, and rely on a well-supported community mental health team to help maintain my wellbeing before things escalate. That’s not just better for individuals; it’s better for families, communities and the NHS as a whole.

Overall, I support these changes and believe a combined push on expanding mental health services, boosting primary care capacity, and building a sustainable workforce is the right approach to improve timely access across the board.

Boost timely access by growing the workforce—targeted recruitment, international hires, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support—while expanding online booking and remote care, but maintaining non-digital options so older or disadvantaged patients aren’t left behind.

I’m responding as someone living in England who wants better, fairer access to GP, community health and mental health services. I don’t think the immediate push towards online booking, e‑consultations and remote care on its own will reliably improve timely access for everyone. Digital options can help some people, but they risk leaving behind others who already struggle to get an appointment or to navigate digital tools. The changes that would really help in my area need to be balanced with strong non‑digital support and clear, easy access routes for those who can’t or won’t use online services.

What worries me most is the digital divide. My own family members include an older relative who still mainly uses a landline and paper reminders. They’re not comfortable with apps or chat functions, and their broadband is inconsistent in the evenings. In practice, when the GP promotes online booking as the fastest route, it often fails them: the online slots are not available, pages crash, or you’re stuck in an endlessly looping queue. I’ve tried booking same‑day online for a minor issue and found it almost impossible to secure a slot; I ended up on hold for 15–20 minutes and still had to book a day later. An elderly neighbour who recently needed urgent attention couldn’t make sense of the online system at all and had to rely on a family member to phone through and advocate on their behalf.

Even when online access works for some, there are real limits with e‑consultations and remote care. Some problems genuinely need a physical check, a quick examination, or the reassurance of a face‑to‑face conversation. With mental health services in particular, I’ve seen situations where a video call just doesn’t capture someone’s distress or provide the level of rapport you get in person. Missing non‑verbal cues or the ability to sense a person’s body language can slow down accurate assessment and timely escalation to urgent help. And for people living in crowded or shared housing, privacy during a remote appointment isn’t guaranteed, which can deter honest discussion about sensitive issues.

There’s also the practical reality of capacity. A lot of clinics now push to a digital‑first model, but the infrastructure across practices isn’t consistent. Some surgeries have robust online booking and rapid e‑consult responses; others are still overwhelmed, with long delays to even get through on the phone. If the aim is to reduce wait times, the system must not penalise patients who can’t or won’t use digital channels. We need a safety net: a clearly advertised, reliable telephone line with short wait times, walk‑in options for urgent cases, and same‑day appointments where possible, including in mental health teams.

What changes would actually improve timely access, in my view?

- Keep multiple booking channels: online, phone, and in‑person front desk/phone triage. No one channel should become the gatekeeper for access.
- Ensure truly available same‑day appointments across GP, community health and mental health services, with proactive allocation of slots for those with urgent needs.
- Invest in digital inclusion: free and easy access to public Wi‑Fi in libraries and GP surgeries, digital‑skills drop‑ins at community hubs, and staff or volunteers to help people book or use remote services. Consider “digital champions” in local communities who can assist vulnerable residents.
- Provide robust non‑digital alternatives alongside digital ones: clear instructions, interpreter and advocacy support, and guaranteed access to a real person who can book or triage on the patient’s behalf.
- Improve the quality of remote care when it is used: establish clear criteria for when a video/phone consult is appropriate, and ensure easy escalation to in‑person care if symptoms don’t improve or concerns remain.
- Address equity and transparency: publish regional wait times, capacity, and access data so communities can see how well services are meeting needs and where gaps lie.

In short, I’m not against digital options. I am against a one‑size‑fits‑all approach that assumes everyone can or wants to go online. The goal should be timely access for all, which means preserving non‑digital access routes, investing in digital inclusion, and designing digital services that genuinely complement, rather than replace, face‑to‑face care. If those protections are put in place, expanding online booking and e‑consultations could be part of a broader, fairer system.

I strongly support the proposed changes to expand community mental health teams, strengthen early intervention, improve crisis response, and widen access to talking therapies. These steps would help reduce waits and bring mental health care closer to parity with physical health in our area. In practice, I’ve seen people waiting weeks for CBT or for a same-day appointment after a crisis. A more integrated community team with rapid assessment, home-visit options, and stronger links with schools and workplaces would make care more accessible and prevent crises from escalating. More flexible therapy pathways, including in-person and online options, would fit busy lives.

On staffing, we need targeted recruitment and retention: international recruitment, better pay and progression, flexible hours, reasonable workloads, and robust wellbeing support. In my experience, staff burnout feeds long waits and lower quality care; stable, well-supported teams would mean patients get timely help and GPs can focus on preventive and holistic care rather than chasing referrals.

Supportive: recruit and retain primary care staff with targeted incentives, international hiring, better pay and flexible, wellbeing‑focused roles; fund co‑located hubs uniting primary, community and mental health with social care partners; widen online booking and e‑consults while offering non‑digital options.

DISAGREE: THE CHANGES THAT WOULD MOST IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS ARE NOT QUICK FIXES LIKE EXTRA APPOINTMENT SLOTS ALONE. THE REAL, LASTING IMPROVEMENT WILL COME FROM GROWING THE WORKFORCE SUSTAINABLY THROUGH TRAINING, RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SUPPORT, APPRENTICESHIPS AND CPD. IN MY AREA, I SEE WAIT TIMES FOR GPS AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES STRETCHING OUT; SHORT-TERM HIRES HELP A BIT, BUT THEY DON’T FIX THE UNDERLYING SHORTAGES OR SKILL MIX.

IF WE EXPAND TRAINING PLACES FOR GPS, NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS, WE CREATE A BIGGER PIPELINE THAT CAN FILL VACANCIES AS COLLEAGUES MOVE ON. RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE PROGRAMMES ARE ESSENTIAL FOR BRINGING SKILLED CLINICIANS BACK AFTER CAREER BREAKS, WITH REFRESHED TRAINING TO MATCH CURRENT PRACTICE. APPRENTICESHIPS OFFER ROUTES INTO CARE ROLES FOR LOCAL PEOPLE WHO MIGHT NOT GO TO UNIVERSITY, PROVIDING A CLEAR PATH TO QUALIFIED STAFF WHO STAY LONG-TERM. CPD KEEPS SKILLS UP TO DATE SO NEW THERAPIES AND DIGITAL TOOLS CAN BE USED SAFELY IN PRIMARY AND COMMUNITY CARE.

FOR EXAMPLE, A LOCAL PRACTICE COULD RUN A NURSING ASSOCIATE APPRENTICESHIP THAT CULMINATES IN REGISTERED NURSE STATUS, BACKED BY A FUNDED RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE ROUTE FOR CLINICIANS WHO PAUSED DURING THE PANDEMIC. WITH SUSTAINED INVESTMENT IN TRAINING AND PROGRESSION, ACCESS BECOMES TIMELIER AND MORE RELIABLE, RATHER THAN A SERIES OF STOP‑GAP STAFFING BURSTS.

From a working‑adult perspective in England, I would welcome evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. When I needed a same‑day appointment for a non‑emergency issue last winter, the earliest slot offered was days away, which caused worry and potentially risk for someone with mounting stress. Extended hours would make GP, community health and mental health services genuinely accessible for families and night‑shift workers.

Continuity of care matters. For my mother, who has diabetes and depression, seeing the same clinician and having longer appointments reduces the need for multiple visits and helps us manage meds and side effects more safely. Longer slots for complex cases support better outcomes and fewer repeat visits.

I also back expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, which save time and cut queues. Yet non‑digital options should remain: a phone line and in‑person slots with staff to help those with limited digital skills or elderly relatives. A flexible, mixed model would genuinely improve timely access while protecting those who need a slower pace of care.

I’d prioritise longer, continuity-led GP appointments for those with chronic conditions and vulnerable patients to reduce repeats, while also boosting training, return-to-practice and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health staff to sustain timely access long term.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains a real concern. I support targeted changes that build capacity for the long term: expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals; and increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots through hiring, session expansion and smarter scheduling. In practice, more clinicians and longer slots for complex or chronic conditions would reduce repeat visits and hospital admissions. For example, my relative has a chronic condition and benefits when they can see the same clinician for 30-minute slots, rather than rushed 10-minute check-ins. Expanding mental health therapy slots and offering flexible options (video/phone) would shorten waits and prevent crises. Protecting continuity of care by ensuring patients see the same clinician where possible, and lengthening appointment times for vulnerable patients, would markedly improve outcomes. These changes feel achievable with a clear pipeline from training to practice, and would make care more responsive for families like mine.

Address access gaps with targeted funding for deprived and minority communities, including interpreters and culturally competent staff; overhaul NHS111 and booking for urgent cases; rely less on generic recruitment and instead recruit internationally, improve pay and flexible hours to retain staff.

absolutely i do not believe that simply increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots will reliably improve timely access. In our area the real hurdle is staffing; there are not enough GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists to fill even the larger number of slots. Without addressing recruitment, retention and workload, more slots will quickly be taken up by backlogged cases or cancelled, and patients will still struggle to get urgent or same-day appointments. For example, when a pilot to extend GP hours was run locally, nearly all additional slots went unfilled by patients who couldn't get transport or who preferred daytime visits, while existing waiting times for routine care remained long. Mental health services illustrate the same issue: weeks or months of waiting for a therapy slot despite longer hours on offer. What would help more: targeted workforce expansion and better pay and progression for nurses, therapists and GPs; more multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, social prescribers, physios); robust same-day triage; smarter scheduling; and reliable digital access. Also track outcomes, not just numbers of slots. Without these changes, simply adding slots risks superficial improvements at best!

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I strongly support expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care. Embedding pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates in GP practices can handle routine issues—medication reviews, minor infections, musculoskeletal problems, and simple follow-ups—leaving GPs free to focus on more complex cases. In Northern Ireland, this approach would mean a quick, appropriate assessment for a sprain or a medicine review by the right professional, reducing delays waiting for a GP appointment.

I also back improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation. A streamlined triage process that directs urgent cases to the correct clinician and offers same-day or next-day slots would cut duplication and confusion. Clear, user-friendly booking and better care navigation would help families balance work, school runs and caring responsibilities. Personally, I’ve experienced delays when trying to access mental health support; earlier identification and faster routing to talking therapies or community services would make a real difference.

Overall, these changes would improve patient flow, lower GP backlogs, and ensure urgent needs are met promptly, while still safeguarding complex care.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area could be improved most by protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. In our organisation we regularly see patients with multimorbidity who must recount history to multiple clinicians, which leads to missed signs, medication errors and avoidable visits. A recent example involved a patient with diabetes, anxiety and heart disease who saw three GPs in four weeks; the lack of a stable care relationship delayed adjustments to their treatment and increased stress.

Proposed changes:
- Guarantee a named clinician for ongoing care and share a patient-centred care plan across the team.
- Extend standard GP appointments to 15 minutes, with 20-30 minutes for mental health reviews and any multi-morbidity case.
- Build stronger multidisciplinary teams in primary care (nurses, pharmacists, social workers) to coordinate care and reduce fragmentation.
- Ensure flexible, longer slots and reserve time specifically for complex cases, including same-week follow-ups when risk is high.
- Improve triage and booking so complex cases aren’t bounced between services; use digital pre-visit questionnaires and remote monitoring to cut unnecessary visits.
- Track continuity and outcomes; fund improvements tied to reductions in repeat visits and urgent referrals.

This would be my organisation’s priority to deliver safer, more effective care.

I STRONGLY AGREE THAT EXPANDING MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS (PHARMACISTS, PHYSIOTHERAPISTS, PARAMEDICS AND PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES) WITHIN GP PRACTICES WOULD SIGNIFICANTLY IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES. IN OUR AREA, ROUTINE CONCERNS LIKE BACK PAIN, SKIN INFECTIONS OR SIMPLE MEDICATION QUERIES OFTEN LEAD TO GP SLOTS FILLED FOR DAYS. IF A PHARMACIST-LED TRIAGE OR A PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATE CLINIC COULD ASSESS AND MANAGE THESE CASES, GP TIME WOULD BE FREED FOR MORE COMPLEX PROBLEMS. I’VE SEEN A NEIGHBOUR WITH PERSISTENT KNEE PAIN BENEFIT FROM AN IN-PRACTICE PHYSIO ASSESSMENT THAT PRODUCED A CLEAR EXERCISE PLAN AND REDUCED THE NEED FOR REPEATED DOCTOR VISITS. A PARAMEDIC-LED HOME VISIT COULD CHECK SOMEONE AFTER A MINOR FALL OR COUGH, PREVENTING UNNECESSARY TRIPS TO URGENT CARE. FOR MENTAL HEALTH, SHORT-ACCESS SESSIONS WITH A WELLBEING PRACTITIONER WITHIN THE TEAM COULD CATCH MILD CONCERNS EARLY AND SIGNPOST TO LONGER-TERM SUPPORT WHEN NEEDED. OF COURSE, ROBUST REFERRAL PATHWAYS AND CLEAR ESCALATION RULES WOULD BE ESSENTIAL IF RED FLAGS APPEAR. OVERALL, THESE CHANGES WOULD SPEED UP ACCESS, REDUCE PRESSURE ON GPS, AND KEEP PEOPLE SAFER AND BETTER SUPPORTED IN THE COMMUNITY.

From where I sit in England, the priority must be to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic, or vulnerable needs. Quick online bookings and short slots may seem convenient, but they often exclude older people like me or my neighbours who struggle with digital tools and need time to explain multiple health issues. In my area, a neighbour with COPD and arthritis sees the same GP every six weeks; when appointments are rushed, small changes go unnoticed and we end up with unnecessary hospital visits. Telehealth can help some, but must be paired with non-digital options—easy phone access, walk-in slots, and in-person clinics for those who can’t use apps. Mental health services suffer similarly when brief calls replace longer, continuous contact with a familiar clinician. We also need interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to deprived communities; language barriers and distrust can delay treatment. Invest in longer consultations, stable GP teams, and targeted outreach; only then will timely access improve for everyone, not just the digitally advantaged.

Expand multidisciplinary teams of pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to manage routine cases, freeing GPs for complex care; pair this with robust handovers, sustainable funding, and local oversight to protect continuity and mental health access.

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute. We are a community-focused organisation operating across England, concerned with how people access GP, community health and mental health services. I strongly support the proposed changes to expand community mental health teams, bolster early intervention, enhance crisis response and widen access to talking therapies. Doing so would reduce waits, prevent crises from escalating, and move us closer to parity between mental and physical health in everyday care.

What would help most to improve timely access in our area:

- Expand and strengthen community mental health teams (CMHTs): Increase multidisciplinary staffing that includes psychiatrists, mental health nurses, psychologists, social workers, occupational therapists and peer support workers. Place CMHTs closer to GP practices and in places people already use, so referrals and assessments happen quickly. Guarantee same-week initial assessments where there are urgent concerns and ensure regular follow-ups within a clearly defined timetable. In our area, people often wait several weeks for an initial CMHT assessment after a GP referral; expanding teams would cut these waits and build continuity of care.

- Speed up early intervention and prevention: Prioritise timely access to Early Intervention in Psychosis and other early-diagnosis pathways. Establish a standard where GP referrals are acknowledged within 48 hours and a formal assessment occurs within two weeks. Provide gatekeeping support for GPs with streamlined referral criteria and clear care pathways so people with emerging symptoms receive appropriate help before crises develop.

- Strengthen crisis response and crisis home treatment: Invest in 24/7 crisis lines and mobile crisis teams that can respond rapidly, ideally within two hours in urban areas and within a reasonable timeframe in rural settings. Ensure these teams are integrated with A&E and CMHTs so people can remain at home safely whenever possible, with hospital-based care reserved for when it’s necessary. We’ve heard from families in our networks that crisis responses can be uneven in response time; consistent, rapid access would prevent preventable admissions and support families better.

- Expand access to talking therapies and stepped-care options: Increase capacity for evidence-based talking therapies (CBT, ACT, IPT, counselling) and offer flexible delivery (in-person, video, and phone). Prioritise low- or no-wait pathways, with clear indications for stepping up or down care based on need. For many, digital or blended provision could make a real difference in rural or work-paced populations, provided it’s clinically appropriate and well-supported by practitioners. Continuity is key: ensure patients do not get lost between services during referral and treatment transitions.

- Improve access within GP services: Offer same-day or next-day mental health appointments through primary care and triage-dedicated slots for urgent mental health concerns. Create faster referral routes from GP to CMHTs and to talking-therapy services. Expand daytime and evening GP access so people can seek help during working hours or after work when symptoms escalate.

- Invest in integrated and co-located services: Co-locate CMHTs, community health teams and GP practices where possible, with shared care plans and common IT systems (with patient consent). This reduces duplicated assessments, speeds up decision-making, and improves information sharing for safer, more holistic care.

- Focus on workforce and retention: Invest in training, recruitment and retention schemes for mental health staff. Support career development, offer better workloads, and provide mental health support for staff themselves. A stable, well-supported workforce is essential to maintaining timely access over time.

- Address rural and digital divides: Use telemedicine where appropriate but ensure digital access doesn’t replace personal contact where it’s needed. Mobile clinics and community hubs can reach people who face travel barriers. Fund appropriate digital options with proper safeguarding, triage, and supervision.

- Transparent funding and measurement: Publish waiting times and outcomes for GP, CMHT and talking-therapy services so communities and commissioners can track progress. Use independent reviews to ensure targets are realistic and that parity with physical health funding is maintained.

From a practical standpoint, these steps would build a more responsive system: GP referrals that don’t get stuck in a bottleneck, quick access to the right kind of mental health support, and a crisis response that can de-escalate situations before they become emergencies. In our experience, where communities see expanded CMHTs, early intervention pathways, and credible talking-therapy options, people wait less, feel listened to sooner, and achieve better outcomes. That is the kind of change that makes a real difference in people’s lives and strengthens communities overall.

I urge policymakers to commit to long-term, adequately funded rollout of these changes, with local flexibility to adapt to different communities, and to prioritise parity between mental and physical health in all commissioning and delivery decisions. Thank you for considering this perspective on how timely access can be improved in practice.

To speed access, recruit more staff through international hires, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support, and expand online booking and e-consults while keeping non-digital options so older or disadvantaged patients aren't left behind.

The changes that would help most are to increase appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding session lengths where appropriate, and optimising scheduling so people can be seen promptly. For example, I recently needed to discuss a new medication; the earliest GP appointment was three weeks away, which caused unnecessary worry given my age and conditions. If there were more GPs and nurse prescribers, I could have been reviewed sooner and my meds monitored without risk. ACCESS TO TIMELY GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES IS A REAL CONCERN IN MY AREA, AND I THINK WE WOULD BENEFIT MOST FROM BUILDING STRONGER MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS WITHIN PRIMARY CARE. THE AIM WOULD BE TO HANDLE ROUTINE, PREVENTATIVE AND BASIC SUPPORT TASKS WITH THE RIGHT PROFESSIONALS, SO GPS CAN DEVOTE MORE TIME TO COMPLEX OR HIGH-RISK CASES WHILE STILL ENSURING SAFE AND SEAMLESS CARE FOR PATIENTS.

MY PRACTICAL SUGGESTION IS TO EXPAND TEAMS THAT ALREADY EXIST IN SOME PRACTICES OR HUBS TO A BROADER MODEL: INCLUDE PHARMACISTS, PHYSIOTHERAPISTS, PARAMEDICS AND PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES AS STANDARD MEMBERS OF A PATIENT-FACING TEAM. THEY WOULD OPERATE WITH CLEAR TRIAGE AND REFERRAL PATHWAYS, SHARED PATIENT NOTES AND AGREED SCOPES OF PRACTICE. THIS SHOULD BE BACKED BY ROBUST TRAINING, GOVERNANCE, AND FUNDED TIME FOR INTEGRATED CARE MEETINGS SO EVERYONE STAYS ON THE SAME PAGE.

IN DAY-TO-DAY TERMS, THIS COULD LOOK LIKE: 
- PHARMACISTS TAKING ON MEDICATION REVIEWS, MINOR AILMENT TRIAGE, AND RECONCILIATION FOR NEW STARTERS OR THOSE WITH COMPLEX REGIMENS. THEY COULD RESOLVE STRAIGHTFORWARD MEDICATION QUERIES DURING A SAME-DAY VISIT OR VIRTUAL CHECK-INS, FREEING GPS TO CONCENTRATE ON DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT OF MORE COMPLEX ISSUES. I’VE ENCOUNTERED INSTANCES WHERE A SIMPLE MEDICATION QUESTION DRAGGED A GP APPOINTMENT OUT OF HOURS; A SKILLED PHARMACIST COULD HAVE RESOLVED THIS QUICKLY, REDUCING DELAYS.
- PHYSIOTHERAPISTS LEADING ON MUSCULOSKELETAL PROBLEMS AND FUNCTIONAL RESTORATION. A PATIENT WITH CHRONIC BACK PAIN OR A SPORTS INJURY COULD BE ASSESSED AND GIVEN A TAILORED EXERCISE PLAN OR A HANDS-ON TREATMENT PLAN WITHOUT WAITING WEEKS FOR A GP SLOT. THAT WOULD LIKELY CUT DOWN REPEAT GP VISITS FOR THE SAME ISSUE AND HELP PEOPLE REGAIN MOBILITY SOONER.
- PARAMEDICS AND PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES PROVIDING TIMELY TRIAGE IN PRIMARY CARE SETTINGS AND URGENT CARE WALK-INS. THEY COULD HANDLE ACUTE, LOW-RISK PRESENTATIONS, CARRY OUT HOME VISITS IF NEEDED, AND ESCALATE TO GPS OR NURSES ONLY WHEN NECESSARY. THIS WOULD BE ESPECIALLY VALUABLE IN RURAL OR UNDERSERVED AREAS WHERE GP ACCESS IS LIMITED AND PATIENTS FEEL COMPELLED TO ATTEND A&E FOR NON-EMERGENCY CONCERNS.
- MENTAL HEALTH STAFF, INCLUDING BRIEF COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL SUPPORT, COUNSELLING AND EARLY INTERVENTION WORKERS, COULD TAKE ON EARLY ACCESS ROLES FOR COMMON CONCERNS SUCH AS ANXIETY, SLEEP PROBLEMS, OR STRESS. QUICK ACCESS TO TALK THERAPIES OR MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING IN A PRIMARY CARE HUB WOULD BE A MEANINGFUL STEP FORWARD, REDUCING WAITS FOR SPECIALIST MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES.

FROM MY EXPERIENCE, WHEN ROUTINE ISSUES ARE DIVERTED TO A CAPABLE MDT MEMBER, THE IMPACT IS TANGIBLE. A SIMPLE REPEAT PRESCRIPTION ISSUE, A MISCOMMUNICATION ABOUT A DOSE, OR A BACK-PACHE THAT RESPONDS TO TARGETED PHYSIO ADVICE CAN BE RESOLVED WITHOUT TYING UP A GP APPOINTMENT. IN CONTRAST, COMPLEX OR HIGH-RISK NEEDS—WHERE A GP’S CLINICAL REASONING AND CONTINUITY ARE ESSENTIAL—REMAIN WITH THE DOCTOR, WHICH HELPS PROTECT PATIENT SAFETY AND ENSURES APPROPRIATE ESCALATION.

THAT SAID, THERE ARE IMPORTANT GUARDRAILS. WE NEED INTEGRATED DIGITAL RECORDS SO A PHARMACIST OR PHYSIO CAN SEE WHAT A GP HAS NOTED AND VICE VERSA; CLEAR REFERRAL CRITERIA; AND TRANSPARENT PATIENT CHOICE ABOUT WHO THEY SEE FOR WHAT. STAFFING MUST REFLECT DEMAND; WE SHOULD AVOID CREATING CHURN WHERE PATIENTS ARE BOUNCED BETWEEN ROLES OR WHERE NEW ROLES ARE INTRODUCED WITHOUT CORRESPONDING WORKLOAD OR FUNDING, WHICH WOULD SIMPLY PUSH DELAYS ELSEWHERE. THE SCOPE OF PRACTICE MUST BE CLEARLY DEFINED, WITH SUPERVISION AND ESCALATION PATHWAYS TO PREVENT FRAGMENTED CARE OR SAFETY GAPS.

IF IMPLEMENTED THOUGHTFULLY, THIS APPROACH WOULD REDUCE AVOIDABLE WAITS, FREE GPS TO MANAGE COMPLEX CASES, AND IMPROVE PATIENT EXPERIENCE BY OFFERING FASTER ACCESS AND MORE CONVENIENT, EARLY SUPPORT. IT WON’T REPLACE GPS, BUT IT SHOULD RE-BALANCE RESPONSIBILITIES ACROSS THE MDT SO PEOPLE GET TIMELY HELP FOR ROUTINE NEEDS AND QUICKER RELIEF FROM LONGER-STANDING ISSUES. I’D SUPPORT THIS DIRECTION WITH CAREFUL ROLLOUT, PERFORMANCE MONITORING AND ONGOING PATIENT FEEDBACK TO REFINE THE MODEL.”

absolutely living in Wales I see a mix of experiences when it comes to getting timely GP, community health and mental health support. Some weeks I hear of neighbours who get same day GP slots, others tell me they’re still waiting two weeks or more. For mental health a friend waited months for a talking therapies referral, and my own family has had to cope with split referrals between NHS and local out of hours services. Because the system varies a lot by town and practice, I’m not sure what single change would fix it everywhere.

Would it help to have more flexible GP access? Perhaps same day or next day appointments, evening and weekend hours, more online triage so you aren’t stuck on the phone for ages. I’ve spent hours trying to get through on the phone in the morning only to be told there are no slots that day. At the same time I worry about overloading doctors and nurses if the hours were extended without more staff. So maybe a combination would be needed: extra staff, better rotation between practices, and clearer information about what you can book and when.

Community health teams could make a difference too: having district nurses, physios and mental health support workers working from local hubs closer to people’s homes would cut travel time and speed up care. In my county some clinics are so far that people without cars struggle, especially older relatives that neighbours help with. A few more community clinics in smaller towns would help but that would need reliable transport links and reasonable appointment times.

For mental health I would value quicker access and more options beyond waiting lists — talking therapies, crisis lines and drop in support. In practice I’ve heard of people starting CBT after a long wait; during that time stress and anxiety can worsen. It would help if initial assessments could happen sooner and then a plan could be put in place quickly, even if follow up is arranged over the next weeks rather than months.

I know there are funding constraints and workforce shortages, and I’m not sure which mix of changes would work best in my area. Perhaps pilots in selected towns to test different models like same day GP slots with nurse triage or virtual GP visits with an option for face to face when needed could shed light on what’s practical. What I would like to see is a clear commitment to improving access that doesn’t just shift pressure around but actually shortens waiting times and reduces the need for people to travel long distances for routine care!

We need extended hours with evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots to help working people. Increase GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots through hires and smarter scheduling. Expand community mental health teams, early intervention and talking therapies to reduce waits and achieve parity with physical health.

AS A SOMEONE AGED 65+ LIVING IN ENGLAND, I WELCOME PROPOSALS TO IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES BY EXPANDING MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS. IF PHARMACISTS, PHYSIOTHERAPISTS, PARAMEDICS AND PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES CAN HANDLE ROUTINE CONDITIONS LIKE CHESTY COUGHS, BACK PAIN, MINOR INJURIES OR MEDICATION REVIEWS, IT WOULD FREE GPS TO CONCENTRATE ON COMPLEX CASES AND CARE PLANNING. A DEDICATED GP CLINIC FOR MEDICATION REVIEWS ALSO HELPS AVOID HOSPITAL VISITS.

LONG-TERM, INCREASING TRAINING PLACES, RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SUPPORT AND CPD FOR GPS, NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH STAFF WILL ENSURE WE HAVE A RESILIENT WORKFORCE AS THE POPULATION AGES. I’VE NOTICED THE VALUE OF OUTREACH PROGRAMMES: INTERPRETERS AND CULTURALLY COMPETENT STAFF, PLUS TARGETED OUTREACH TO DEPRIVED AND MINORITY COMMUNITIES, SO EVERYONE CAN ACCESS SUPPORT WHEN NEEDED. IN PARTICULAR, INTERPRETERS AT APPOINTMENTS AND TRANSLATED MATERIALS REDUCE CONFUSION AND HELP PEOPLE SEEK HELP EARLY, WHICH MAKES A REAL DIFFERENCE TO OUTCOMES.

I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. In practice, that means a single front door where a trained navigator assesses my needs and routes me to the most appropriate option—be that a same‑day GP appointment, a nurse‑led walk‑in, or a mental health support slot—without me having to repeat information to several teams.

THIS APPROACH WOULD PROMOTE PARITY WITH PHYSICAL HEALTH SERVICES AND DELIVER TIMELY HELP WHEN IT IS MOST NEEDED, REDUCING DISTRESS FOR INDIVIDUALS AND FAMILIES IN MIDLIFE AND BEYOND.

i really think i’m writing as an older resident living in England, and I want to flag that simply expanding community mental health teams, pointing to early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, or rolling out telehealth hubs, will not by itself deliver timely access for people like me. I have seen how well-meaning changes can drift into fragmentation unless they are joined up with the everyday reality of GP practices, local clinics and people’s transport needs.

First, expanding mental health teams sounds good in theory, but in practice it can create more moving parts without a stable point of contact. In my town, a new community mental health team arrived with promises of quicker assessments, only to find scheduling and record-sharing between the team and my GP practice were still not aligned. People waited weeks for an initial contact, then had to tell their story again to someone else, and I worry this repeats for others, delaying genuinely needed support. If we are to rely on more teams, we must guarantee continuity of care: a named clinician, a single updated care plan that travels with the patient across services, and real investment in the staff who sustain those relationships over time.

Second, early intervention and crisis response can be valuable only if they are timely and properly resourced. I’ve seen colleagues and neighbours deteriorate because a crisis line or out-of-hours service wasn’t able to provide rapid help. The risk with a broader mandate is that thresholds for access become stricter as demand grows; people in urgent need fall through the gaps. We should not assume that more services automatically equate to faster access. Instead, we need a structure where crisis teams are genuinely 24/7, with clear pathways back to ongoing care, and where primary care teams are trained and funded to recognise and escalate mental health needs without stigma or bureaucracy.

Third, talking therapies and early interventions are welcome, but they must be age-appropriate and locally available. Some older patients prefer in-person conversations, not screens or apps, and many still struggle with digital literacy or broadband access. If telehealth hubs are introduced as a substitute for in-person visits, we risk leaving behind people who are less comfortable with technology or who live in areas with poor connectivity. Any expansion should preserve flexible options: face-to-face when requested, telephone support, and, where appropriate, blended models that respect patients’ preferences and mobility constraints.

Transport, parking and premises continue to be substantial barriers, especially in rural or mobility-limited areas. Mobile clinics and outreach can help, but they must be reliable and well-coordinated with existing services. A weekly mobile clinic that is late or cancelled frequently is more frustrating than helpful. Likewise, telehealth can bridge some gaps, yet if there is no safe, accessible place to use it or if reading and hearing difficulties aren’t accommodated, it becomes a barrier instead of a bridge. I would like to see real investment in practical transport solutions—subsidised travel to appointments, community taxis, better bus links to health hubs—and improvements to physical premises so that parking is available and the premises are welcoming and accessible to older people.

Most importantly, for those of us with complex, chronic or multiple health needs, the focus must be on continuity of care and adequate time with clinicians. The current norm of brief appointments with frequent handoffs simply doesn’t work for managing multiple conditions or medications safely. Longer, regular appointments with a consistent clinician would reduce unnecessary return visits, improve outcomes, and free up resources in the longer term. In my experience, when I have had a longer appointment to discuss several issues, the doctor can adjust care more effectively and I avoid repeating complaints at subsequent visits.

If the aim is to improve timely access, the backbone should be stronger than new teams or trendy models. I would prioritise:
- stable, adequately funded primary care with named GPs and longer appointments for complex cases; a genuine commitment to continuity of care.
- integrated care records and clear, well-resourced pathways between GP practices, mental health teams, and community services to prevent duplication and gaps.
- real investment in workforce retention, training in geriatric mental health, and flexible care options that respect older patients’ preferences.
- practical transport solutions and accessible premises, plus thoughtfully designed mobile outreach that is predictable and coordinated with local clinics.
- age-appropriate mental health services that offer in-person, telephone or blended therapy, ensuring parity with physical health in terms of prompt access and ongoing support.

In short, I want changes that are coherent, locally accountable and sustainable, not merely additional services that risk fragmentation or unequal access. If these guardrails are put in place, I would welcome improvements; without them, I fear the proposed changes will merely shuffle the problem rather than solve it."

To improve timely access, I think we should protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients. When clinicians can spend 15-20 minutes with someone who has long-term conditions, mental health concerns, or multimorbidity, outcomes improve and people stop needing repeat urgent visits chasing the same issue. For example, in our practice a longer follow-up in diabetes care reduced unnecessary phone calls and stabilised blood pressure without extra trips to A&E. Longer slots also allow mental health specialists to pick up warning signs early and coordinate with social care. 

But there are real barriers: transport, parking and premises deficits make getting to appointments harder, especially for those in rural areas or with mobility limits. Practical changes could include mobile clinics visiting housing estates and village hubs; outreach workers coordinating with hospitals; telehealth hubs at community centres, libraries, or GP co-working spaces; and incentives for practices to offer some extended-hours slots. 

Additionally, flexible transport vouchers or coordinated local transport links would help. In short, combine longer, continuous care for complex cases with accessible, community-based and digital options to reach people who currently slip through the cracks.

absolutely i disagree with relying mainly on online booking and telehealth. In rural Wales, transport, parking and digital exclusion create barriers. Prioritise mobile clinics, outreach, interpreters, culturally competent staff, and non-digital options alongside remote care!

Access to GP, community health and mental health services is inconsistent and often leaves people needing to juggle work and care. I would welcome evening and weekend clinics in my area and a guaranteed same-day urgent slot for non-emergency issues. For someone who works full-time, the current daytime-only pattern means you either take time off or wait days for a check-up, which isn't practical for anything urgent but not life-threatening. A few months ago, I had a sudden chest-like symptom and struggled to get a same-day appointment; I ended up waiting and felt anxious, which could have been avoided with a quick slot. 

In the longer term, I think we need to sustainably grow the workforce: more training places for GPs and nurses, plus return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and good CPD, so the quality of care remains high even as we open hours wider. Rural and coastal areas will need targeted schemes to attract clinicians. Funding and IT must keep pace with expanded hours to avoid burnout and ensure safe triage. 

Overall, small-scale changes now plus a clear plan to grow the workforce would help not just me but families who rely on timely support.

it's outrageous that as a youth-led organisation in England, we welcome the goal of improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but we strongly disagree that the proposed focus alone will deliver real change. 

Reason 1: Interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential, but without expanding the base capacity we will just swap bottlenecks. In our city, many people cannot get a same-day appointment because practices are closed or booked weeks ahead; even when interpreters exist, confusion and missed slots persist. 

Reason 2: Targeted outreach to deprived and marginalised groups is necessary, yet it must be backed by sustained funding and integrated into the core service—not as a separate add-on. We've seen outreach programmes start but then fade when funding stops, leaving gaps again. 

Reason 3: Expanding community mental health teams and early intervention is good in theory, but results depend on timely access to initial assessments. Waiting months for a referral means early signs escalate into crisis; we need same-day crisis response and more on-campus or community-based drop-in spaces, with clear pathways. 

Examples: local GP clinics still offer limited after-hours; language access lines are sometimes unavailable; students struggle with mental health support during exam periods. 

So our priority is a holistic capacity plan: more GPs and nurses, longer hours, reliable interpreters, integrated mental health hubs in schools and community centres, and transparent waiting-time targets!

i really think in my town in England, the main barrier isn’t simply that GP and mental health services aren’t open late; it’s getting through on the phone, getting an appointment and knowing where to go. Targeted resources for interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential, but they must be embedded locally with clear funding and measurable results. Without active outreach into deprived and ethnic minority communities—through local partners, faith groups, and bilingual workers—many people simply don’t access services or don’t trust them.

Evening and weekend clinics would help working people, but only if there is sustainable staffing and proper triage to avoid burnout and backlogs. Guaranteed same-day urgent slots sound attractive, but they rarely work if they’re used for non-urgent issues and don’t connect quickly to crisis support when needed.

Expanding community mental health teams and early intervention is good in principle, but it must be timely, well integrated with GP practices, and give rapid access to talking therapies; otherwise waits in mental health will stay as long as physical health access gaps.

In short: commit to targeted funding for outreach and interpreters, durable staffing, strong integration, and clear crisis pathways, rather than relying on longer hours alone!

As an older resident of England, I’ve learned that timeliness isn’t just about squeezing more GP slots into the day. In my village, even when a GP is available, getting there can be tricky in winter, and information about what help is actually on offer is often hard to understand. A neighbour waited three weeks for a mental‑health listening service, and the local bus timetable stops early, so access depends on a kind neighbour rather than a reliable system. I’d like to see changes that aren’t just about queue lengths: better transport links to clinics, more home visits for those with mobility issues, and stronger coordination between GP practices, social care, and local volunteers to prevent crises. I also worry about digital systems that assume everyone has broadband or knows how to use apps. If there’s a path forward, it should include clear information in plain language, more predictable out‑of‑hours contacts, and straightforward steps for joining up services locally. Which changes help most will depend on local realities, not one‑size‑fits‑all targets.

absolutely i welcome proposals to make GP, community health and mental health services more timely and accessible across Scotland. Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care is sensible, especially for people with mobility limits or busy care duties. In my practice, online booking and a nurse‑led e‑consult have sped up routine requests, but I also rely on non‑digital routes: a telephone line at reception and paper forms I can fill with help from a neighbour if needed. We must ensure no one—especially older or financially stretched households—gets left behind; offer in‑person help at the surgery, libraries, or via local volunteers to assist with digital access. Evening and weekend clinics would help those who work or care for others, and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would ease worries when someone suddenly deteriorates. Improvements to NHS111, better clinical triage, streamlined booking systems and a clear care‑navigation pathway would prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and speed patient flow, making the system feel calmer and more reliable for communities across Scotland!

I welcome mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs to improve access for rural and mobility‑impaired residents, but timely care also hinges on attracting and retaining staff—better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support, plus targeted recruitment and international hiring where needed.

Online booking and e-consults can help some, but they risk excluding older or disadvantaged patients. Protect continuity of care and longer appointments for complex cases, including mental health, and keep non-digital options and in-person support to avoid widening access gaps.

I LIVE IN ENGLAND AND I’M RESPONDING AS AN INDIVIDUAL CONCERNED ABOUT TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES FOR PEOPLE LIKE ME AND MY FAMILY. I STRONGLY AGREE THAT THE CHANGES PROPOSED COULD MAKE A REAL DIFFERENCE TO HOW QUICKLY PEOPLE GET HELP WHEN THEY NEED IT, WITHOUT COMPROMISING QUALITY OF CARE. IN MY VIEW THE BEST WAY TO SECURE QUICKER ACCESS IS TO TACKLE THE ROOT CAUSES—MORE TRAINED PROFESSIONALS, SMARTER USE OF DIGITAL TOOLS WITH INCLUSIVE OPTIONS, AND BETTER TRIAGE AND NAVIGATION SO URGENT NEEDS DON’T GET STUCK IN THE SYSTEM.

1) GROW THE WORKFORCE IN A SUSTAINABLE WAY
- INCREASE TRAINING PLACES ACROSS GPS, NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS, NOT JUST IN THE SHORT TERM BUT WITH A CLEAR, LONG‑TERM PLAN. IF MORE MEDICAL SCHOOL PLACES ARE FUNDED AND SUPPORTED WITH ACCESSIBLE SIXTH-FORM AND LOCAL OUTREACH PROGRAMMES, MORE TRAINEES WILL STAY IN PRACTICE IN AREAS WHERE SHORTAGES ARE MOST ACUTE.
- EXPAND RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE SUPPORT AND APPRENTICESHIPS. MY LOCAL PRACTICE HAS STRUGGLED WITH STAFFING GAPS AFTER RETIREMENTS OR LONG‑TERM ILLNESS LEAVES; TARGETED RETRAINING, BRIDGING COURSES AND SUPPORTED RE-ENTRY COULD AVOID PROLONGED WAITS FOR ROUTINE CARE AND ENABLE EXPERIENCED CLINICIANS TO CONTRIBUTE QUICKLY.
- PRIORITISE CPD AND CAREER PROGRESSION FOR EXISTING STAFF. WHEN NURSES AND MENTAL HEALTH WORKERS HAVE REGULAR UP‑SKILLING OPPORTUNITIES, THEY ARE BETTER PLACED TO MANAGE INCREASING DEMAND, TRIAGE APPROPRIATELY AND STAY MOTIVATED IN DEMANDING ROLES.

2) MAKE ACCESS EASIER THROUGH DIGITAL TOOLS WHILE KEEPING NON‑DIGITAL OPTIONS
- EXPAND ONLINE BOOKING AND E‑CONSULTATIONS, INCLUDING VIDEO AND ASYNCHRONOUS MESSAGING, SO PEOPLE CAN ARRANGE URGENT OR SAME‑DAY SLOTS MORE FLEXIBLY. FOR MANY WORKING ADULTS, QUICK ONLINE ACCESS IS A REAL TIME SAVER AND REDUCES THE PRESSURE ON TELEPHONE LINES.
- AT THE SAME TIME, PROVIDE ROBUST NON‑DIGITAL PATHWAYS. NOT EVERYONE CAN ACCESS OR NAVIGATE DIGITAL SERVICES EASILY—OLDER PEOPLE, THOSE WITH LIMITED CONNECTIVITY, OR PEOPLE IN RURAL AREAS CAN BE LEFT BEHIND. IN PRACTICE THAT MEANS CLEAR TELEPHONE TRIAGE LINES, IN‑PERSON APPOINTMENT SLOTS, AND HELP DESKS IN LOCAL HUBS TO GUIDE PEOPLE THROUGH THE PROCESS.
- SUPPORT DIGITAL INCLUSION LOCALLY. I’D LIKE TO SEE PILOT SCHEMES WHERE COMMUNITY CLINICS OR LIBRARIES OFFER ‘ASSISTED DIGITAL’ SESSIONS, WITH STAFF WHO CAN HELP PATIENTS REGISTER, BOOK, AND USE ONLINE SERVICES. THIS WOULD PREVENT EXCLUSION WHILE STILL DRIVING EFFICIENCY.
- ENSURE CONTINUITY OF CARE. DIGITAL SYSTEMS MUST BE INTEROPERABLE ACROSS GP PRACTICES, COMMUNITY SERVICES AND MENTAL HEALTH TEAMS SO A PATIENT’S RECORDS TRAVEL WITH THEM AND AVOID REPEATED QUESTIONNAIRES OR TESTS.

3) IMPROVE TRIAGE, BOOKING SYSTEMS AND CARE NAVIGATION TO PRIORITISE URGENT NEEDS
- INVEST IN NHS111 AND CLINICAL TRIAGE WITH EXPLICIT PATHWAYS TO URGENT PRIMARY CARE OR MENTAL HEALTH INTAKE WHEN NEEDED. A MORE ACCURATE AND COMPASSIONATE TRIAGE SYSTEM WOULD MEAN PEOPLE IN CRISIS OR WITH RED‑FLAG SYMPTOMS COULD BE FAST‑TRACKED TO THE RIGHT CLINICIAN RATHER THAN LANGUISHING IN QUEUES.
- CREATE EFFECTIVE CARE NAVIGATION ACROSS THE WHOLE PATIENT JOURNEY. A DEDICATED NAVIGATOR CAN HELP PATIENTS MOVE FROM NHS111 TO THE RIGHT APPOINTMENT, CONFIRM WHETHER A SAME‑DAY SLOT IS AVAILABLE, AND COORDINATE ACROSS GP, MENTAL HEALTH AND COMMUNITY SERVICES TO AVOID DUPLICATION.
- SIMPLIFY PATIENT FLOW. REDUCING MULTIPLE HANDOFFS, REPEATED DATA ENTRY AND FRICTIONS BETWEEN SERVICES WOULD SPEED THINGS UP. WHEN A SHARED, PATIENT‑CENTRED PATHWAY EXISTS, URGENT CASES ARE LESS LIKELY TO BE DELAYED BY ADMINISTRATIVE BOTTLENECKS.
- USE DATA TO DRIVE IMPROVEMENTS. REGULAR MONITORING OF WAIT TIMES, REFERRAL OUTCOMES AND CONVERSION TO URGENT APPOINTMENTS CAN HIGHLIGHT BOTTLENECKS (FOR EXAMPLE, WHERE MENTAL HEALTH REFERRALS STALL IN TRIAGE) AND GUIDE TARGETED FIXES.

PERSONAL EXPERIENCE SUPPORTS THESE POINTS. A FAMILY MEMBER NEEDED MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT AND WE FOUND ONLINE APPOINTMENT BOOKING QUICK FOR ROUTINE CHECKS, BUT URGENT CASES STILL FACED WEEKS OF WAITING. IF THERE HAD BEEN A CLEARER TRIAGE ROUTE, WITH CARE NAVIGATORS GUIDING US STRAIGHT TO THE APPROPRIATE SERVICE AND A NON‑DIGITAL OPTION AVAILABLE, WE COULD HAVE ACCESSED HELP SOONER. LIKEWISE, WHEN MY LOCAL PRACTICE RAN SHORT OF GPS, A STRONGER TRAINING AND RETURN‑TO‑PRACTICE PIPELINE WOULD HELP FILL GAPS MORE QUICKLY, REDUCING CANCELLED OR DELAYED APPOINTMENTS.

OVERALL, I BELIEVE THESE CHANGES WOULD LEAD TO TIMELIER ACCESS WITHOUT COMPROMISING QUALITY. A SUSTAINED COMMITMENT TO GROWING THE WORKFORCE, COMBINED WITH FLEXIBLE, INCLUSIVE DIGITAL ACCESS AND SMARTER TRIAGE AND NAVIGATION, WOULD NOT ONLY SHORTEN WAITING TIMES BUT ALSO IMPROVE THE PATIENT EXPERIENCE AND OUTCOMES FOR PEOPLE WITH COMPLEX NEEDS. I’M ENCOURAGED BY THE DIRECTION OF TRAVEL AND HOPE THESE MEASURES ARE SUPPORTED WITH RELIABLE FUNDING AND CLEAR DELIVERY PLANS SO THAT COMMUNITIES ACROSS ENGLAND SEE REAL IMPROVEMENTS SOON.

absolutely timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people like me who juggle work and family. I strongly support expanding multidisciplinary primary-care teams, including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, to handle routine cases. This would free GPs to devote time to complex conditions and prevention. In practice, a minor knee strain, repeat migraines or a skin infection could be managed by the appropriate team member after quick triage, reducing GP waiting times and follow-ups. For mental health, early access through a stepped model with trained practitioners in the same team would prevent issues from escalating.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are real barriers, especially in rural or mobility‑limited areas. Mobile clinics visiting village hubs, outreach to care homes, and telehealth hubs in community centres or libraries would bring care closer to people. Incentives for practices to extend hours and co‑locate services can ease parking and space pressures and support integrated care. In my area, a weekly mobile clinic and a local library teleconsultation point would make a real difference to patients like my elderly neighbour and my busy colleague who can't spare long journeys!

From my experience in Northern Ireland, where deprivation exists in pockets and many migrant communities rely on basic GP and community services, the main barriers are language, trust and awareness. Changes that would most improve timely access include targeted resource allocation to deprived areas to fund extra GP and mental health slots and to support outreach through community organisations already trusted by local families. Providing interpreters—on-site or via video/phone—during GP, nurse and mental health consultations is essential so people can describe symptoms accurately and feel understood. Training reception staff and clinicians in culturally competent communication, plus recruiting bilingual staff or trusted liaison workers from local communities, would bridge gaps and reduce refusals or delays in care. Outreach should bring services to people: mobile clinics in neighbourhood hubs, extended hours, and information in multiple languages at workplaces, faith groups and community centres; clear, multilingual signposting to mental health services. Ensure multilingual digital booking and reminders, and collect data to monitor wait times by language and background to target improvements. In short, make services closer, approachable and responsive to marginalised groups to improve timely access for all.

Living in Scotland, I want timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The biggest win would come from targeted recruitment and international hiring to fill shortages, plus incentives and improved pay to attract staff to rural and underserved areas. Flexible working patterns, including evening and weekend clinics, and robust wellbeing support would help retain people in the long run. When staff aren’t stretched, there’s real relief for patients who struggle to get same-day advice.

Also essential is expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals sustainably.
