A single hub or closely linked network would enable a patient to see a GP, a district nurse, a mental health practitioner, and a social-care worker in one visit or with one triage process, reducing waiting times and multiple trips. In my area in Wales, transport and navigating services can slow down care, so keeping services nearby is crucial, especially for older or working‑age adults with caring responsibilities.

I also support protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex cases. Longer slots and a named clinician or care co‑ordinator can prevent repeated crises and down‑stream hospital visits. However, success depends on proper funding, robust data sharing with patient consent, and avoiding the creation of new silos. Digital access should be inclusive, with options for face‑to‑face for those who can’t use online systems and reliable transport links to hub sites. If done well, these changes could shorten waits and improve outcomes for physical, mental health and social needs.

I live in a town in England and I strongly support changes that will improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by creating co‑located hubs. When services are spread across separate buildings and scattered phone lines, patients can easily fall through the cracks. A local hub integrating primary care, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners would make it possible to see multiple professionals in one visit or within the same day, reducing travel, repeating information and wasted time. In my experience, booking mental health support or social care alongside a GP appointment would have saved weeks of delay. 

To make this work we need to grow the workforce: targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support to attract and retain staff in general practice and community services. I’d also like to see evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots so working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs aren’t stuck waiting. If these changes are funded and implemented well, people in our area will get timely, joined‑up care at the right place, first time.

BETTER NHS111 TRIAGE, CARE NAVIGATION AND SIMPLER BOOKING WOULD HELP URGENT CASES, BUT WE SHOULD ALSO EXPAND MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS TO HANDLE ROUTINE CARE, FREEING GPS FOR COMPLEX NEEDS; CO-LOCATED HUBS COULD HELP WITH SEAMLESS LOCAL ACCESS.

Our organisation supports timely access improvements across GP, community health and mental health services. Transport, parking and premises constraints remain a major barrier in rural and mobility‑limited areas. We back investment in mobile clinics and outreach teams that visit village halls and care homes, plus telehealth hubs linked to local GP surgeries. Providing incentives for practices to open in under‑served locations and offer extended hours would boost same‑day access and reduce travel burdens for patients.

We also support improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and smooth patient flow. A dedicated care navigator at triage can steer patients to the right service, while a single digital booking system minimizes multiple calls and enables timely slots.

On workforce, increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Our pilots show funded placements and strong mentorship cut wait times and improve retention.

In our area, mobile clinics have delivered weekly GP clinics to remote communities, telehealth hubs in community centres link to mental health specialists, and streamlined triage shortened urgent referral times. We urge funding for a joined‑up plan so people can access timely care locally and safely.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services would improve if we tackled staffing and outreach together. I think we need targeted recruitment and retention of primary care staff, including sensible international hiring and incentives, fair pay, flexible working patterns and genuine wellbeing support so experienced nurses and GPs stay in town rather than move away. At the same time, resources should be directed to interpreters and culturally competent staff so people from deprived or migrant backgrounds feel understood and supported when they present with concerns.

Transport, parking and premises are a barrier in my area. Mobile clinics visiting rural and mobility‑restricted residents, outreach teams, and local telehealth hubs would help reduce trips and waiting times. For example, a weekly mobile clinic in our village would mean older neighbours could get blood tests or mental health check-ins without long journeys. Clear triage and same‑day appointments for urgent issues would also curb delays.

Overall, I support a package that grows the workforce, expands accessible services, and reaches people where they live, with funding tied to measurable improvements in timely access.

From where I’m living in England, it’s clear that the biggest wins on timely access would come from expanding community mental health teams, boosting early intervention, strengthening crisis response, and widening access to talking therapies. When these areas are well funded and properly connected to GPs and local urgent care, people get help sooner and don’t fall through gaps that push them into A&E or crisis rooms. I’ve seen how delays turn small worries into bigger problems, so I’m convinced these changes would make services fairer and more efficient.

What I’d like to see in practical terms:

- Expand and diversify community mental health teams. Increase multidisciplinary staff in every locality (psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, nurses, social workers, peer support workers) and ensure teams operate with flexible hours, including evenings and weekends. These teams should do home visits where needed and work closely with GP practices to smooth referrals. In my area the community team is stretched; people I know have waited weeks just to be allocated a therapist or to get a joint call with a nurse and a social worker. More capacity would prevent small problems from becoming crises.

- Strengthen early intervention services. Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) and other early-intervention pathways should be available promptly, with clear referral routes via GP and urgent care. Reducing the duration of untreated illness not only helps people recover more quickly but also reduces hospital admissions down the line. I’ve heard stories from friends who felt their early signs weren’t picked up quickly enough, leading to needless anxiety and higher care needs later. Adequate staffing and predictable wait times would change that for many.

- Improve crisis response and access. Crisis Resolution and Home Treatment Teams (CRHT) should be available 24/7 with same-day crisis assessments and rapid home treatment where appropriate. Right now, weekend or after-hours access is inconsistent in some areas, which can send people to A&E unnecessarily. A robust, well-publicised 24/7 crisis line, plus mobile teams that can reach people at home, would make a real difference and reduce avoidable hospital stays.

- Widen access to talking therapies and make it user-friendly. The IAPT model is essential, but capacity often doesn’t meet demand and waits can be long. I’d like to see more therapists trained in a range of therapies (CBT, ACT, DBT, interpersonal therapy) and more support for people with complex needs, including neurodiversity and language or cultural barriers. We should also formalise remote and self-referral pathways so people can start therapy quickly from home, while still offering in-person options for those who prefer them. More integration with schools, workplaces, and community groups would help reach people earlier.

- Ensure parity with physical health in funding and accountability. Mental health services still struggle for parity with physical health in both budget and perceived priority. Ring-fenced funding, clear local targets for wait times, and public dashboards showing how long people wait for initial assessment and for ongoing treatment would build trust and accountability. I’d like to see local health partnerships publish data on waiting times by area and routinely review where bottlenecks occur.

- Improve GP-level access and triage. GPs should have direct, timely pathways to mental health professionals, with rapid triage to appropriate services (IAPT, CRHT, CAMHS when relevant). Quick GP-to-specialist referrals and integrated care plans would stop people bouncing between services and help stabilize conditions before they escalate.

In short, these changes aren’t just about shorter queues; they’re about giving people timely, compassionate care that responds to what they’re experiencing right now. If these services are funded, staffed and measured with the same urgency as physical health care, we’d likely see fewer emergency visits, better outcomes, and people feeling heard and supported when they first reach out for help.

I disagree that the answer lies in tinkering with one bit of the system. For many young people in England, real gains would come from overhauling NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation so urgent cases are prioritised and you’re not shuffled between services. In my experience, NHS111 often ends up directing people to wait for a GP slot that isn’t available the same day, which pushes people into A&E or leaves mental health concerns untreated for longer. When I’ve tried to access mental health support, repeated forms and conflicting triage advice across services meant I had to explain things twice and still didn’t get timely help.

What would help more: a single, interoperable care-navigation hub that can see a triage outcome, check real-time GP and urgent mental health slots, and guide you to the right service first time. Interoperable records would stop duplicating questions and referrals; you’d only need to give consent once and your information would follow you through primary care, community health and crisis services. Real-time booking across practices, predictable same-day slots for urgent needs, and stronger out-of-hours hubs would also stop the endless chasing of appointments.

These changes would deliver timely access more effectively than simply adding more clinicians without fixing the flow and triage.”

A smoother flow means fewer people calling multiple times or turning up at A&E for problems that could be managed in primary care. In our area, the triage process has started to steer patients toward the most appropriate service quickly, whether that’s a GP appointment, a nurse-led clinic, or a mental health service. A strong care navigation role—reception staff or dedicated care navigators—can help patients choose the right appointment the first time, avoid multiple calls, and reduce backlogs.

For mental health services, timely access is particularly crucial. Online access to talking therapies or remote counselling saves travel and makes it easier to fit sessions into busy lives, but must be balanced with options for in-person meetings when preferred or necessary. It is important that targeted outreach also helps people recognise early warning signs and seek help promptly, not only when a crisis occurs.

In practice, I would welcome: more guaranteed access to non-digital booking channels alongside online options; funded training in cultural competence and interpreters; community outreach to raise awareness of services in accessible languages; and robust, well-publicised care-navigation pathways that guide people to the right service first time. I’d also like to see evaluation measures that track both access and outcomes for older and digitally excluded residents, so we know what’s working and where more help is needed.

Thank you for considering these changes. With steady investment and thoughtful planning, we can improve timely access for everyone—keeping people healthy and connected to the care they need, when they need it most!

To improve timely access, changes should prioritise continuity of care for complex and vulnerable patients and extend appointment lengths. Short appointments and frequent handoffs frustrate patients with multiple conditions and can worsen outcomes, leading to more visits later. In our local area a young person with diabetes and episodes of anxiety waited two weeks for a 15 minute GP slot, then had to chase referrals to community nursing and psychology, creating gaps and extra trips to the clinic. Longer appointments of 20 to 30 minutes for those with chronic or mental health needs would allow a real plan to be made, reduce repeated visits, and improve adherence. 

We also need to protect continuity by letting patients see the same clinician or a small, stable team. That might mean protected time for complex cases, and care coordinators who oversee a plan across primary care, community services and mental health. Integrated community teams that can offer counselling, pharmacy checks and social support in one path are essential. 

Digital triage and same day access are useful but must not replace face to face assessments when necessary. If implemented with care, these changes could reduce hospital admissions and save time and stress for young people.

From my experience in England, the biggest barrier to timely access isn’t just the number of slots, but how they’re allocated and staffed. Yes, we need more GP, nurse and therapy slots, but promising hiring without lasting funding, retention plans and smarter scheduling will just reproduce the same bottlenecks. In our area, GP practices run limited hours and routine appointments can be two weeks away; same-day access is rare. Expanding capacity must go with better triage, longer consultations when needed, and smarter use of digital and phone access so people aren’t pushed into hospital visits for simple issues. For mental health, expanding community teams, early intervention and crisis response is essential; waiting times for talking therapies stretch into months, and crisis lines still struggle after supporting hours end. I know someone who waited eight weeks for CBT and another who felt their risk wasn’t acted on promptly.

What would help is a funded plan with realistic staffing targets, protected training and retention budgets, ring-fenced funding, extended hours (including weekends), and integrated care records. We also need clear national standards for wait times and better regional planning to avoid postcode lotteries. Without these safeguards, more slots won’t automatically translate into better care or real parity with physical health services.

Agree. To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I support expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but with robust non-digital options so no one is left behind. Online booking and video or phone triage can cut waiting times and reduce travel for many people, which is especially helpful for busy families and those with mental health concerns. I’ve personally benefited from booking slots online and using a short video check‑in for follow‑ups, but I’ve also seen neighbours struggle with digital access. Practices should offer strong telephone booking, walk‑in slots and in‑person triage at community hubs or pharmacies, with staff available to assist people navigating the system.

Equally important is targeted support for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Local clinics should provide interpreters and culturally competent staff, multilingual appointment reminders and outreach in trusted community venues. In my area, clinics that offer Urdu, Polish and Somali interpreters at peak times see higher attendance and fewer missed appointments. I’d also like to see funded training for reception teams on cultural sensitivity and clearer signposting to mental health services, plus flexible hours and transport support so people can access timely help without barriers.

Overall, a blended approach that scales digital access while safeguarding non‑digital routes will deliver timely care for everyone.

i strongly believe timely access is obviously important, but I’m skeptical about relying primarily on NHS111, triage, and reforming booking systems as the main fix. In practice, NHS111 in our area can be slow, and the triage advice often pushes urgent concerns into phone consultations that end with “book an appointment” weeks later. I’ve had to chase test results and speak to a clinician several times because the initial call didn’t capture the seriousness of symptoms. 

Online booking and care navigators can help, but they often confuse older patients who struggle with digital portals or who receive conflicting guidance from different staff. A neighbour, in their 60s, spent days trying to arrange a simple repeat prescription because the booking system redirected her to multiple teams with no single point of contact. 

As for multidisciplinary teams taking routine cases, it risks fragmenting care and eroding GP continuity, which matters for those with long-term conditions. If a patient sees a different clinician each time, important information can slip through the cracks, and medications can be duplicated or missed. Better to fund longer GP hours, stable care coordinators, and integrated records that keep a single clinician responsible!

From our organisation working with adults across England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is shaped by more than clinic lists. People tell us travel to appointments can be long, parking is scarce and evening/weekend slots are patchy, so getting in quickly isn’t just about “more appointments.” Even with online booking, digital access is a barrier for those with limited broadband, low digital literacy or caregiving responsibilities. In mental health, waits for talking therapies can be months, which means people deteriorate before help arrives; in social care and community nursing, staff shortages push routines back and people struggle with continuity of care when the same clinician isn’t available. We also see how transport difficulties and the need for reliable community supports around the home push people toward emergency services, which isn’t efficient for anyone.

What would help, though not a single fix: ensure stable staffing and salary models (including practice-based pharmacists and mental health workers) so GPs can focus on urgent and continuity care; extend hours at local hubs to cover evenings and Saturdays; improve transport links and parking near clinics; maintain multiple booking routes (phone, in-person, digital) with proactive reminders; and strengthen links between primary care, community services and voluntary sector to keep people well at home and reduce avoidable hospital visits. We need local, joined-up solutions that reflect real-world daily barriers.
We need evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, plus more GP, nurse and therapist appointments by hiring and smarter scheduling to stop long waits for working people.

Agree. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to manage routine cases would free GPs for complex care and speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area.

i strongly believe agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential, and I believe the right changes to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation could make a real difference in my area. My experience suggests that urgent needs are too often slowed by fragmented booking and repetitive information, while people in distress may fall through the gaps between services. There are practical steps that could improve patient flow, reduce duplication and prioritise those in urgent need.

NHS111 and clinical triage
- Expand the capacity and quality of triage in NHS111 with highly trained clinicians—nurses or GPs—backed by robust online tools. A clear, consistent set of criteria for what constitutes urgent or red-flag symptoms would help ensure the right decisions are made at the first point of contact.
- Ensure triage decisions are linked directly to real-time booking options, so urgent cases can be offered same-day GP slots, urgent care access, or rapid mental health assessment when needed. This should apply equally to physical health and mental health concerns.
- Improve the handoff from NHS111 to primary or community services by eliminating the need for patients to repeat information. An integrated digital record for triage notes should be visible to the clinician who takes the next step in the pathway.

Booking systems and access
- Create a unified, real-time booking platform that all GP practices and community services can access. Patients should be able to see earliest available slots for urgent issues, book mental health triage appointments quickly, and cancel or reschedule online without losing their place in the process.
- Allow cross-service booking so someone referred from GP to physiotherapy or district nursing can stay in the same queue and not start from scratch again. A single, shared wait-list for urgent care could dramatically reduce repeated contacts and confusion.
- Improve access outside traditional hours where appropriate, with protected urgent slots in the evenings or weekends and flexible options for video or phone consultations. This would reduce the need for non-essential in-person visits and speed up urgent assessments.

Care navigation and reduced duplication
- Introduce trained care navigators in every GP practice and in major community hubs who can assess needs, guide patients to the right service first time, and streamline referrals (e.g., to mental health teams, social prescribing, or district nursing). They could handle pre-consultation checks to avoid multiple appointments.
- Promote a single referral path and common referral forms, so a patient’s information moves smoothly between GP, community health, and mental health services. This would reduce duplication of history-taking and tests, and shorten the time to the first appropriate intervention.
- Invest in shared electronic records and information governance that supports safe data sharing with proper consent. Navigators and clinicians would be able to access essential information quickly, minimising repeated questions and re-tests.

Focused improvements for urgent and mental health care
- Expand urgent care hubs and multidisciplinary clinics that combine GP expertise with nurse practitioners, physio, and mental health staff in a single setting. This would be especially helpful for patients like me with multi-faceted needs who currently bounce between services.
- For mental health, speed up initial access to talking therapies (IAPT) and ensure crisis pathways are straightforward and well signposted. A same-day triage process should be available for those experiencing acute distress, with clear handoffs to appropriate levels of support.
- Ensure district nurses and community teams can respond quickly to home-care needs to prevent avoidable hospital visits, especially for older family members or those with chronic conditions.

A few personal observations and expected outcomes
- I’ve spent time on calls with NHS111 only to be told to book a GP appointment weeks later, then had to repeat the story when I finally reached a clinician. A seamless triage-to-book flow would have reduced anxiety and saved time for everyone.
- When information isn’t shared between services, I’ve seen duplicate forms, repeated histories and longer waits for tests. A unified system would cut down on bureaucracy and help people receive the right care faster.

In summary, by strengthening NHS111 triage with clinical input, delivering a real-time, inter-operable booking system, and embedding capable care navigators who guide patients through a streamlined, joined-up pathway, we can prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and improve the overall flow from first contact to appropriate treatment. These changes would make a tangible difference to patients and families in our area who are trying to navigate multiple services under pressure.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is crucial for us in England, especially as we age. I strongly support changes that expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs to focus on more complex care. Pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can manage many everyday concerns, triage referrals, and oversee medication reviews, which should shorten waiting times and boost continuity of care. In our area, a pharmacist-led clinic for minor illnesses and a physiotherapist-led musculoskeletal triage have already reduced the number of same‑day GP slots used for simple matters, and elderly patients get quicker advice without travelling.

To grow and retain primary care staff, targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support are essential. For example, offering part-time and staggered shifts for clinicians, providing relocation packages for international recruits, and ensuring protected time for training, reduces burnout and improves retention. Embedding more mental health practitioners in GP hubs and enabling social prescribers to work within community teams would mean timely support for people before crises develop.

Overall, these changes would help deliver timely, compassionate care closer to home while keeping our NHS sustainable.

I live in England and, like many neighbours, I’ve noticed how delays for GP appointments can push people to seek care elsewhere. Expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care—including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—would make timely access far more realistic. They could handle routine cases and simple follow-ups, freeing GPs to focus on complex conditions.

Practically, this means a person with a back strain could see a physiotherapist for evaluation and exercises, while a pharmacist could adjust a prescription or answer medication questions on the same day. A mental health concern could be triaged by a nurse or psychologist within a community hub, with rapid signposting to therapy if needed. In urgent but non-emergency situations, a paramedic-led home visit or an urgent care clinician in the hub could prevent unnecessary trips to A&E.

In my experience, local clinics with this model have reduced waiting times and kept people moving with the right support. If rolled out consistently in our area, it would noticeably improve access and reduce pressure on hospital services while maintaining high-quality care.

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and talking therapies to reduce waits and parity with physical health. I also want NHS111, triage and booking simplified to prioritise urgent cases, and continuity protected by longer appointments for complex, vulnerable patients.

I strongly support the plan to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. For many of us who work full-time, slots during the day don’t fit, so evening and weekend clinics would make a real difference without the need to take time off work. A guarantee of same-day urgent slots for urgent but non-emergency needs would prevent small concerns from growing into bigger problems and take pressure off urgent care departments.

Improving NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation is essential to prioritise urgent cases and to simplify patient flow. If NHS111 can triage efficiently and direct people to the right service first time, we avoid ringing round clinics and reduce wasted time. A single, easy-to-use online booking system with clear, real-time availability would cut confusion and duplication. Trained care navigators could help people choose the most appropriate service—GP, mental health, or community teams—and organise appropriate follow-ups, which would also help reduce avoidable delays.

In my own experience, better after-hours access and clearer triage would have saved hours of calls and worry. When a relative needed urgent mental health support, a quicker triage path and direct referral could have made a real difference. These changes feel achievable and would benefit many working families like mine.

Disagree: simply increasing appointment slots won’t fix delays unless NHS111 triage, booking systems and care navigation are improved to prioritise urgent cases and simplify flow. Long-term, expand training, return-to-practice support and CPD to grow staff.

Agree. To improve timely access, protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, so clinicians can address needs in one visit, reducing repeat consultations and improving outcomes across GP, community and mental health services.

Timely access to GP, community health, and mental health services in my area isn’t just about demand—it’s about staffing and how we organise work. The changes that would make the biggest difference for me are practical, long-term steps to grow and retain primary care staff. First, targeted recruitment: establish strong pipelines from medical schools, nursing courses, and local colleges, with clear career tracks into general practice and community roles. Second, expand international hiring but with robust, accelerated registration, culturally competent induction, and sustainable visa pathways so new clinicians can settle and stay. Third, pay improvements and retention incentives that reflect the full scope and hours of on-call work, plus targeted extra support during peak periods. Fourth, more flexible working patterns: job-sharing, longer evening clinics, and part-time GP slots to attract a wider workforce without sacrificing continuity of care. Fifth, comprehensive wellbeing and professional support: protected time for supervision, mental health resources for staff, and realistic admin loads so clinicians can spend time with patients. Sixth, empower non-physician roles (nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists) to handle triage and routine care. In practice, I’ve seen same-day slots vanish and burnout rising among colleagues; these measures could help keep care timely and sustainable.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. Our organisation supports actions that will make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services a reality across England. When people can get seen promptly, it reduces anxiety, prevents deterioration of conditions and can avert hospital admissions. With that in mind, the changes proposed would bring real benefits in our area by increasing capacity, broadening the skill mix in primary care and ensuring services are accessible to everyone, including those facing language or cultural barriers.

First, increasing the number of appointment slots and overall session capacity is essential. This means recruiting more GPs, practice nurses and therapists, expanding session lengths where clinically appropriate, and using smarter scheduling so slots aren’t left unused or duplicated. Practical steps could include more flexible hours, such as early mornings and later in the evenings or at weekends, and stronger use of triage to direct people to the most appropriate clinician quickly. In our experience, even modest investments in extra nurse and therapist slots can dramatically reduce wait times for common concerns like colds, sleep problems, back pain or anxiety. Digital tools should support this, with reliable online booking, real-time wait-time indicators and efficient telephone triage that redirects people to the right level of care first time.

Second, expanding multidisciplinary teams will help manage routine cases and free GPs to focus on complex care. Pharmacists can handle repeat prescriptions, minor illnesses, and medication reviews; physiotherapists can lead on musculoskeletal and rehabilitation concerns; paramedics can run rapid-access clinics for urgent but non-urgent issues; physician associates can see routine cases under supervision. When teams operate cohesively, patients receive stable, timely care without unnecessary delays, and GPs have more bandwidth for complex or high-risk cases. We’ve seen pilot arrangements where pharmacist-led medication reviews caught potential drug interactions before harm occurred, and where physiotherapist-led pathways reduced GP visits for back and joint problems. Scaling these models could yield meaningful system relief if supported with appropriate supervision, CPD and clear referral protocols.

Third, targeted resources to reach deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups are critical to closing access gaps. This means funding interpreters and translation services as standard, recruiting and training culturally competent staff, and designing outreach that meets people where they are—through community hubs, schools, workplaces and places of worship. In practice, this could include multilingual appointment letters, on-site interpreters for longer consultations, and community health workers who can navigate people through the system, explain what to expect from services, and help with follow-ups. Outreach and flexible access points should be paired with culturally appropriate care pathways, including mental health services that acknowledge stigma and language barriers. When families from migrant backgrounds can access timely advice and support without excessive paperwork or fear of discrimination, health gains accumulate quickly.

To implement these changes successfully, sustained funding and clear accountability are essential. Long-term workforce planning is needed to maintain expanded teams, and data-sharing agreements must protect patient confidentiality while enabling responsive scheduling and service design. It would also help to build strong partnerships with local voluntary and community sector organisations to support outreach and help people navigate services.

In summary, expanding capacity, widening the multidisciplinary team, and prioritising interpreters and culturally competent outreach will collectively shorten waits and improve outcomes for GP, community health and mental health services in our area. We welcome a programme that brings these elements together in a coherent, well-resourced plan that ensures timely, equitable access for all residents.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a priority for me as a local resident. In our area, transport options can be limited and parking at busy practices can be a real barrier, especially for older neighbours and those with mobility issues. Premises sometimes feel cramped or not fully accessible, and that can deter people from seeking help when they need it. I believe the best way to improve access is to combine several practical approaches: mobile clinics, outreach work, well‑screened telehealth hubs, sensible incentives for providers, and robust non‑digital options so no one is left behind.

Mobile clinics could make a real difference, particularly in rural or sparsely serviced parts of our county. A GP van that visits a village hall or school weekly, offering routine check‑ups, vaccinations, wound care and mental health screeners, would cut travel time dramatically for many families. It would also help people who are nervous about visiting a traditional clinic, by providing a familiar, community setting. To work well, these services should be published in advance, with clear booking options and accessible transport arrangements. The presence of on‑site interpreters or multilingual staff would help with inclusivity too.

Outreach and integrated care teams are key. Regular health‑visitor and nurse outreach to care homes, workplaces and community groups would catch issues earlier and reduce avoidable GP visits. For mental health, mobile or outreach counselling and crisis support in convenient community settings could stabilise situations before they escalate, while still offering rapid in‑person care when needed. Where possible, pairing outreach with social support services—housing, debt advice, nutrition—creates a more holistic safety net which improves engagement with health services.

Telehealth hubs are another important pillar, provided that access remains genuinely flexible and inclusive. Establishing telehealth hubs in libraries, community centres or within GP practices—equipped with user‑friendly devices, free Wi‑Fi and trained staff to help people login and book appointments—would expand choices. A hub could host video or telephone triage, allowing nurses or GP assistants to direct patients quickly to the right service. For chronic or long‑term conditions, remote monitoring and e‑consultations can reduce unnecessary trips to clinics, freeing up slots for those who truly need in‑person care.

Of course, incentives must back these changes. Longer or weekend clinic hours, more flexible appointment slots, and rural recruitment packages can make working in or serving rural areas more attractive. Extra funding to support travel time, locum coverage, and shared working spaces would help GP practices offer timelier care without burning out staff. Encouraging co‑location or partnerships with pharmacists, community pharmacies and voluntary groups could also improve aftercare and compliance, which in turn reduces repeat visits.

Expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care is essential, but non‑digital alternatives must remain strong and accessible. Online booking and e‑consults can streamline routine issues and triage, shortening wait times. However, not everyone can use digital tools—older patients, those with sensory impairments, or people without reliable internet may struggle. A robust phone triage line, paper forms, and in‑person walk‑in slots should be retained. Staff in each facility could offer “digital‑champion” support for those who want to learn, and carers or family members should be able to help with consent and scheduling if the patient agrees.

In my experience, online booking has helped with smaller, non‑urgent concerns and allowed our family to secure a same‑day appointment when a child was unwell at short notice. But my elderly neighbour finds the apps confusing and would prefer a simple phone call or a visit if needed. A local practice that runs a monthly outreach clinic at the village hall has been popular, yet it is not always easy to coordinate transport. If we could scale up such outreach, with a regular predictable timetable and clear signposting, it would reduce stress for families and individuals who are already juggling work, childcare and caring responsibilities.

A practical plan in our area could include: (1) a published weekly schedule for mobile GP and mental health van visits with extended hours; (2) a network of telehealth hubs supported by trained staff to assist with login, device use and privacy; (3) incentives for clinics to extend hours and to recruit staff willing to work in rural or mobility‑limited settings; (4) continued strong booking and triage options by phone and in person, alongside online services; (5) partnerships with community spaces (libraries, community centres, schools) to host drop‑in clinics and information sessions.

Overall, I want care to come to people, not always require people to come to care. A blended model that prioritises timeliness, respects different levels of digital access, and keeps personal, local contacts at the heart of care will improve outcomes, reduce unnecessary hospital attendance and, importantly, support people when they need it most. I welcome proposals that deliver practical, funded, and scalable versions of these changes, with clear timelines and measurable benefits for patients across our communities.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP and mental health services is uneven, especially outside cities. Changes that would help include growing the primary care workforce through targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, and practical incentives like better pay, flexible hours, and solid wellbeing support to keep staff from burning out. This needs to be paired with ongoing training and realistic workloads so gains aren’t temporary. For mental health, more integrated teams and local crisis and early-intervention options would make a real difference.

We also need smarter triage and booking. NHS111 and clinical triage should route urgent cases quickly, with clear same-day GP slots, better care navigation to steer people to the right service, and less duplication across systems. A shared digital booking platform with real-time availability and straightforward reminders would reduce missed appointments and confusion.

Addressing transport, parking and premises deficits is essential for rural and mobility‑restricted residents. I’d back mobile clinics, outreach at community hubs like libraries, and telehealth hubs, plus incentives for practices to provide extended or weekend appointments in hard-to-reach areas. In my view, a blended package—staff recruitment and retention, smarter digital systems, and accessible local services—offers the best path to consistent, timely care. For someone juggling shifts, these changes could genuinely reduce delays and stress.

Agree. Expanding multidisciplinary teams in GP practices across Wales would greatly improve timely access to GP, community health, and mental health services. When I had a minor back problem last year, a physio assessment via a GP-led triage would have saved days of waiting. Having pharmacists and physiotherapists handle routine reviews, injections, minor injuries, and medication reconciliations would free GPs to focus on complex or vulnerable patients. Paramedics or physician associates embedded in primary care could see routine cases quickly, with robust handovers to GPs when issues escalate, reducing unnecessary A&E visits.

Protecting continuity of care and extending appointment times for those with chronic conditions or mental health struggles is vital. For my relative managing diabetes and anxiety, longer, same-clinician appointments would improve management, reduce hospital admissions, and prevent repeated tests. Consistent relationships enable better medication adherence, early recognition of complications, and safer deprescribing where appropriate.

I’d also value reliable digital booking and triage so people in rural areas aren’t waiting days, and community teams linked to GP practices to support home visits where needed. Overall, this approach seems to deliver better outcomes and efficiency.

I welcome a clear focus on making timely GP, community health and mental health services more accessible. In practice, the main barrier I’ve seen is the mismatch between demand and the hours and capacity available. My area often has a limited number of appointment slots, and after-work hours are particularly tight. That means families like mine end up juggling work, school runs and urgent needs while trying to secure a reasonable, same-week appointment. I’ve also heard from neighbours about long waits for talking therapies, and I’ve watched the stress this creates for people trying to stay on top of chronic conditions.

I think the most effective changes would combine expanding capacity with smarter scheduling, plus targeted options for evenings and weekends. Specifically, I’d support measures to:

- Increase appointment slots and session capacity across the board by hiring more GPs, nurse practitioners, and therapists, expanding session lengths where appropriate, and improving scheduling systems. In practice this could mean longer-term recruitment from GP training pipelines, better retention packages for experienced clinicians, and more flexible use of allied health professionals such as physiotherapists and pharmacists to handle appropriate cases. A more efficient front desk and triage process—so people are directed to the right clinician first time—would also cut wasted slots and keep the service moving.

- Introduce evening and weekend clinics, with guaranteed same-day urgent slots where clinically appropriate. For working people, late openings and Saturday slots would be a real lifeline for non-urgent but time-sensitive issues, reducing the need to take time off work or wait weeks for a visit. The key here is genuine guarantees: if something is urgent, there should be a same-day or next-day slot with a clinician who can assess and triage appropriately. I’d expect this to be rolled out as pilots in several practices first, with clear metrics on access, wait times and patient satisfaction before wider rollout.

- Improve mental health access by expanding the capacity of IAPT and community mental health teams, and by combining that with flexible delivery models. My experience and hearing from others is that waiting times for therapy can be long, even when a referral is made. A practical improvement would be same-day or rapid access triage with a clinician who can offer brief, evidence-based interventions and fast-tracking to longer-term therapy where needed. Video or phone appointments should be available as a standard option, alongside in-person sessions, to reduce barriers for those who work irregular hours or have caring responsibilities.

- Strengthen community health services and integration: more district nursing capacity, physiotherapy and occupational therapy available through integrated clinics, with stronger care coordination so patients don’t have to repeat information to multiple teams. A pharmacist-led approach to minor ailments and medication reviews could also relieve GP pressures where appropriate. When services work together smoothly, a patient can be routed to the best professional without delays.

- Ensure equity and patient safety: expansion must reach rural as well as urban areas and must be accessible to people with disabilities or limited digital access. Any increase in hours should be matched with staffing plans that protect clinicians from burnout and maintain high standards of care. Frontline staff will need robust IT, administrative support and clear escalation paths for urgent cases.

From personal experience, a few concrete changes would make a real difference: an agreed after-hours GP slot for non-emergency issues, predictable and publicly posted wait times, and a system that confirms urgent slots within hours when a medical need arises. For mental health, a guaranteed quick triage pathway and more community-based options would reduce crises and improve outcomes. For chronic conditions, more flexible scheduling and shared-care plans—so patients can see a nurse practitioner or physiotherapist for routine issues without waiting for a GP appointment—would be highly beneficial.

I’m supportive of these changes in principle, but they must be implemented with proper funding, workforce planning, and ongoing evaluation. There should be pilot schemes with transparent reporting on access, outcome measures, and workforce wellbeing, followed by scale-up only where there is demonstrable improvement and sustainability. If done thoughtfully, this approach could make timely care a reality for more people, reduce avoidable crises, and create a more resilient local health system for the long term.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven in our area. I’d favour a package that makes today’s triage and booking work more smoothly, while also planning for the longer term. In the short term, a more reliable NHS111 and clinical triage system that properly flags urgent cases and routes people to the right service is essential. Real-time GP availability, same-day slots where appropriate, and a booking system that cuts out duplication and repetitive calls would remove a lot of the friction people experience. A clear care-navigation pathway would help patients choose the right service first time, reducing wasted appointments and bottlenecks.

For the medium term, expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will help sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. In my experience, capacity constraints are felt most acutely in mental health waiting times and after-hours access.

Equity must be at the core. Increasing interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus targeted outreach to deprived, ethnic minority and migrant communities, are essential to close access gaps. Practical steps include multilingual information, outreach in community venues, and monitoring wait times by demographic group to ensure improvements are shared fairly.

Overall, I’d support a coordinated approach that improves triage today, expands the workforce for tomorrow, and tackles language and access barriers in tandem.

I want to see changes that deliver real, practical improvements now, rather than relying mainly on longer training pipelines. In our area, many people struggle to get a same-day GP appointment, and mental health referrals can take weeks. My sister waited over a month for a routine check-up last autumn, and a relative with anxiety waited 3–4 weeks for talking therapies to start. The immediate fixes matter most. 

I do understand the argument for longer-term strategies to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals through more training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. However they won’t fix today’s delays and may divert funding away from current services if not carefully managed. Therefore I’d prioritise: 1) targeted recruitment incentives and better local contracts to attract staff where shortages hit hardest; 2) wider use of qualified allied professionals (pharmacists, physiotherapists, mental health practitioners) to handle routine and urgent cases; 3) extended hours and community urgent care hubs to take pressure off GP clinics; 4) faster and safer return‑to‑practice pathways with clear competency checks; 5) improvements to appointment booking and triage systems so urgent cases are prioritised. 

In short, combine practical short‑term fixes with the long‑term workforce plan, but don’t let the latter delay the former.

We support strengthening NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and streamline patient flow, improving timely access across GP, community and mental health services.

Living here, I know how hard it can be to get timely GP, community health or mental health support. The changes that would help most, in my view, are a mix of extended hours, a reliable same-day urgent slot, and a stronger, well-supported workforce.

Evening and weekend clinics would make appointments possible for people like me who work part-time or care for a partner, without sacrificing daytime commitments. I disagree with the idea that simply piling more GP appointments will most effectively improve timely access. In my area, waits for a GP can be long, but many of those visits could be handled by other professionals who are trained for common issues. If we expanded teams with pharmacists to do medicines reviews and minor illness triage, physiotherapists to manage musculoskeletal problems, paramedics and physician associates to handle triage and follow-ups, GPs would have more time for complex cases and safety checks. For mental health, a joined-up hub with a mental health nurse and qualified counsellor providing same-day triage would hasten support and reduce crises. We also need to grow appointment slots across disciplines through targeted recruitment, extended hours, and smarter scheduling, including weekend clinics and same-day triage blocks. In rural Wales, a community clinic where a pharmacist, physio and nurse share slot space alongside GPs would cut travel, shorten waits, and keep people out of hospital. This coordinated approach is what would really improve timely access.

Access to timely GP, nurse and therapist appointments is uneven in our area. I think increasing slots and session capacity is essential—more GPs and practice nurses, plus longer or additional mental health sessions. In rural Scotland waits for routine appointments can stretch to weeks, so extending hours (evenings and weekends) and smarter scheduling would help, provided it’s matched by solid workforce planning to avoid burnout and maintain quality. 

I also support strengthening NHS111, clinical triage and the booking system so urgent cases are prioritised and patients don’t bounce between services. A reliable triage process that links directly to GP and therapist slots could cut duplication and reduce pointless journeys. In my experience, tangled booking messages can create delays and confusion, especially for those with mobility issues.

Transport, parking and premises gaps still bottleneck access. Mobile clinics and targeted outreach for remote communities, plus telehealth hubs in community spaces with some practical IT and transport support, could bridge gaps. Incentives for practices to expand premises or improve parking, and shared care navigation to steer people to the right service first time, would help those of us who struggle to travel. A couple of concrete pilots—e.g., a nurse/physio van visiting every two weeks and a local telehealth point at a library—would be a good start, with monitoring and local input.

I think the changes proposed to improve timely access are right, and I’d support them strongly. Prioritising urgent cases through better NHS111 and clinical triage, combined with streamlined booking and care navigation, would cut duplication and get people to the right service quickly. An integrated online system that shows real-time GP, nurse, and urgent care slots would save hours of phone calls and anxiety; it could direct non-urgent cases to digital care where appropriate while fast-tracking those with urgent needs.

Protecting continuity of care and allowing longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients would also pay dividends. When people see the same clinician for follow-ups, outcomes improve and repeat visits fall. Longer slots for long‑term conditions and mental health checks should be standard practice, with sensible routing to specialists when needed.

To deliver this, we need to grow and retain primary care staff: targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, fair pay, flexible hours, and robust wellbeing support. More GPs, practice nurses, and integrated mental health and community teams are essential so patients aren’t left waiting.

In my experience, a coordinated system that blends triage, booking and continuity delivers timely, safer care and reduces the stress of navigating NHS services.

Living in England and juggling a full-time job with family and caring responsibilities, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services isn’t a luxury – it’s a necessity. I’d support changes that make it easier to get seen when it’s urgent and to keep people out of hospital by addressing both supply and continuity of care. In practical terms, that means several concrete steps that would fit well with what many practices are already trying to do, but require systemic backing to work reliably.

First, we need more flexible appointment options. Evening and weekend clinics should be normal, not exceptional. I’m not asking for a luxury; I’m asking for routine after-work slots and a guaranteed same-day urgent slot when people have a sudden flare-up or a non-emergency problem that simply can’t wait. In my area, it’s common to miss work to attend a daytime appointment, or to wait two weeks for a non-urgent slot. If practices could offer at least two evenings per week and a Saturday morning clinic, with the option of same-day triage for urgent issues, that would make a real difference to working people and to families with school-age children. To make this workable, clinicians could use a robust telephone or video triage system to identify those who truly need to be seen the same day and to direct others to the most appropriate care (pharmacy advice, online resources, or a planned appointment).

Second, we must address the recruitment and retention of primary care staff. The workload on GPs, nurses and other staff is unsustainable in many areas. A package of targeted recruitment, smart international hiring, enhanced pay where warranted, flexible working patterns, and strong wellbeing support would help attract and keep the teams we need. In practice, this could include streamlined visa routes and relocation incentives for international candidates, longer-term contracts that offer predictability, and banked or pool cover so practices aren’t left short when a clinician is off sick or on leave. Local practices benefit from flexible shift patterns that protect time with patients rather than packing days with back-to-back, pressurised slots. And crucially, wellbeing and supportive supervision should be built into every role so staff feel valued and supported, reducing burnout and turnover.

Third, protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. For many people, especially the elderly, those with long-term conditions, or those with mental health needs, continuity makes a big difference to outcomes. I would support extending the standard consultation length for complex cases—ideally 20 minutes for general practice and longer for mental health evaluations—so clinicians can gather full histories, review medications, and coordinate with community services in one sitting. Named GP arrangements and stable patient lists help families build trust and reduce the need for repeat visits. When a patient sees a familiar clinician, the chances of miscommunication drop, and the opportunity to spot subtle changes early increases, which can avert crises and hospital visits.

I’ve seen how gaps in access push people toward A&E or urgent care services, often for problems that could be managed in primary care with better scheduling and more time. For instance, a family member with a chronic condition needed a rapid review after a medication change, but we were offered a 15-minute slot two weeks later. A longer appointment with continuity would have allowed the clinician to review the medication interaction, adjust plans and teach self-management skills, reducing downstream visits. With better after-hours access and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, more issues could be resolved before they escalate.

Finally, meaningful integration with community health and mental health services is essential. GP practices should have closer links with district nurses, social care, pharmacy teams and mental health professionals to coordinate care plans. For mental health, that means same-day access to an initial assessment when someone presents with acute distress, dedicated time slots with a clinician trained in early intervention, and a clear pathway to rapid follow-up or crisis support if needed. Home visits or community outreach for those with mobility issues or low digital literacy can prevent deterioration in health and reduce hospital admissions.

If these changes are implemented, I’m confident we’d see fewer avoidable visits to urgent care, better management of chronic conditions, and improved outcomes for vulnerable patients. It would take coordinated funding, workforce planning and a commitment to flexible, person-centred care, but the benefits to patients, families and the health system would be tangible and lasting.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in Scotland remains uneven, and I’ve felt the strain personally. To improve this, I’d prioritise expanding community mental health teams with robust early intervention, crisis response and accessible talking therapies. When people get timely support, it reduces hospital admissions and helps achieve parity with physical health services. In my area, waits for a GP appointment can stretch to two weeks, and mental health services often have month‑long delays before assessment. Strengthening crisis teams and offering same‑day phone or video triage would keep people out of A&E and prevent deterioration.

There’s value in expanding multidisciplinary teams that include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine cases and free GPs for more complex care. But this must be coupled with clear supervision, integrated notes and defined handovers to avoid fragmentation. Growth of the GP, nurse and mental health workforce must be sustainable—more training places on their own won’t fix things unless there’s return‑to‑practice support, CPD, apprenticeships and real career progression. In rural Scotland, extra funding for transport and digital connectivity would help people access services where distance worsens delays. Overall I’d like a coherent plan that reduces waits, aligns mental and physical health pathways, and remembers frontline staff need manageable workloads.

From my experience in England, the strain on GP services is evident. Too many people wait weeks for routine appointments; mental health care often lags behind physical health in access and urgency. I would like to see a substantial expansion of community mental health teams, with robust early intervention and crisis response, plus more accessible talking therapies so people aren't left waiting while their condition worsens. When crisis lines are swift, outcomes improve and hospital admissions fall.

Equally, expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates working alongside GPs—would let routine cases be managed quickly and efficiently, freeing GPs to focus on complex or high-risk patients. In my practice area, patients with simple musculoskeletal issues or medication queries could be routed to a clinician with the right skills, rather than clogging GP time.

On access, transport and premises are real barriers. I support mobile clinics, outreach in supermarkets or community hubs, and telehealth hubs, especially for rural or mobility‑limited residents. Incentives to attract staff to rural posts would help too. All changes must be underpinned by seamless data sharing and consistent care pathways.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area, I would prioritise targeted resources for those most likely to be blocked by language, culture or deprivation. Key changes would include:
- Expand interpreters and translation across GP practices, triage lines and mental health services, including urgent calls, with clear funding for in-person, phone and video interpretation so language is not a barrier to timely care.
- Recruit and retain staff from local communities and deliver mandatory cultural competence training for all frontline staff, with anti-racism and anti-discrimination standards.
- Proactive outreach via trusted community organisations, faith groups, schools and community hubs to raise awareness of services, explain referral pathways and co-design solutions with marginalised groups.
- Bring services closer to people: mobile clinics and pop-up sessions in deprived areas, extended hours (evenings/weekends), and simplified appointment booking for non-English speakers.
- Improve digital and paperwork accessibility: multilingual online booking, simple forms, and carer support to assist with navigation.
- Strengthen data and accountability: collect and publish waiting-time data by language and ethnicity, with quarterly targets and review.

In experience, families with limited English report delayed mental-health referrals and access due to scarce interpreters; where local groups partner with clinics, uptake improves and waits shorten. A dedicated funding stream for interpreters, culturally competent training and co-designed outreach would make these changes feasible and effective.

From our organisation in England, I welcome a blended approach to improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In the long term, expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is essential to sustainably meet demand and reduce burnout. In our area, where gaps in workforce have caused longer waits, the introduction of nurse practitioners and supported return-to-work clinicians has noticeably shortened response times for urgent issues and relieved pressure on GP clinics. 

At the same time, practical improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation are urgently needed to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and streamline patient flow. Better online booking, clear same-day triage and transparent care pathways would stop patients bouncing between services and help them access the right care faster. Importantly, we must protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients; longer slots and stable clinician pairs reduce repeat visits and improve outcomes. 

Any reform must be accompanied by robust metrics and user-friendly feedback loops to track wait times, equity of access and patient satisfaction across communities, so we can course-correct quickly where things aren’t working.

Agree. To improve timely access in our area, I’d prioritise targeted resources and workforce development. First, ensure interpreters and culturally competent staff are available across GP surgeries and community health services. In practice I’ve seen families struggle because there’s no translator for a diabetes review, and information about mental health support isn’t shared in a language they understand. Local outreach via community groups, schools and places of worship could inform people about services and help reduce stigma. Also, extend opening hours, including evenings and Saturdays, and provide mobile clinics in deprived estates to reach those far from the health centre.

Second, grow the long-term workforce. Increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals; expand return-to-practice schemes to help experienced clinicians rejoin; create apprenticeships and funded CPD so staff keep skills up to date and can take on new roles in primary care and community mental health.

Additional steps: easier online booking with language options, triage that routes urgent cases to same-day slots, and longer appointment times for complex cases. These changes would reduce wait times and improve care for marginalised groups while building a sustainable workforce for the future.

From a young resident of England, I back targeted changes that speed up urgent access but still keep care inclusive. Strengthening NHS111 and clinical triage to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplications, and simplify patient flow could stop people chasing appointments for days. For example, last term I needed a same-day GP slot and ended up on several calls and a looping path before being told to book online; a clearer, safer triage route would save everyone time and reduce stress.

I support expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care, but only if there are non-digital routes and support for those without reliable internet, smartphone access, or private space. In my student household I can use online slots; a friend relies on phone bookings and a walk-in clinic. We also need privacy safeguards; clinicians should combine triage with proper clinical judgement, not rely on automation alone.

Practical steps: a single care-navigation service to guide people through GP, mental health and community services; integrated appointment systems that avoid repeating information; more same-day slots outside standard hours; clear communication about expected wait times. Pilot these locally and learn what works for younger people and for family members who aren’t digitally connected.

it's outrageous that expanding multidisciplinary teams to manage routine cases could free GPs for complex care, but requires stable funding and clear governance. Prioritise targeted recruitment, international hiring, pay improvements, flexible hours and wellbeing support. Also offer evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots for working people's needs!

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for my area. The main barriers are transport, parking and the limits of premises in rural or mobility‑restricted settings. Practical changes would include mobile clinics visiting villages on a regular schedule, outreach into schools and care homes, and telehealth hubs housed in local libraries or community centres. These would cut travel time, ease parking pressures, and keep people connected with care when a full clinic visit isn't possible. In addition, offering incentives to attract and retain GPs, nurses and mental health clinicians—targeted recruitment, international hires where appropriate, better pay, flexible shifts and wellbeing support—would fill gaps and reduce burnout. For the long term, more training places, return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD are vital so staff can specialise and stay locally. In my experience, a telehealth hub nearby reduced unnecessary trips, and a pop‑up mobile clinic helped my neighbour access a quick check without a long journey.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains a major concern. A routine GP appointment last year was two weeks away, and a mental health referral after a crisis took several weeks to even triage. Fragmentation between services means I often have to repeat my history and chase different teams separately.

The changes that would help most are: first, invest in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners. If a hub offers same-day triage, rapid referrals, and a shared care plan, with staff able to access a single, up-to-date record, care becomes seamless and less stressful for patients.

Second, increase capacity by expanding appointment slots and session lengths through hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, and smarter scheduling, including some evenings and weekends to fit work patterns. Improving triage so urgent needs are prioritised is essential.

Third, to sustain improvements, use targeted recruitment plus international hires where appropriate, offer incentives, flexible working arrangements and wellbeing support to retain staff. Clear governance and patient involvement in service design are critical to ensure changes work for people like me.

With the right funding and leadership, these approaches could substantially reduce waits and deliver more holistic care in our community.

absolutely as an organisation representing local health and social care networks in England, we support moves to improve timely access, but we have serious concerns about how this would work on the ground in rural and mobility‑limited areas.

Transport, parking and premises deficits remain the biggest barrier. Patients face long drives, unreliable bus routes and scarce parking near clinics, which compounds delays for GP, community and mental health appointments. We welcome the idea of mobile clinics visiting village halls and care hubs on a rotating schedule, plus targeted outreach by community nurses and pharmacists. Telehealth hubs, with booked slots at accessible community venues, could cut unnecessary travel if funded and staffed adequately. Incentives to attract GPs, nurses and therapists to rural roles—relocation grants, enhanced salary bands, protected sessions—are essential; without them, flexible models will not stick.

Co‑located community hubs integrating primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners could streamline care, reduce duplication and improve information sharing. However, success hinges on clear governance, data sharing agreements, ring‑fenced funding and patient choice. Start with pilot hubs in a few areas, measure patient outcomes, and ensure privacy and accessible spaces.

Finally, ramping up capacity—more appointment slots, longer sessions, optimized scheduling and staffing—we should pursue in parallel but tied to the above transport and hub models. In practice, a blended approach feels most workable, with real local co‑production and clear timelines!

I support expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine care, freeing GPs for complex cases. Also increasing appointment slots and improving triage/booking through NHS111 to prioritise urgent needs and reduce waits.

As an organisation working with communities across England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven and frustrating for many residents. In our area, routine GP appointments are often booked weeks ahead, mental health assessments can take several weeks, and community physiotherapy slots are booked solid well in advance.

- Increase capacity now: recruit more GPs, practice nurses and therapists; expand session lengths and extend opening hours (including some evenings and Saturdays) to offer additional slots and reduce bottlenecks. Implement robust same‑day triage so urgent cases aren’t left waiting.
- Improve scheduling and care pathways: adopt smarter appointment systems, greater cross‑practice rosters or multi‑practice hubs, and digital triage to ensure people are routed to the right clinician first time; use reminders and flexible booking to reduce missed slots.
- Long‑term workforce planning: expand training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals; grow return‑to‑practice programmes, apprenticeships and CPD; fund retention and supportive work environments to stabilise the workforce.
- Mental health and community teams: invest in faster triage and more front‑line therapists; strengthen integrated community teams to handle more care locally and reduce unnecessary hospital referrals.

Evidence from our network shows a local GP practice could operate around 40 extra hours weekly with more staff; a parent reported waiting three weeks for a GP slot; someone else faced a two‑month wait for initial mental health support. These changes must be matched by sustained funding and governance to deliver reliable access.

i strongly believe access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area is often slow, especially for urgent mental health needs. I would strongly support expanding community mental health teams, with quicker access to talking therapies, early intervention, and a robust crisis response. By linking GPs with psychologists, social workers and youth specialists, we can reduce waits and improve outcomes. Guaranteed same-day urgent slots and dedicated crisis hubs for evenings and weekends would help working people and those with non-emergency but urgent needs.

Staffing is the bottleneck. I back targeted recruitment, including international hires, better pay, flexible working, and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care teams. In practice, a local clinic offering extended hours—late evenings or weekend slots—would cut down missed work and prevent unnecessary A&E visits. From my experience, longer appointment times for complex cases and consistent GP continuity would also build trust and reduce repeat visits.

Overall, this combination would shorten waits, improve parity between physical and mental health services, and keep care local and timely!

While I recognise the aim to improve timely access, I’m not convinced the current package will deliver in my area. Expanding community mental health teams and early intervention is essential, but it will fail without a solid plan to recruit, train and retain staff. In the last year our GP practice relied on locums, and appointments have shrink-wrapped into two-week slots; a same-day urgent slot is too often unavailable. Extending hours to evenings and weekends could help working people, but only if there’s enough staff to cover those hours and protect wellbeing—otherwise it adds burden, not access. 

I welcome targeted recruitment, including international hires and pay improvements, yet I fear numbers promised won’t translate into stable teams. Flexible working is good in principle, but it must be backed by real buffers, telephony triage and dependable wellbeing support so staff don’t burn out. 

For mental health, crisis response and talking therapies are vital, but waiting times for CBT or counselling remain unacceptable. I’d like to see guaranteed same-day urgent slots at local hubs, clear rapid triage pathways, and real investment to keep services integrated across GP, community and mental health. Without that, changes risk being cosmetic.

absolutely support investing in co-located hubs that blend GP, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners for seamless local care, plus expanding training and return-to-practice routes to sustain staff!

I don’t think simply increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots will automatically deliver timely access, and I’m not convinced current plans have the right balance between expanded capacity and real-world feasibility. In my experience, waits aren’t just about how many slots exist on paper—they’re about who fills them, how consistently care is delivered, and whether people from marginalised groups feel able to use the system without risking delays or misunderstandings.

Firstly, boosting the number of slots sounds straightforward, but it presumes we can recruit and retain staff fast enough to keep them filled. The NHS is already struggling to recruit GPs, nurses and therapists long-term; even when new posts are advertised, it can take many months to fill them and longer to build a stable team. Hiring more locums or short-term contractors can fill the gap temporarily, but it ruins continuity of care, which matters for chronic conditions and mental health. My local practice has added a few evening slots on paper, yet the actual appointments are often with different clinicians week to week, making it hard to build trust and to manage ongoing treatment effectively.

Second, there’s a risk that “optimised scheduling” ends up benefitting the system more than patients. If triage and booking rely on complex digital systems, some people—particularly older residents, those with limited broadband or digital literacy, and those who speak little English—are left behind. A good booking system needs to be simple, reliable and backed by human support. In practice I’ve seen situations where a phone call is answered by a voicemail during peak times, or where interpreter requests create bottlenecks and delays simply because there isn’t enough staff to handle multilingual bookings smoothly.

On the issue of interpreters and culturally competent staff, increasing staff slots without ensuring quality, language access and cultural trust will not close the gaps. Interpreters are essential for many in deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups, but simply increasing the number of appointments isn’t enough if language barriers still derail the consultation, or if patients fear stigma, discrimination or privacy concerns.
