Outreach programmes can help, but they require sustained funding, long lead times and genuine community involvement. In some areas, outreach projects exist in name but are thin on the ground in practice, leaving people to navigate a system that feels alien and unfriendly.

Moreover, access gaps aren’t only about language. Transport, work patterns, childcare, and flexible hours affect when people can attend. In communities I know, people struggle to attend daytime GP slots because they’re essential workers or carers. Expanding slots without also offering truly accessible after-hours services or location-embedded community hubs won’t reach those who most need care.

So what would work better, in my view? I’d prioritise a holistic workforce strategy: long-term investment to train and retain GPs, nurse prescribers, and therapists, with stable teams rather than a churn of contractors. Fund dedicated care navigators who can help patients book across GP practices, community health teams, and mental health services, taking language and literacy needs into account. Ensure interpreters are available across all contact points, with consistent scheduling capacity, so language isn’t a barrier to timely care. Invest in culturally competent recruitment, including bilingual staff from local communities, and support ongoing cultural competency training for all front-line staff. Build stronger, community-based access points in areas with high deprivation, where trusted relationships with local groups can streamline referrals and reduce avoidable hospital visits.

Finally, any expansion should come with clear, measurable targets: reduce average wait times by a defined percentage, improve continuity of care scores, and demonstrate better access for non-English speakers and marginalised groups. Without that, we risk paying for more appointments that still don’t land where they’re needed most.

Thank you for considering these points. I want improvements, but I’m concerned the current emphasis on sheer slot numbers won’t deliver equitable, timely access without addressing recruitment, continuity, language access and genuinely inclusive outreach.

In Northern Ireland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most with a hybrid model that combines expanded online booking, e-consultations and remote care with strong non-digital options and support. Online systems are convenient for many, but they risk excluding older people, those with limited broadband or without devices. I’ve seen neighbours struggle to get a quick appointment when the online slot was taken and phone lines were busy; a simple multilingual phone line or a paper form would have resolved it sooner. For mental health, triage via digital means can help, but there must be rapid in-person assessment pathways where needed.

We also need targeted resources to reduce access gaps: more interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach teams in deprived or migrant communities. Mobile clinics, community hubs and extended hours in GP practices would help people who cannot attend standard daytime slots. Data monitoring by area and ethnicity would help identify gaps and drive local outreach. A robust hybrid system, with non-digital access options and ongoing investment in interpreters and community engagement, should be the default so no one is left behind.

I think the most effective changes would be to invest in the people who deliver these services. Increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals in Scotland, with funded posts in rural and community settings, would steadily grow capacity and improve reliability of access. A robust return-to-practice offer—paid refresher courses, flexible re-entry timelines and strong mentoring—would bring skilled clinicians back into practice more quickly and safely. 

We should also expand apprenticeships so more practice nurses, healthcare assistants and mental health workers can train on the job, with clear career progression. Coupled with ongoing CPD funded by NHS boards, staff can keep up-to-date without bearing extra financial strain, which is vital for long-term retention. 

In my area, when the local GP vacancy is long, patients experience delays and stress. I’ve seen a retired nurse in the community re-train through a short refresher and return to work in a local hub, helping triage and support mental health referrals. A network of co-located teams and supported digital triage would reduce unnecessary waits. 

If these changes are funded and delivered, we would see steadier access to daytime GP appointments, timely community nursing care, and earlier mental health support, especially for our older residents.

From a youth-focused community organisation in England, I disagree that simply expanding online booking will fix timely access. The biggest gains come from protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When a patient with long-term mental health issues sees the same clinician who understands their history, outcomes improve and repeat visits fall. Short slots and frequent handoffs just push problems into the next appointment. 

We also need to grow and retain primary care staff. That means targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible working and wellbeing support to stop burnout and vacancies we’ve seen locally. A stable, well-supported team is the backbone of timely access.

Finally, keep online options but ensure non-digital routes remain. The digital divide excludes older people and those with limited data or devices. A hybrid system with online booking and e-consults, plus robust phone triage and in-person slots, would work best in practice, with clear triage guidance about when each path is appropriate. If changes prioritise continuity, staffing and hybrid access, they’ll genuinely improve timely access and reduce avoidable crises.

In Scotland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will come most quickly from growing and retaining the workforce while expanding capacity. I support targeted recruitment, including international hiring, with attractive pay, flexible working options (job sharing, late clinics, weekend slots) and robust wellbeing support so staff stay motivated and healthy. A package of relocation grants and return-to-practice schemes would help fill vacancies faster. I also back expanding appointment capacity by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists and by extending session lengths and hours. Practical steps would be more early-morning and late-evening slots, additional GP partner roles, nurse-led clinics and more community therapy hours. Digital triage plus reliable same-day booking would reduce wasted slots and patient frustration. In my area, a local practice trialled extended hours and added two therapists; wait times for talking therapies dropped noticeably and same-day GP slots increased. With sustained investment and good management, these changes should bring faster, local care for families and reduce pressure on hospital services.

Agree: mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs would reach rural and mobility-limited patients, plus better transport and parking. Also expand training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff long-term.

I’m glad the focus is on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely. Expanding community mental health teams, boosting early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies would reduce waits and help parity with physical health. If there were larger, integrated teams with straightforward access for urgent mental health issues, someone could be seen within 24 hours instead of waiting weeks. Early intervention for anxiety or emerging psychosis can stop deterioration and cut hospital admissions. I’ve seen friends struggle to secure timely talking therapies; a guaranteed pathway to CBT or EMDR within a few weeks would make a real difference.

Improving NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation would prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and simplify patient flow. A single, efficient triage process that guides people to the right service saves time and stress. And offering evening and weekend GP and mental health clinics, with guaranteed same-day urgent slots for non-emergency needs, would really help working people and those who can’t take time off during the day. These changes would build a smoother, more reliable route to care when people need it most.

I’m supportive of changes to improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services in Wales. To make this work, we should: 1) increase training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. More trainees on placement in our practice tends to open up appointment slots sooner and keeps staff from leaving. 2) invest in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners. A hub with GP, district nursing, talking therapies, pharmacy and carers’ support in one place would cut travel and waiting times. 3) protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Longer, ongoing appointments with the same clinician reduce repeat visits and hospital admissions. These changes would strengthen local, sustainable care for families and people with long-term needs, and help prevent crises before they arise. Please consider them in the policy.

I live in England and, like many others I know, I want timely, holistic care that doesn’t feel like navigating a maze. I strongly support the changes proposed to improve access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. The combination of co‑located hubs, expanded multidisciplinary teams and greater appointment capacity could genuinely transform how people experience local care.

Co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners would make a real difference to day‑to‑day health needs. When services sit in one place with a shared care plan, you avoid the back‑and‑forth between different buildings and phone lines. In areas where I’ve seen pilots of this approach, people can be triaged on the same day, referrals are coordinated quickly, and a consistent point of contact is established for complex needs. It reduces stress, saves time, and means families don’t have to chase multiple teams separately. I’d like to see more hubs with genuine ease of access—same‑day triage, same‑week appointments, and clear routes to social support if someone needs it.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams to include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates would allow routine cases to be treated outside of GP time, freeing GPs to focus on more complex care. For example, a pharmacist can review medications and adjust doses or flag interactions during a short consult, which often prevents problems from escalating. A physiotherapist can assess and manage common musculoskeletal issues, which often means quicker relief for patients and fewer GP visits. Paramedics and physician associates could handle home visits or quick check‑ins, which is invaluable for people who are frail, live in rural locations, or struggle to travel. In practice, this means a patient presenting with a knee pain or a persistent cough could receive expert input from the most appropriate team member within days rather than waiting weeks, with a clear plan all in one place.

Increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots and session capacity through targeted hiring, session expansion and optimised scheduling would bring down the long waits that frustrate patients and disrupt work and family life. Our practice has started some extended hours and online booking, which helps a little, but it isn’t enough across the board. If every practice could offer a mix of longer chronic‑disease review slots, more same‑week mental health appointments, and flexible evening or weekend slots, people would access early help and problems wouldn’t snowball into bigger crises. Better scheduling—simple triage pathways, visible wait times, and real‑time capacity updates—would also reduce unnecessary trips and wasted journeys.

Of course, delivering this at scale requires solid funding, strong governance and secure, interoperable IT systems so information can be shared safely between providers. It must be designed to work for rural residents, people in urban deprivation, and those who rely on VOSE partners for social support. Privacy protections and consent processes need to be clear, but with sensible data sharing agreements and common standards, care won’t be duplicated and patients won’t fall through gaps.

In summary, investing in co‑located hubs, expanding multidisciplinary teams and increasing appointment capacity would make access to GP, community health and mental health services more timely, predictable and person‑centred. I hope the programme is rolled out widely and kept under ongoing review so it can adapt to communities’ needs rather than becoming a one‑size‑fits‑all solution.

From my experience here in England, simply setting up evening and weekend GP clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots would not by itself deliver timely access, and could put unsustainable pressure on staff. Extending hours without enough clinicians and support staff risks cancellations, lower quality care, and burnout among receptionists and nurses I’ve spoken to. My local practice ran a weekend slot for a few months, but attendance was patchy and the extra shifts stretched the team thin; when the follow-up was needed, it still couldn't be guaranteed, and records weren’t always seamless with weekday GPs. 

What would help more is: a robust triage system by phone or online that directs urgent cases to the right clinician first time; guaranteed same-day urgent slots only if funded with extra permanent staffing; more practice nurses, physiotherapists and mental health professionals who can see patients quickly without always waiting for a GP; and integration with community services to avoid hospital referrals. Also practical issues like transport and local travel help for older residents. I want access, but not at the cost of quality or staff wellbeing.

Yes, I support expanding community mental health teams, improving early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waiting times and bring mental health on a similar footing to physical health. In our area, people often wait weeks for GP slots, and some turn to A&E when crises hit because timely community support isn’t available. Strengthening community mental health teams with rapid triage, home-based assessments and consistent follow-up would catch problems early and keep older residents safe at home. A friend with depression and a neighbour feeling isolated both benefited from timely talking therapies, but the wait was too long. Robust crisis-response services that can visit in the evenings or at weekends would prevent avoidable hospital admissions and give families reassurance.

On the workforce side, increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals long-term. I know clinicians who paused work to care for relatives; with proper retraining and flexible schemes they could return, easing shortages. More local recruitment and clear career progression would deliver stable, responsive services for years to come.
i really think more flexible GP booking and extended hours could help, but I’m unsure what mix would work best in my area!

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services could be improved by a balanced mix of more appointment slots and smarter delivery, plus targeted outreach where transport is a barrier. In my area, increasing capacity by hiring more nurses and therapists and expanding session lengths would help reduce waiting times, especially for ongoing care. Practical steps would include same-day triage slots, a few extended morning or evening clinics each week, and guaranteed follow-up within 48 hours for urgent concerns. It’s important these slots are backed by proper staffing and support so clinicians aren’t stretched thin and patients don’t face repeated cancellations.

On accessibility beyond the clinic walls, I’ve seen how parking and travel can delay care. Mobile clinics visiting village halls, town centres on market days, or healthcare vans staffed with nurses and mental health workers could reach rural residents and those with limited mobility. Telehealth hubs in community venues, with on-site assistance to use equipment, would help people who can’t easily travel. Incentives to attract clinicians to underserved areas, plus reliable IT systems that share notes across GPs, community services and mental health providers, are essential to make these changes work.

Overall, a combined approach—more slots with sensible scheduling, and mobile/telehealth options—would improve timeliness without compromising care quality for most people in the area.

i strongly believe from where I sit in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services could be significantly improved by two linked strands: a sustainable workforce expansion and targeted outreach that truly reaches deprived and minority communities. Key changes would include increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus enhanced return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD to grow capacity long term. It’s vital we fund robust supervision and mentoring so new staff are retained and skilled quickly across practices, community teams and remote hubs, not just in big cities. 

Equally important is targeted outreach: ensuring interpreters, multilingual booking lines, and culturally competent staff are readily available; employing patient navigators from local communities; and directing outreach to ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups who often face practical and language barriers. In my area we’ve seen real benefits when a bilingual nurse helped coordinate care and explain treatment options, while times when interpreters were unavailable led to missed follow-ups. I’d also support mobile clinics and home visits to reach those with transport issues or poor digital access, plus extended hours for urgent mental health triage.

In the short term, smarter scheduling and improved digital triage, backed by human support, would help while the workforce expands. Overall, I back long‑term workforce growth paired with focused outreach to close genuine access gaps!
Access should not be rushed; prioritise continuity and longer consultations for complex patients to reduce repeat visits and improve outcomes, even if this slows overall appointment availability.

In my area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if resources were targeted to deprived and marginalised communities, with robust interpreter support and staff who reflect local cultures. Practically this means ensuring on-demand interpreters (phone or video) across practices and translating appointment letters and patient information, plus deliberate recruitment and ongoing training for culturally competent staff. I’ve seen how language barriers lead to missed appointments and delayed care, especially for migrant families.

I’d also back genuine outreach: monthly pop-up clinics in community centres, faith venues and housing associations, staffed by multilingual health workers, with walk-in slots and straightforward sign-ups. Continuity of care matters, so patients should have a named GP or small care team and longer appointment times for complex or chronic conditions (20–30 minutes) to prevent repeat visits and fragmentation.

For mental health, faster access pathways and better integration with primary care are essential—same-day or rapid-access slots, shared care plans, and supported digital access with interpreters. Collecting data on wait times and language groups would help refine these efforts and ensure progress is visible to communities.

I strongly support policies to boost timely access by growing and retaining primary care staff, and by safeguarding continuity of care for those with complex needs. Key changes would be targeted recruitment and international hiring with streamlined visas, improved pay, and incentives, plus more flexible working patterns and meaningful wellbeing support. In my area, turnover and vacancies have left GP slots hard to come by and community nurses stretched thin, driving delays for routine checks and mental health triage. If practices could recruit faster—using targeted campaigns, short-term visa routes, relocation help and progression pay bands—we’d see more GPs and district nurses on the rota, with capacity for same- or next-day slots. Flexible hours, part-time options, and strong wellbeing programmes would help staff stay long-term. Equally important is protecting continuity of care and extending appointment times for complex, chronic or vulnerable patients to improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. I’ve seen the benefit when a named clinician manages a multi-condition care plan and when mental health workers are co-located in primary care, offering longer, coordinated appointments. Expanded integrated teams and better out-of-hours access would make a real difference.

it's outrageous that i strongly support evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, plus mobile clinics and telehealth hubs to reach rural areas, and expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care and free GPs for complex cases!

I think the changes that would most improve timely access are about smoothing patient flow and strengthening the frontline triage, not just increasing the number of appointments. In practice, that means a more robust NHS111 with clinical triage and capable care navigation to direct urgent cases to the right service first time. A single, transparent booking system that shows real-time GP, nurse, mental health and community slots would cut duplication and reduce the waiting around after a phone call. My own experience often involved multiple calls or being re-directed before I found someone who could help quickly; a streamlined digital pathway would have saved time and anxiety.

I also welcome the expansion of community mental health teams, with early intervention, crisis outreach and accessible talking therapies. In Scotland, rapid access pathways for young adults, and reliable crisis response teams, would help parity with physical health and prevent escalation. It’s important these services are well funded and staffed, including in rural areas, and that patient choice is preserved. My caveat is that we must guard against overreliance on digital triage without human oversight and ensure robust governance, privacy, and continuous feedback to prevent new bottlenecks as systems scale up.

From where I sit in England, the biggest gap is not just getting an appointment, but getting the right appointment with the right clinician who knows you and your history. My experience over the last few years is that urgent access can be okay, but for people with long-term conditions or complex needs, the system often feels rushed and fragmented. I’ve had episodes where I’ve seen a different GP every time for the same issue, and the notes don’t always travel smoothly between visits. I’m convinced that protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex or vulnerable patients would improve outcomes and reduce repeated visits to the doctor or even to A&E in the long run. This is not just about more time; it's about the quality of the interaction and the coherence of the care plan.

What changes would most improve timely access in my area? A mix of practical scheduling, stronger integration, and a shift in what happens within the practice day-to-day. First, guarantee a named GP for patients with chronic or multiple conditions, supported by a stable small team (nurse, health practitioner, or pharmacist) who know the patient. For those with complex needs, longer initial and follow-up appointments should be the default, not the exception—20 minutes minimum for standard GP consults, and 30 minutes or more when dealing with polypharmacy, multi-morbidity, mental health issues, or social care concerns. This would allow proper medication reviews, risk assessment, and time to discuss anxieties or social determinants that affect health outcomes.

Second, restructure how we schedule. Rather than a one-size-fits-all timetable, clinics could allocate protected blocks for complex cases. It would mean the same clinician regularly reviewing your file rather than a string of different doctors; this continuity reduces the need for repeat investigations and clarifies care plans. I’ve seen how a consistent clinician can spot when a symptom pattern is shifting and adjust care without a cascade of referrals. It should be complemented by flexible same-day triage, but with a guaranteed follow-up with someone who knows the patient, not just a phone call with an anonymous triage line.

Third, expand the model of care within general practice by embedding multidisciplinary teams. A practice-based pharmacist to review medicines, a district nurse for home care, and a mental health practitioner who can join a patient’s care plan would make a real difference. When someone has COPD and depression or anxiety, a coordinated approach (medication review, breathing support, and talking therapies) can reduce hospital admissions and the cycle of repeated GP visits. Not every problem needs a hospital referral; more on-site support means patients can get help sooner and stay healthier at home.

Fourth, strengthen access to mental health services. Timely talking therapies are crucial, but early access in primary care is just as important. If a patient can’t get a timely assessment with a mental health clinician who understands their history, crises become more likely and the demand on GPs grows unsustainably. I’d like to see rapid access pathways—ideally within two weeks—for those with mounting concerns, plus integrated care plans where mental health professionals are readily available in the same practice setting.

Fifth, invest in smarter use of digital tools without losing the personal touch. Virtual check-ins and remote monitoring can help with stable conditions, but they must complement, not replace, in-person assessments for complex cases. The key is a hybrid model where digital contacts are used for quick updates and escalations, while longer, face-to-face appointments are reserved for deeper reviews and care planning with a familiar clinician.

Sixth, ensure equity of access, especially in rural or deprived areas where distance and staffing pressures are highest. This could include outreach clinics, mobile services, or partnerships with community hubs and pharmacies so people don’t have to travel long distances for routine reviews. The goal is to shorten the time to a meaningful appointment rather than merely offering a convenient slot.

Finally, funding and governance must reflect these priorities. Longer appointment times and multidisciplinary teams require sustainable staffing and administrative support, with clear performance measures that reward continuity and patient outcomes, not just throughput. If we get the balance right—continuity, time for complex cases, integrated teams, and sensible use of technology—we should see fewer hospital visits and better overall health in our communities.

In my experience, the most effective changes would be those that recognize a patient’s ongoing journey rather than treating each visit as a standalone event. The system needs to adapt so that a person with chronic illness or vulnerable mental health needs can see the same clinician over time, with enough time to address the full picture. If implemented thoughtfully, these changes could deliver more timely access, but only with proper funding, workforce planning, and safeguards to ensure fairness for all patients.

absolutely from my point of view living in England and aged 65+, I understand the aim to improve access, but the three elements described risk not delivering timely care in the short term. Increasing training places and return-to-practice support is essential for the long term, but it won't help me or my neighbours get an appointment next week. In our town, GP slots are scarce; last winter I waited two weeks for a routine appointment, and a neighbour with a back problem waited a month. Evening and weekend clinics would help many who work or volunteer; but they must come with proper staffing and predictable slots, otherwise it just shifts the problem. The idea of guaranteed same-day urgent slots sounds good, but in practice many urgent cases end up at A&E when practices can't triage or book a slot. We also need sustained investment in interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to deprived and migrant communities, not just a one-off project. These resources must be ongoing, well funded and meaningfully linked to local services, including community hubs. Overall, these changes are a start, but without immediate recruitment and fair distribution, timely access will remain poor!

I agree. Expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine cases would free GPs for complex care, speeding access. Also targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support are essential to grow and retain primary care staff.

I understand the push to speed access, but I strongly oppose making online booking and remote care the default without solid non‑digital options. In our area many older people still rely on a simple phone call, and broadband can be patchy. A neighbour aged 78 struggled for weeks to book a GP appointment because the online system wouldn’t accept her postcode, and she had to borrow a phone from a relative. Last winter our practice’s online booking collapsed for hours, leaving busy phone lines clogged and urgent concerns unaddressed. 

Evening and weekend clinics could help working people, but only if they are properly funded and staffed to offer guaranteed same‑day urgent slots; otherwise they become a luxury that the elderly and those without flexible hours cannot use. For mental health and other urgent non‑emergency needs, a reliable three‑tier approach with clear in‑person or telephone options is essential.

NHS111, clinical triage and care navigation must be improved to prioritise true emergencies and reduce duplication. In my experience, better triage is possible but requires trained clinicians and an integrated patient record so people are not asked the same questions multiple times or directed to the wrong service. Overall, choice must be preserved and supported with real, human access points for those who need them most.

I disagree that only workforce expansion will fix access; the key is tightening NHS111 triage, faster booking, and better care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and cut duplication, while also funding return-to-practice schemes and CPD to grow GPs, nurses, and mental health staff.

Disagree. Streamlining NHS111 and triage risks more misrouted appointments and longer waits for urgent cases; we need real frontline capacity: more GPs and nurses, longer hours, simpler walk-in/phone access, and properly funded community hubs with staff present daily.

Agree: expand online booking, e-consults and remote care, with non-digital options for older or rural patients; plus targeted recruitment, international hires, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support to retain staff and improve timely access.

Timely access would improve most if we had co‑located community hubs that bring GP, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. A single visit could triage on the day and link patients to housing, debt advice or a local charity, reducing multiple trips. In my area, people often wait weeks for a mental‑health slot and then repeat information to different teams; a hub would prevent that duplication with a named navigator coordinating care.

I also welcome expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, especially for busy working people. But non‑digital options must remain: telephone triage, in‑person slots, and support for older or less tech‑savvy residents. For chronic issues, remote monitoring and quick nurse messages would cut trips and speed up treatment.

In short, integrated hubs plus flexible digital access would cut waiting times, improve prevention, and give people reliable, local support when they need it most.

Expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care can offer convenience, but I don’t think we should push them at the expense of real, non‑digital access. In my area the problem isn’t just whether someone can click a button; it’s getting seen quickly when you’re unwell, especially for GP, community health and mental health services. Online slots fill up fast and busy phones often block easier routes for people who aren’t comfortable with digital tools or who lack reliable internet.

What would help more than anything is a true hybrid system that keeps all channels open. Expand online options, but also guarantee well‑staffed, easy-to-use phone lines and enough same‑day in‑person slots for urgent issues. Invest in digital inclusion: digital champions at practices, simple step‑by‑step guides, and community hubs or libraries offering free access and support. Targeted outreach for older people and those on low incomes is essential so no one gets left behind.

Mental health access needs urgency too—e‑consults may work for low‑risk cases, but crisis or complex needs should be seen promptly in person or via video with a clinician who can assess risk properly. More capacity from GPs, nurses, and community teams is also critical to reduce waits. I’ve seen neighbours miss appointments or wait weeks because digital options were confusing or unavailable; a flexible, inclusive system is needed.

Thank you for focusing on timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. I strongly support increasing appointment slots and session capacity through hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding appointment lengths where needed, and smarter scheduling. In our area waits for routine GP reviews can be a week or more, and mental health support is stretched thin; more clinicians and quicker access would prevent minor issues from escalating and ease pressure on urgent care.

Concrete steps could include recruiting additional GPs and practice nurses, plus dedicated therapist slots, extending weekday hours and adding a Saturday morning clinic so older residents with transport challenges can attend. Keeping longer appointment times for chronic conditions would reduce repeated visits. A central online booking system with triage would ensure urgent calls get next-day slots, and a small pool of locums could cover absences to stop gaps opening in the timetable.

Personally, last winter I had a chest infection and the earliest GP appointment was several days away, which left me uncomfortable and concerned. If there had been more flexible hours and greater clinician capacity, I could have been seen sooner and avoided a trip to urgent care. With these changes, people in our community would receive timely care and stay healthier, reducing hospital visits.

absolutely increase GP, nurse and therapist slots by hiring and expanding sessions, with smarter scheduling to cut waits; for rural or mobility‑limited residents, boost mobile clinics, telehealth hubs and outreach, plus better transport and parking at premises!

These changes alone won't deliver timely access. Even with more GP slots and co-located hubs, without stable staffing, funded long-term, and real transport options for rural and mobility-limited people, waits will persist. Prioritise mobile clinics, telehealth hubs, and integrated service networks now.

I disagree that only short-term tweaks will help; we need sustained investment in training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus funded interpreters and outreach to reach deprived and minority communities.

absolutely i strongly support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The priorities that matter most to me are continuity of care and longer appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. When patients can see the same clinician and have a proper slot to discuss multiple long‑standing issues, outcomes improve and avoid avoidable hospital or emergency visits. As an older person, I’ve seen how rushed 10‑ or 15‑minute slots miss key details about medications or new symptoms, leading to follow‑up calls and trips. Longer appointments and dedicated slots for high‑needs patients would make a real difference.

I also welcome targeted resources to tackle access gaps among deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In our community, language barriers and limited familiarity with NHS processes can delay care. Providing interpreters, culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach, including mobile clinics and community health workers, would help people attend appointments and understand care plans. For mental health, timely access and integrated support with primary care would prevent crises and support staying independent at home. These changes would mean better, fairer care for everyone and fewer avoidable holds on NHS resources!

As an organisation representing older people in Scotland, we believe that protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients would markedly improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. In practice, many of our members with multiple conditions rely on a named GP and a small care team. Short 10–15 minute slots frequently lead to follow-up calls or extra visits, causing delays and anxiety. We welcome proposals that enable samr-day triagr for urgent concerns and ensure patients are seen by their usual clinicians. Extending consultations to 25–30 minutes for chronic cases, with flexible slots for medication reviews, mental health checks and social support planning, would improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. We also urge investment in integrated community teams and robust administrative systems so appointments aren’t lost and care plans are coordinated acros GP, district nursing and mental health services. In rural areas, a named link worker and improved digital scheduling that preserves continuity would help our older residents stay well at hom and out of hospital.

I welcome a sustained focus on mental health as part of timely, local care. Expanding community mental health teams, with stronger early intervention, crisis response and expanded talking therapies, would help people get support before situations deteriorate and move parity with physical health on waiting times. I’ve seen friends struggle for months to access CBT through NHS providers; quicker access to evidence‑based talking therapies would make a real difference rather than waiting for a referral to come through A&E. I also see value in investing in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners. When you can access GP, nursing, counselling and social support in one place, it reduces confusion and travel and supports people holistically. However, this requires solid workforce planning, robust data sharing, and clear governance to avoid fragmented services. To grow and retain primary care staff, targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, pay improvements, flexible working and strong wellbeing support are essential. In my area, pockets of improvement followed from better staff wellbeing and shorter shifts, but we need those measures system‑wide to deliver timely access.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I support three practical changes working together: expand the primary care workforce, fix booking and triage, and grow community mental health supports.

First, grow and retain staff in primary care. This means targeted recruitment, including international hiring, better pay, flexible working (part‑time GP slots, more locums with guaranteed hours) and strong wellbeing support so clinicians aren’t burnt out. In my area, evenings and weekends are often booked full months ahead and new graduates drift away for better conditions elsewhere; these steps would help keep services local and available fast.

Second, NHS111, triage and booking should prioritise urgent cases and simplify patient flow. A streamlined system with effective care navigators and improved online booking would cut duplication between GP, urgent care and hotlines, so someone with a real emergency gets seen quickly.

Third, expand community mental health teams, with early intervention, crisis response and more talking therapies to reduce waits and parity with physical health. I’ve seen friends wait months for counselling; extra teams and faster access would make a real difference.

Overall, these changes would make timely access more realistic for people like me.

As an organisation representing older residents across England, we are concerned by the idea of expanding GP services mainly through evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, and by a heavy emphasis on increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD as the core long-term solution. While the intention is to improve timely access, the practical implications risk making care less personal, less reliable, and less affordable for those who rely most on steady, familiar handling of their health needs.

First, the proposal to run longer hours and guarantee same-day urgent slots sounds helpful for working people, yet it can erode the continuity of care that many older patients value and rely on. For years, my neighbours and family members have spoken about the importance of seeing a GP who knows their medical history, medications, and the nuances of their conditions. When appointments are reshuffled to fit evening or weekend slots, patients often end up with clinicians who do not know their background, or with staff who have not had time to review a full chart before making decisions. In our area, extended hours at one practice led to longer waits in the reception and a backlog of requests for home visits, simply because the day had to be reset to accommodate the new pattern.

The logistics are not trivial. Evening and weekend clinics require extra staffing, secure premises, and robust rostering to avoid staff burnout. Doctors, nurses and reception teams already feel pushed to the limit by workload, administrative burdens, and the need to cover shifts across inconsistent patterns. Asking them to operate at a high intensity during evenings or Sundays could, paradoxically, worsen availability at other times if staff choose to reduce hours or leave the profession. This is especially true in rural and semi-rural areas where recruiting a full team outside core hours is already difficult. For older people who depend on reliable access to a named clinician and to timely medication reviews, there is a real risk that “more hours” translates into “less continuity” and not the quick, confident reassurance patients expect.

Secondly, the stated goal of guaranteed same-day urgent slots neglects the real problem of triage and the pressure on urgent care pathways. Urgent slots can become a bottleneck if every urgent demand is treated as an immediate GP appointment, diverting time away from chronic disease management, diabetes reviews, and polypharmacy checks—services crucial to older patients. In practice, urgent care must be properly integrated with other professionals (nurse practitioners, pharmacists, mental health workers) and with social care to prevent over-medicalising non-emergency problems and to avoid unsafe rushed decisions. The risk of creating a “fast-track” system for urgent issues is that the wrong issues are escalated, or the right issues are treated too quickly without sufficient consideration of a patient’s full history.

On the long-term strategy of expanding training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD: while we cannot deny the need to replenish the workforce, the plan as described risks chasing numbers without guaranteeing the conditions required for those new or returning clinicians to stay and to practise safely. Training places take years to bear fruit, and there is little point in swelling numbers if there are not enough jobs, support, and appropriate working conditions for newly qualified staff. We have seen talented junior clinicians move away or reduce hours because of unsustainable workloads, leading to persistent gaps in care longer term.

Similarly, return-to-practice schemes can help, but they must be matched with real, attractive posts and retraining that fits local needs. Apprenticeships and CPD are valuable, but they should not become a workaround to underfunded services. If we train more staff without addressing pay, workload, admin support, and the availability of appropriate senior supervision, we will simply train people to leave or to take on tasks they cannot safely manage solo.

What would help in the here and now—and be more equitable—would be a more holistic, sustainable approach. Invest in non-clinical support so GP practices are not buried in admin; expand multidisciplinary teams within primary care so a patient can see a nurse, pharmacist or mental health worker who knows their history and can escalate appropriately; strengthen home visit capacity and community-based services so that frail older people don’t always need a GP appointment for every issue; and ensure any extension of hours is financially and organizationally protected, with clear guarantees about continuity of care and patient choice.

In addition, any training expansion should be closely linked to clearly available posts, good remuneration, and supportive supervision. There should be robust evaluations of pilots to identify where extended hours truly improve timely access without compromising safety or continuity. Without these safeguards, the proposed changes risk creating a two-tier effect: those who can adapt to the new system and those who cannot, particularly older residents who may struggle with changes in routine, transport, or digital access.

We support a patient-centred strategy that values continuity, safety and dignity in care. To genuinely improve timeliness, the focus must be on sustainable workforce planning, smarter use of the wider health and social care system, and meaningful engagement with older people about what works best for them in daily practice, not just a race to extend hours or to push more training through the pipeline alone.

From my chair by the fire, my thoughts drift beyond the question of which changes would best speed up GP, community, and mental health slots. In our village, the biggest obstacle isn’t the clinics as such but getting there. The bus runs only a couple of times a day, and when winter wind rattles the panes I worry about travelling for a same-day appointment. A neighbour waited weeks for a mental health assessment after a difficult patch, and the family carer’s energy is wearing thin as we juggle phone triage and repeat prescriptions. Digital booking helps some, but my sister, like many of us older folks, struggles with online forms and video calls due to hearing and eyesight. I’d value more home visits and better liaison with pharmacists, who can flag issues before they become crises. I know these are tangential points, but for many of us, transport, straightforward admin, and time with staff underpin care far more than new clinics alone.

While I recognise the aim to improve timely access, I’m not convinced the proposed changes will help people like me across England, especially in rural areas. Expanding multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases could remove the GP’s central role and create confusion over who is responsible for my care. If a pharmacist or physiotherapist handles routine checks, who keeps the overall plan, and who do I contact when issues crop up? Continuity matters; I want to see the same clinician who knows my history. Fragmented contacts risk mistakes and delays for those with multiple, long‑standing conditions.

Targeted resources for deprived groups are important, but they must not come at the expense of GP capacity. Without clear accountability and sufficient staffing, outreach and interpreters may be underused and the benefits will slip away in practice.

Transport and premises deficits are real barriers. Mobile clinics and telehealth hubs could help, but many older people struggle with travel, safety, and digital literacy. In rural areas a 20–30 minute drive to a hub remains a barrier; we need reliable transport, better parking, and accessible, well‑located surgeries.

My priority would be to boost GP numbers, ensure same‑day access when needed, and make sure any MDT work supports continuity of care with clear contact routes and proper funding for transport and premises.

To improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services, I’d support a dual‑track approach: expand online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, while guaranteeing non‑digital options and help for those who need them. In practice, faster online triage could shorten queue times and free up in‑person slots for urgent cases. My older relative struggles with portals, so there must be clear phone support, simple guides, and protected in‑person slots as a baseline. Expanding evening and weekend GP clinics, nurse‑led same‑day sessions, and accessible walk‑in hubs would help reduce waits.

For mental health, increase community mental health teams with strong early intervention in schools and workplaces, robust crisis response and shorter‑term talking therapies to improve parity with physical health. I’ve seen friends benefit from timely counselling, but waiting lists remain a barrier. It’s essential to fund interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus targeted outreach to deprived and migrant communities to close gaps. Proactive contact in digitally excluded groups—through paper forms, community venues and drop‑in clinics—would also help.

Overall, blend tech‑enabled access with reliable real‑world support, ensure adequate funding for interpreters and outreach, and equip local teams to coordinate care so people get timely help regardless of background or digital ability.

I live in Wales and, as someone juggling work and family, I’m sceptical these changes will automatically improve timely access without creating new problems. Expanding multidisciplinary teams may free GPs, but in practice it can fragment care and erode continuity. A routine cough or sprain might end up bounced between a pharmacist, physiotherapist and physician associate before a GP is involved, delaying escalation for complex cases and creating confusion for patients who value a single clinician they know. 

Evening and weekend clinics could help when you work full-time, but in rural areas staffing those slots is challenging. Last winter, a weekend clinic in our town had to close twice because of staff shortages, leaving people with nowhere to go on a Saturday in pain. A guaranteed same-day urgent slot sounds right but could squeeze already stretched services and push people into A&E rather than primary care. 

Digital options are good, but I’ve elderly neighbours who can’t use online booking and lack broadband. We must preserve non-digital routes and provide support to avoid exclusion. If these changes go ahead, they must be backed by sustained funding, clear referral pathways, and protections for GP continuity.
Disagree that long-term training alone will fix timely access; we need immediate staffing boosts, flexible GP shifts, and improved triage while training capacity scales up.

Invest in co-located hubs that bring GP, community and mental health together with social care and VCSE partners for seamless local care, and protect continuity with longer appointments for complex patients to improve outcomes and reduce repeats.

In my area, and as someone in their early 20s living in England, I think the biggest wins on timely access would come from targeted investment and a real focus on continuity of care for people who are most likely to fall through the cracks. It isn’t just about booking slots faster; it’s about making sure people can actually use the services without facing language barriers, cultural barriers, or a care system that feels like it resets every time you need help. I’ve seen friends and family struggle with this in practical ways, which makes me wary of plans that look good on paper but don’t address those gaps directly.

One clear problem is access for deprived and minority communities. When you don’t speak English well, relying on online or phone-only appointment booking can be a barrier. Interpreters are often hard to get, booked last minute, or limited to certain times, which means people delay contacting a GP until problems become urgent. I’ve witnessed a friend with chest pains wait days for an interpreter to be available, and by the time they could communicate properly, the symptoms had intensified. In another example, a migrant family received information about mental health services only in English, and the forms and guidance pages were inaccessible, so they didn’t even know where to start seeking help. These aren’t just “nuisances”—they’re real obstacles that push people toward crisis services instead of early, preventive care.

To address this, changes need to be targeted and locally tailored. It’s not enough to say “improve access” without resources to match. We should see dedicated funding for language and cultural support embedded in primary care networks, not as an afterthought. That means:

- Interpreting and translation made reliably available in GP practices, hospitals, and community health services, with funded slots booked in advance rather than rely on ad hoc arrangements.
- Recruitment and training of staff who reflect the communities they serve, including bilingual receptionists and clinicians who understand cultural nuances around symptom reporting and help-seeking.
- Outreach teams or community health workers who operate in local hubs—schools, mosques, community centres, migrant help desks—to help people navigate the system, signpost to the right services, and build trust.
- Easy-to-understand, translated information about GP, community health, and mental health services, plus clear guidance on how to access urgent help when needed.

In practice, these measures would reduce the confusion and delay that currently drive people away from timely care. They would also close the gap between what is available in theory and what people can actually access in their own communities.

Equally important is protecting continuity of care and allowing longer appointment times for complex or vulnerable patients. Fragmentation—seeing different GPs, re-explaining the same issues, or being handed a new care plan with no follow-up—leads to missed signals and repeated visits. For young people with chronic conditions or mental health concerns, continuity isn’t a luxury; it’s a clinical necessity that improves outcomes and reduces the likelihood of escalations that land you back in urgent care.

Concrete improvements here include:

- A named GP or a consistent care team for each patient, whenever possible, so that patients don’t have to re-educate new clinicians about their history every visit.
- Longer appointment times for complex cases, with flexible scheduling that protects time for a thorough mental health assessment, social determinants of health discussions, and care planning.
- Clear care plans with agreed follow-up steps, including a designated point of contact (a care coordinator or nurse) who tracks progress, coordinates between primary care and mental health services, and checks in between appointments.
- Integrated digital and in-person pathways so patients can switch between modes without losing continuity—e.g., a patient can have a telehealth check with a familiar clinician if it suits their circumstances, while still receiving in-person support when needed.

I’ve also seen how timely, well-organised care can reduce repeat visits. When a young person with anxiety and a sleep disorder could access a longer appointment with a clinician who already knew their history, the clinician could address multiple linked issues in one session and offer a supported step-by-step plan. On the flip side, when access is rushed or the same questions are asked repeatedly by different clinicians, symptoms worsen and trust in the system declines.

So, in short, improvements that will most reliably boost timely access are those that (a) allocate targeted resources to reduce language and cultural barriers, (b) bring in community-facing roles to bridge gaps, and (c) guarantee continuity and longer appointments for complex needs. Without these, faster booking or more digital features won’t translate into better outcomes for all, especially the most marginalised groups. If the government is serious about improving access, it should tie funding and performance to concrete measures on interpreter availability, cultural competence, and sustained clinician-patient relationships across GP and mental health services.

I strongly agree that the changes proposed would meaningfully improve timely accrss to GP, communityy healthh and mental health services. In my area of England, access gaps hit hardest for people in deprived communities and for migrants and ethnic minorities who often face language barriers and confusion about how to navigate NHS services. Providing interpreters and employing culturally competent staff would remove a major obstacle, whilee targeted outreach through schools, faith groups and community organisations would help people know what support exists and how to access it. Transport, parking and premises deficits aree a real barrier for many; I’d like to see more mobile clinics in housing estates and rural hubs, outreach teams visiting busy centres, and telehealth hubs in libraries or community venues to reduce travel time. Flexible options such as evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would make a big difference for working people and urgent non-emergency needs. A mobile clinic visiting our estate for vaccines last year showed how accessible services can be when barriers are lowered. If implemented, I’d also want careful monitoring of uptake by ethnicity, deprivation and rural/urban areas to ensure no groups are left behind.

In Scotland, our organisation sees real merit in expanding multidisciplinary teams to manage routine care and free GPs to focus on complex cases. But any expansion must come with clear scopes, robust supervision and guaranteed access to patient records so pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can triage safely without fragmenting care. A local practice has shown how a pharmacist-led triage or physiotherapist-led assessment could reduce waiting times for common musculoskeletal and minor respiratory issues, provided there is real-time sharing of notes and timely escalation when red flags appear. Without these safeguards, co‑ordination breaks down and risks patient safety.

We also recognise the value of longer-term workforce strategies—more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD—but these need service-ready roles and protected time for learning. Otherwise, trainees simply shift bottlenecks rather than relieve them. Clear career pathways, funded supervision and integrated placement in community teams are essential for sustainable growth of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals.

Finally, targeted evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots could help working people and urgent non‑emergency needs, but only if backed by adequate staffing (including mental health practitioners) and safe triage with data-driven evaluation. Pilot this in diverse urban/rural sites to refine impact before broader rollout.

Thank you for asking for views on how to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my experience living in England, I’m not convinced the main levers in your consultation will deliver the changes people actually need, quickly or equitably. I think the problem is more systemic and layered than simply hoping recruitment drives and more online booking will miraculously free up waiting times.

First, the proposed focus on targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support is sensible in principle, but it feels like a slow burn. Training a new GP or nurse takes years, and people currently waiting weeks for routine appointments are not going to be helped by cohorts trained in the next Parliament. Relying on international hires raises real questions about integration, language and culture, and it can be unstable if visa and regulatory requirements change. In my area we’ve already seen a few locum-heavy periods where appointments disappear for weeks; those gaps aren’t solved by promises of “more staff later.” What would help much sooner is a robust retention strategy: pay recognition that matches workload, reduced bureaucratic tasks for clinicians, protected time for professional development, and predictable rosters that prevent burnout. Without that, even new recruits won’t stay long enough to stabilise access.

Second, increasing appointment slots and session capacity sounds obvious, but you can’t expand slots if there isn’t physical space, daytime capacity or reduced demand from duplicative administrative work. I’ve heard of practices trying to run near-capacity clinics with multiple short slots, and the result is frequent cancellations, rushed consultations, and worse continuity of care. A real solution would involve expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physician associates, physiotherapists, mental health practitioners) who can handle common issues, leaving GPs to manage more complex cases. Group education sessions for chronic conditions and longer wellbeing clinics can also move people through the system faster, without compromising quality. But this needs ring-fenced funding for space, staff, and back-office support, not just promises of “more slots later.”

Third, expanding online booking and e-consultations is a double-edged sword. I’ve seen the benefits: quicker triage for some issues, fewer phone queues, and easier access for people who work irregular hours. But it also risks marginalising the elderly, those with limited digital literacy, and households without reliable broadband. In my street, my neighbour struggled to navigate an online portal after a recent eye operation, and two other relatives found the digital check-in process confusing and off-putting. Non-digital alternatives must be guaranteed and genuinely easy to use: a well-staffed telephone line with reasonable wait times, clear in-practice booking windows, and in-person triage where needed. If we press ahead with digital by default, we must fund digital inclusion measures and provide ready-made assistance (things like patient-led digital mentors or front-desk help to guide people through online systems).

Fourth, the combination of online booking and remote care must be accompanied by strong local delivery that actually reaches disadvantaged groups. Remote care can improve convenience for some, but it can also create a two-tier system where the well-connected get timely virtual help while those with transport difficulties, caring responsibilities or language barriers end up wait-listed or pushed into crisis services. In practice, I’ve seen remote triage push people into a waiting list for face-to-face assessment anyway, which defeats the purpose. A successful path would align remote and in-person services in a seamless continuum, with clear pathways for urgent care, supported by community-based services, social care integration, and clear patient information about what to expect and when to escalate.

In terms of what would genuinely make a difference, I’d prioritise:
- a credible workforce strategy that combines realistic recruitment with robust retention measures, improved working conditions, protected time for training, and reduced bureaucracy; ensure services in my area are not reliant on short-term locums.
- expansion of multidisciplinary teams and flexible models of care (e.g., nurse-led clinics, group sessions, same-day triage) to increase capacity without simply piling more appointments on GPs.
- a truly inclusive digital access plan, with strong non-digital options and practical support for those who are digitally excluded; targeted outreach in communities most likely to be left behind.
- urgent, locally tailored investment in primary and community care spaces and in-stream funding to support rapid improvements, rather than waiting years for large-scale workforce changes to take effect.

As things stand, I’m concerned that the main thrust of your changes would improve the headline numbers but not the lived experience of people who need timely care today. The system needs a credible, well-funded plan that tackles workforce stability, expands capacity in a sustainable way, and ensures digital innovations don’t leave anyone behind. Until then, I remain wary that these changes will merely shift the bottleneck rather than remove it.

I welcome the aim to improve timely access in Scotland, but I am concerned that the proposed fixes still lean too heavily on more GPs or digital fixes without practical steps to shift routine care to teams and to rural access. The biggest gains come from expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle routine cases, triage, and follow-up, freeing GPs to concentrate on complex problems. But this must be backed by secured funding, clear scopes of practice, and integrated information sharing so patients do not face duplicated visits or confusion. 

Crucially, transport, parking and premises deficits remain a daily barrier in many rural and mobility-limited communities. We need mobile clinics and community outreach visiting outlying villages on regular schedules, plus telehealth hubs in local community venues with reliable transport links and accessible parking. Incentives to attract and retain staff in rural posts, plus investment in fit-for-purpose premises and co-location of services, are essential for sustainable change. 

In our area, long bus gaps and scarce parking cause missed appointments, and a weekly nurse-led clinic only reached part of the population. A mobile team with a pharmacist and physio could have kept chronic conditions stable and avoided unnecessary hospital visits.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for a healthy, young population. From where I sit, the most advertised fixes—extending hours and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots—are not enough on their own. You can book a weekend slot, but if there aren’t enough qualified staff to fill it, consultations become rushed, wait times persist and clinician burnout rises. The real fix has to start with growing and retaining the people who deliver care, not just tinkering with the timetable.

Firstly, even with evening or weekend clinics and guaranteed urgent slots, capacity grows only as fast as the frontline workforce. International recruitment and targeted recruitment with incentives and pay improvements are essential, but they’re not quick fixes. Visa processes, language Maths, induction and ongoing professional development, and long‑term retention are real challenges. In our area, efforts to recruit overseas have filled vacancies temporarily, but without a robust retention package those staff leave for better conditions elsewhere. And the cost of agency cover to plug gaps is unsustainable and doesn’t build lasting capacity.

Secondly, while increasing training places, return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals are absolutely necessary for a sustainable pipeline, they take years. We cannot wait for a whole generation to come through before patients see real relief. We need parallel short‑term actions that deliver now while building a longer‑term workforce, so people aren’t left waiting or forced into urgent care channels for routine needs.

What would work better in practice is a multi‑pronged plan that combines workforce growth with smarter care delivery:
- A credible national workforce strategy with clear targets and timetables to raise numbers of GPs, practice nurses, pharmacists and mental‑health workers, funded and overseen by a dedicated delivery body.
- Robust pathways for international recruitment with strong induction, language support, mentorship and long‑term retention incentives, ensuring newcomers are distributed fairly and stay in primary care.
- Real improvements in pay and flexible working conditions, backed by wellbeing and peer‑support systems, so staff aren’t forced to burn out or leave early.
- Expansion of mid‑level and allied health professionals (nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists, therapists) to handle routine care and triage, freeing GPs to focus on more complex cases.
- Safe, evenly staffed extended access—where clinics operate as part of a network or hub rather than in one practice only—so capacity is shared and not solely dependent on one surgery’s staffing.
- Smarter digital tools and triage systems that direct patients to the right professional first time (online booking, video checks, nurse‑led triage) to reduce bottlenecks and wasteful visits.
- A strengthened mental‑health pathway, including school and community links, rapid access teams and evening/weekend slots for urgent needs, but anchored by sufficient staffing to avoid delays.
- A robust return‑to‑practice and CPD framework that makes it feasible for clinicians who paused training to re‑join and upskill quickly.

On the ground, I’ve seen how delays to appointments hit working students and young people who rely on daytime services between lectures or shifts. In my area, when a GP slot is delayed or a mental health request has to wait weeks, people turn to urgent care or online self‑care, which isn’t a substitute for timely, coordinated care. A lasting fix must combine workforce growth with smarter care models and credible funding that doesn’t just “patch” the system.

I want policymakers to back a comprehensive plan that delivers both near‑term relief and long‑term resilience, with transparent reporting on workforce numbers, access metrics and patient outcomes. We should invest now in people, not just in extending hours, so that improvements in access aren’t temporary but built to last for students, workers and families across England.

From my vantage in an area where travel can be difficult for older folk, the changes that would help most are a mix of co-located community hubs and stronger community mental health provision. I would welcome a local hub that brings together GP surgeries, district nursing, social care staff and voluntary sector partners in one place or through seamless links. In practice, this would mean being able to see a GP, a nurse, and a mental health worker, and getting social support for housing or carers in one appointment or coordinated visits. At present I often have to travel to several places, which is hard on mobility and timing. 

I also think expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis support and talking therapies would help reduce waits and restore parity with physical health services. That said, any expansion must come with genuine capacity to offer timely appointments and clear roles across teams to avoid confusion and preserve continuity with my own GP. In-person access remains important, though telehealth can help, especially for routine checks, so long as it suits those less comfortable with technology.

From my experience living in England, the most effective improvements to timely access won’t come from simply cramming more services into new co‑located hubs or throwing more appointment slots at a system that’s already strained. Any gains will only materialise if there is real, practical integration, realistic workforce plans and patient choice at the heart of design.

Co-located hubs sound sensible in principle—bringing GP, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. In practice, however, they often become another layer of management with separate funding streams, IT systems and referral routes that don’t align. The result can be slower rather than faster access, because a patient may be passed between teams with no single, accountable plan. In my area last year, a hub opened with fanfare, but access across services remained patchy; staff were overstretched, referrals stalled, and people with complex needs still faced repeated hand-offs instead of a coordinated care plan. For some, the hub is convenient; for others it’s a detour that adds travel time and confusion over who to contact. If co-location is pursued, it must be backed by robust joint governance, unified IT and funding, and a clear, patient‑centred care pathway that preserves choice and avoids turning access into a bureaucratic bottleneck.

Similarly, simply increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots without solving the underlying staffing and administration bottlenecks is not a cure. Recruitment for GPs, nurses and therapists remains challenging in many parts of the country, so promises of more slots risk being hollow if there aren’t enough trained professionals to fill them long term. Also, more hours don’t automatically mean better access if clinicians spend more time on bureaucracy or if the non‑clinical admin load eats into the time available for patients. In my practice, talk of weekend or extended hours sounded good, but actual availability fell short because locum staffing and admin requirements couldn’t be sustained. And even when therapists are added, long waits persist if triage and referral pathways are slow or unclear, leaving people waiting weeks for a first contact that still doesn’t address their primary needs.

What would actually improve timely access, in my view, is a balanced mix of practical tweaks and targeted, well‑designed reforms:

- Smarter, more reliable triage and same-day access within existing GP services: quick phone or video triage by a clinician, same-day nurse or GP assessment where appropriate, and rapid escalation for mental health crises. Extend hours only where staffing is stable and funded, not as a stand‑alone promise.
- Sustainable workforce planning: invest in training and retaining clinicians, with clear career progression and appropriate pay, so that extended hours do not simply shift the problem elsewhere. This should include mental health staff who can operate within primary care without always requiring separate, additional appointments.
- Practical digital and administrative improvements: real-time online booking, streamlined referrals, and shared care plans across GP, community and mental health teams, with robust but privacy‑conscious data sharing.
- Targeted, evaluated co‑location: pilot co‑located hubs with strong governance, transparent evaluation, and guaranteed patient choice. If the data show real, tangible benefits for specific populations or pathways, scale with caution; if not, don’t force consolidation.
- Local, patient‑led design with VCSE involvement: ensure social prescribing and community outreach are embedded from the start, with clear performance metrics and accountability.

In short, I’d prioritise faster, simpler routes into care now, backed by sustainable staffing and clear accountability, rather than a wholesale push for more hubs and longer lists that may not translate into real improvements for most people. The goal should be reliable access that works for diverse communities, not a one‑size‑fits‑all rebuild that risks creating new barriers.

More online booking and remote care risk leaving pensioners like me without access; must keep walk-in slots, phone triage, and home visits alongside investments in training, return-to-practice schemes, and longer-term GP staffing to ensure timely care for all.

Access to GP, nurse and therapist appointments in my area could be improved most effectively by increasing appointment slots and expanding session capacity through more staff and smarter scheduling. I’ve experienced a two-week wait for a standard GP appointment and similar delays for mental health support, which can let small health issues become bigger problems. If practices could hire more GPs and practice nurses, extend opening hours into weekday evenings and weekends, and create protected slots for urgent reviews, it would reduce uncertainty for families like mine. Implementing robust triage via online booking and same-day nurse triage calls would help direct patients to the right clinician quickly. Expanding therapy capacity—by recruiting more therapists, offering group sessions for mild anxiety, and providing digital options where appropriate—would also cut wait times. Local investment in extended hours, better rostering, and administrative support to keep schedules accurate would make a real difference, ensuring timely care and preventing crises rather than reacting to them.

To improve timely access, target funding for interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus active outrrach in deprived and minority communities. Mobile clinics and extended hours should be available, with clear information in multiple languages to close access gaps for migrants and marginalised groups.

In my area in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains inconsistent. I’ve had friends and family struggle to get a same‑day GP slot, and a relative waited many months for mental health support. To make access genuinely timely, I think we need to grow the workforce sustainably by expanding training places, strengthening return‑to‑practice routes, promoting apprenticeships and ensuring robust CPD.

Concretely, more GP registrar places and practice‑based training hubs with funded supervision would help fill a pipeline that currently peaks and troughs. Return‑to‑practice schemes, with structured upskilling and mentoring, would bring skilled clinicians back sooner after breaks. Apprenticeships should be widened into nursing, allied health and mental health support, offering paid, hands‑on routes for school leavers and career changers to enter these essential roles.
