CPD must be protected with real time off and practical, interdisciplinary learning that aligns across GPs, nurses and mental health professionals rather than ticking boxes.

In practice, a local community health centre could host a shared training hub where clinicians rotate between GP, nurse prescriber and mental health teams, paired with expanded tele‑triage to direct patients efficiently while keeping essential face‑to‑face slots for those who need them. Long‑term, stable funding and regional workforce planning are crucial so these roles are distributed fairly in towns and rural areas, reducing waits across the board.

Resources must be targeted to deprived and minority communities with interpreters and culturally competent staff; expand outreach and non-digital options to avoid excluding the elderly, rather than relying mainly on online booking and remote care.

I understand the aim to speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I’m not convinced the proposed broad expansion will deliver reliably or safely, and I’m worried it could actually widen gaps for some patients. In particular, shifting routine care to multidisciplinary teams, expanding mental health teams, and pushing more services online risks fragmentation, misses the point of continuity, and risks excluding people who aren’t comfortable with digital ways of getting help.

First, about multidisciplinary teams: bringing in pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle “routine” cases sounds efficient in theory, but in practice it can break the thread of ongoing care. I’ve seen cases where a patient with long-term conditions ends up seeing several different clinicians who don’t have a single, up-to-date view of meds and past tests. Notes aren’t always shared smoothly across providers or across different practices, so the patient ends up repeating history and risking drug interactions or duplicative tests. The idea of a free‑standing routine slot for a non-GP clinician only works if there is a clearly defined care lead for each patient, with access to a unified medical record and robust governance. Without that, patients may receive well‑intentioned but inconsistent advice, and GPs—already juggling heavy workloads—could feel undermined or unable to coordinate the overall plan. If this approach is pursued, it must be accompanied by a clear clinical leadership model, shared IT systems, and guaranteed patient choice (you should still be able to see your own GP if you want to).

Second, expanding community mental health teams and early intervention sounds laudable, but there are real capacity limits and funding gaps. In my area, crisis and urgent mental‑health responses can’t always reach people quickly; waiting times for therapy remain uncomfortably long, and parity with physical health won’t be achieved just by deploying more staff on paper. Training more staff without ensuring proper supervision, integration with primary care, and reliable access to timely interventions risks creating more handoffs and fewer sustained outcomes. I’d rather see targeted, well‑funded investments that guarantee 24/7 access to crisis lines, closer integration with GPs, and co‑located services where possible, so a person in crisis isn’t bounced from one team to another. I’d also want clear guidelines to avoid over‑pathologising everyday distress and to set measurable targets for improvement in waiting times, with patient feedback driving the service redesign.

Third, the push toward online booking, e‑consultations and remote care is welcome in some contexts, but not as a one‑size‑fits‑all solution. Digital access can genuinely relieve pressures, but it risks excluding older patients, those with limited digital skills, or people without reliable internet or devices. I know neighbours who struggle with online booking portals or can’t navigate complex apps, and for some physical examinations or mental‑health conversations, a phone call or in‑person visit offers essential nuance that a screen can’t capture. Online triage can also misjudge urgency when symptoms aren’t easily described, leading to delays. If we push digital first, we must back it up with real non‑digital options: telephone triage and appointment lines with longer call times, walk‑in clinics, and home visits where appropriate. We also need to ensure robust data security and staff training so patients feel confident their information is protected.

What I’d call for is a blended, patient‑centred approach: keep a strong GP‑led model with clear care coordination, ensure any expanded teams have properly funded, backed‑up support and integrated IT; invest in mental‑health parity with timely, accessible services and crisis response that actually works in practice; and roll out digital options alongside universal non‑digital access, with proactive support to help people engage. Before any significant rollout, there should be local pilots with independent evaluations, patient involvement at every stage, and explicit equality assessments to prevent widening health disparities.

I want to see improvements that are tangible for everyday patients: shorter waits, clearer pathways, and care that feels coherent rather than shuffled between different providers. I’m not convinced the current proposals, as stated, will deliver that without substantial safeguards, funding, and a strong emphasis on keeping the patient’s experience at the heart of the system.

I support mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs to reach rural patients; increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots through hiring and better scheduling, incentives for staff, and expanding community mental health teams and talking therapies to reduce waits and ensure parity with physical health.

As a pensioner living in England, I want timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I’m concerned that pushing more online booking and remote care will leave many of us behind. My own attempts to book online are not reliable: the system times out, and when I ring the practice line the queue is long and staff are rushed. An elderly neighbour without sturdy broadband struggles with e-consults and fears missing an urgent appointment. 

What would help most is a mix of digital and non-digital options, not a replacement of the old ways. Keep telephone booking, same-day nurse triage by phone, and clear in-person appointment access at local clinics. Provide practical help for those who need digital support—trained care navigators in surgeries, volunteers, and carers who can assist with devices and forms so nobody is left waiting in silence. Improve NHS111 with simpler menus, quicker routing to the right service, and a direct link to GP calendars to avoid duplicating requests. Make booking systems straightforward so patients go through one clear process rather than juggling multiple platforms. 

Mental health services also deserve timely responses; offer face-to-face options when needed and ensure remote care supplements—not replaces—human contact. In short, expand access channels thoughtfully, cut duplication, and guarantee urgent cases are prioritised while protecting the digitally excluded old and vulnerable in our communities.

I strongly support changes that grow and retain the primary care workforce and extend access hours to GP, community health and mental health services. This should include targeted recruitment and international hiring, with clear visa pathways, incentives and pay improvements to attract and keep clinicians in local practices. In our area there are noticeable vacancies across GP partners and practice nurses, so better pay, structured progression, and dedicated recruitment campaigns would help fill posts more quickly and reduce waiting times. Flexible working patterns and robust wellbeing support are essential to prevent burnout and maintain quality patient care. 

Providing evening and weekend clinics, along with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would make it much easier for working people to get timely care without taking unpaid time off. For mental health, same‑day triage and rapid access to talking therapies or brief interventions would prevent crises and ease pressure on emergency services. A straightforward online triage that directs patients to the right service would also cut down wasted appointments. Overall, these changes would deliver faster, more convenient access and better health outcomes for our community.

Thank you for inviting views on this. I’m writing as a long-time resident of England, kindly trying to make sure we don’t swap one set of problems for another in the name of “improving access.” I’m afraid I can’t back the idea that the best way to speed up GP, community health and mental health care is to push everything into co-located hubs. In practice, that approach risks making access less flexible, less local and less reliable for many people, especially older ones like me who rely on familiar GPs and home visits.

Why I’m wary:
- Travel and transport realities. Many people in my area have limited mobility and rely on local buses or family, not a central hub that’s miles away or hard to reach. If services are concentrated in a hub, we might have longer journeys, not shorter waits. That’s a real barrier for someone with arthritis or dementia who can’t easily get to a distant site.
- Continuity and trust. Seeing the same clinician builds understanding of a patient’s history, medications and concerns. If staff are moved into a hub with rotating teams, that continuity – so important for managing long-term conditions and mental health – can feel lost. People don’t always want to be shuffled between professionals who don’t know their story.
- Capacity and staffing realities. The NHS is stretched. Building or expanding hubs requires more staff, space and funding. If the money isn’t there to staff them properly, we’ll just trade queueing at a GP for queueing at a hub, possibly with longer waits and less personal attention.
- Local governance and integration hurdles. Co-locating primary, community and mental health with social care and voluntary groups sounds ideal in theory, but in practice it needs seamless IT systems, agreement on data sharing, and strong local leadership. Too often these pieces don’t align quickly enough, leading to muddled pathways rather than smooth care.
- Risk of centralisation. Co-located hubs can end up pulling services out of smaller practices that people have used for years, leaving rural or peripheral communities with even fewer local options. We should be wary of creating a two-tier system where some people enjoy easy access and others lose local, known services.

What I’d prefer and what could actually work better
- Strengthen what already exists. Invest in capacity and support for individual GP practices to run more efficient triage, same-day appointments and longer allocations for complex cases. Put in place better care coordinators to navigate patients through GP, community and mental health services without forcing them into a hub.
- Embed teams locally, not centrally. Rather than one big hub, create small, linked teams that include GPs, district nurses, mental health practitioners and social care workers attached to each area or locality. They can work together with social prescribers and VCSE partners but remain rooted in the community where patients live.
- Flexible access, including home visits and digital options. Expand safe, simple digital consultations and telephone triage while preserving the option for home visits when needed. Ensure patients can choose the mode of access that suits them best.
- Transport and outreach. For rural or bus-challenged areas, pilot mobile clinics and outreach teams that visit villages on set days, with clear routes and contact details. This keeps care local without forcing people to travel to a distant hub.
- Mental health integrated at practice level. Staff mental health professionals within primary care teams can reduce delays and keep care person-centred, while still enabling rapid referral to specialist services when needed.
- Respect patient choice and privacy. Any model should preserve patient choice, ensure continuity of care and protect privacy. If hubs exist, they must be options, not requirements, with transparent information on how you can access services.

In my experience, improvements have often come from bolstering the existing pathways and adding practical supports—not from centralising everything into large hubs. The goal should be timely, local, person-centred care that respects how people actually live and travel, not a one-size-fits-all solution.

If a hub model is pursued, it must be implemented with strong local involvement, clear patient choice, robust IT and governance arrangements, and a guaranteed capacity to preserve continuity with familiar clinicians. Otherwise, I fear we’ll swap one set of delays and frustrations for another, and older people will be the ones who pay the price.

I support improving timely access by lengthening appointments for complex patients expanding multidisciplinary teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to treat routine cases, and increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots—protecting continuity of care and reducing waits through hiring, session expansion and optimised scheduling.

Prioritise training and return-to-practice programmes, apprenticeships and CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff; expand online booking and e-consultations while ensuring non-digital options for older or disadvantaged patients; and fund co-located hubs integrating primary, community, social care and VCSE partners.

From my experience living in England, getting timely GP, community health and mental health care can feel uneven, especially outside town (as if that will ever happen). I welcome plans to expand multidisciplinary teams so routine cases are handled by pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, freeing GPs to focus on complex care. I’ve benefited when a pharmacist sorted a medication issue quickly, a physio-led session reduced my back pain without a GP visit, and a paramedic-supported triage helped me access urgent care after a minor fall with a shorter wait. 

Transport and access remain barriers in rural and mobility-limited areas. Mobile clinics that visit community halls or estates, outreach nurses, and telehealth hubs in libraries could dramatically cut travel and parking stress. In my neighbourhood, a weekly GP telephone triage followed by same-day or next-day face-to-face with a nurse or physio would be ideal. Incentives for practices to run outreach clinics, subsidised transport to appointments, and investment in premises that accommodate digital access would make a real difference. Data sharing across teams must be robust but seamless to avoid repeated tests or conflicting advice.

Overall, a blended model—local, easy-to-access multidisciplinary teams with strong GP involvement for complex cases—would improve timeliness and continuity of care without compromising safety, while genuinely addressing the practical barriers many of us face.

Yes, invest in co-located community hubs that integrate GP, community health, mental health with social care and VCSE partners to deliver seamless local care. This should include protected funding for flexible appointments, transport support, and staffing continuity to prevent delays and inequities.

I live in England and I value timely access to GP and community mental health services. I welcome expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, provided there are non‑digital options and support for those less tech‑savvy, especially older people. For instance, an online appointment with a phone back‑up option would help when I can't travel, and simple triage should never replace a proper face‑to‑face check when needed. 

Expanding multidisciplinary teams makes sense: pharmacists to review medicines, physiotherapists for rehab after falls, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine checks and minor illnesses, freeing GPs to focus on complex care. In my experience, a local clinic with a physio and nurse practitioner reduces waiting times and avoids unnecessary GP visits. 

Targeted outreach: ensure interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to deprived and ethnic minority groups. Clinics in community centres, translation services at appointments, and mobile units would help those who are struggling to access care. Overall, these changes would improve timeliness while keeping care safe and respectful for older patients like me.

From our organisation's perspective, I strongly support targeted resource allocation to GP, community health and mental health services. In our area, there are communities with language and cultural barriers that lead to delays; investing interpreters and culturall competent staff, and running outrrach clinics in deprived neighbourhoods would reduce access gaps for ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physicia associates—would handle routinee cases, freeing GPs to devote time to complex care and high-risk patients, which should improve timely access. We have seen success where pharmacists run chronic disease checks and triage minor issues; patients then get quicker access to medicines or definitive advice. I disagree with relying on daytime weekday appointments alone; please fund evening/weekend clinics, guaranteed same-day urgent slots, interpreters, and expand teams (pharmacists, physios, paramedics) to handle routine care.

Agree. For our community, increasing appointment slots with more staff and smarter scheduling, plus evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would help everyone, including working people. Invest in targeted recruitment and wellbeing for primary care teams to attract and keep good clinicians.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for someone like me juggling exams, part-time work and the everyday pressures of growing up. In my area there are times you can get a GP appointment quickly, but more often there are long waits for mental health support and community health services. Early support saves problems from escalating, so the changes I’d push for are practical, well-resourced and focused on equity.

First, expand community mental health teams and strengthen early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. If there were more mental health workers embedded in primary care, schools and community hubs, you’d have quicker triage and a better chance of catching issues early. A real improvement would be a rapid-access pathway: same-day triage in GP practices with a mental health nurse or trained counsellor who can set up next steps within days, not weeks. Alongside this, invest in a broader menu of talking therapies—CBT, counselling and newer approaches like ACT—offered in person and online, with options that fit busy student schedules. Where possible, there should be crisis-response teams that can reach a person within hours and coordinate with the GP to prevent hospital admissions.

Second, close gaps in access for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups through targeted resources and culturally competent delivery. In many communities language barriers and a lack of interpreters create delays and misunderstandings about available support. I’d like to see funded interpreters and multilingual staff, plus clear information in multiple languages about how to access services. Local outreach matters too: pop-up clinics in community centres and housing estates, partnerships with faith groups and student unions, and a community navigator role to help people move through the system. These steps would help ensure someone who is new to the country or who speaks English as a second language isn’t left behind when a GP or mental health service is under pressure.

Third, I recognise the importance of continuity of care, especially for complex, chronic or vulnerable patients. While expanding services is vital, we must protect continuity and build stability. That means longer appointment times for difficult or ongoing issues (think 20–30 minutes for mental health reviews or complex physical health cases), a named GP or care coordinator, and better handovers between community teams and hospital services. Reducing repeat visits and fragmented care should be a core outcome, not an afterthought.

From my own experience, waiting for CAMHS was a real challenge for friends during deadlines and exams, and some people end up paying for private therapy because NHS waits are too long. I’ve found value in school-based mental health supports that act as a bridge to NHS services, but the system shouldn’t depend on luck or a particular school. Quick referral routes and early access to talking therapies made a big difference for me when stress started to spiral—and I know that if more peers had those pathways, fewer would slip through the cracks.

Beyond mental health, I’d like to see GP services improve as well: same-day or next-day urgent slots, more nurse-led clinics for chronic conditions, and clear pathways that guide people from initial contact to ongoing care without excessive delays. Night-time and weekend access would be a real help for students with irregular hours.

In summary, the changes that would most improve timely access are: more community mental health teams with strong early-intervention and crisis capacity; expanded, flexible talking therapies with rapid referral options; targeted outreach and interpreters to close access gaps for marginalised groups; and a firm commitment to continuity of care with longer consultations and named clinicians for those with complex needs. These should be built with local voices—patients, families and community organisations—to ensure practical, equitable and sustainable improvements across GP, community and mental health services.

In our area, getting timely access to GP and community health services feels inconsistent. You can sometimes book online, but same-day GP slots are rare and I’ve been redirected to ring back or come back tomorrow. My concern extends to mental health support for family and friends, where waiting lists still push people toward emergency routes, which is distressing. There are practical snags too: occasional long queues at the local practice, and the extra time needed to travel to appointments when bus services are infrequent and parking is costly. It all compounds when you also need pharmacy or physio follow-ups on the same day. I worry about relying too much on digital channels when not everyone, especially older residents, has reliable internet at home or feels comfortable with online triage. My instinct is that improving access will need more than a single lever—earlier, friendlier triage, more flexible transport to clinics, closer cooperation between GP surgeries, mental health teams, and community nurses, and clear information about what to do after hours. But I’d like to see concrete evidence that changes will reach people who are not online all day.

As an older resident in England, I have seen how difficult it is to get timely help when you need it. GP appointments can be booked days away, mental health services often have long waits, and when you fall between services you feel left hanging. I welcome steps to expand multidisciplinary teams, including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to treat routine or minor conditions. That could free GPs to focus on complex cases and ensure quicker access, provided there is clear supervision, consistent prescribing practices, and good handovers so patients don’t have to repeat their story.

I’m also concerned about mental health access. Expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis response is vital to parity with physical health. In my area, waits for talking therapies can stretch into months, and families worry when crisis lines aren’t immediately available. More robust crisis support and quicker referrals would help.

Finally, investing in co-located community hubs that bring together primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners is sensible. The hubs must be truly accessible—ground-floor rooms, good transport links, and seamless data sharing so you don’t repeat tests.

With proper funding, governance and local involvement, these changes could improve timely access significantly.
it's outrageous that target resources for deprived and minority communities, expand community mental health teams, and streamline NHS111 and triage to cut waits!

From my small town in England, expanding online booking and e-consultations sounds convenient for some, but it risks leaving older people behind. I’ve tried online systems; pages stall, forms time out, and passwords get forgotten. In our area many pensioners have limited data and struggle with smartphones. A neighbour waited weeks for a mental health referral after the practice shifted to online triage. My own experience with a simple prescription call showed that moving to screens often means someone younger is on the other end, not someone who can talk through a problem.

What would help most is a genuine mix of options. keep clear telephone booking lines with patient‑friendly staff who can triage and book, and keep same-day or walk-in slots where possible. provide non-digital help in libraries or community centres to set up online accounts; offer printed reminders and simple paper forms for those who want them; and arrange home visits for the housebound. For mental health, quick-access phone or face-to-face routes should be maintained, with straightforward referral steps.

If policies fund both digital access and robust non-digital support, and invest in local volunteers or staff to assist older people, I think timely access would improve without excluding anyone.

Extending GP hours into evenings and weekends and guaranteeing same-day urgent slots would, I fear, shift the burden rather than fix it. The real problem is under-staffing among GPs and trained nurses. Without more frontline clinicians, longer hours simply spread the same workload thinner and raise burnout, which hurts patient safety and continuity of care. 

Even with a guaranteed same-day urgent slot, issues remain. People often end up seeing a different clinician each time, which is not ideal for managing chronic conditions or mental health needs. And after-work slots may not be reliably staffed, leaving patients to wait again or go to A&E for non-emergency concerns. 

I work full-time and know others who struggle to fit daytime appointments around work and childcare. If we want real timely access, we should invest in recruiting and retaining more GPs and practice nurses, fund stable long-term posts, and expand robust same-day triage by phone or video to direct people to the right level of care. We also need stronger community mental health teams and nurse-led urgent care hubs that operate within core hours, coordinated with primary care, not just extended hours.

Thank you for inviting views on how to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. I live in England and am part of the 65-plus generation, and I’ve seen how waiting for care can become a real worry, not just for myself but for neighbours who are less mobile. Transport, parking and the quality of premises are often the first barriers, especially in rural or semi-rural areas where buses are infrequent and parking at the small surgeries is cramped or hard to access. I’ve also noticed that even when a service exists, the journey to reach it can mean days without a check-up, which is risky for people with chronic conditions or recent mental health concerns. Given these realities, I’d like to see a mix of approaches rather than one-size-fits-all fixes.

What changes would most improve timely access? Here are some practical ideas that would work well in my area, with the emphasis on mobility and local integration:

- Mobile clinics and targeted outreach: A regular, predictable schedule of mobile GP and district nurse sessions visiting villages, care homes and market towns would bring basic health checks, wound care, vaccinations and mental health check-ins closer to people’s homes. When I’ve seen mobile clinics operate, the turnaround time for getting an appointment dramatically improves for those who cannot travel easily. Pairing these with simple diagnostic tests and on-site pharmacies would cut days of waiting. We should also boost outreach for mental health, with trained workers meeting people in community spaces (libraries, churches, community centres) on a rotating basis so people feel safer and more inclined to engage without the stigma of a clinic door.

- Telehealth hubs with real local support: Telehealth can shorten waiting times and triage effectively, but many older residents need help to use the technology. I’d welcome telehealth hubs in village halls or community centres that are staffed by friendly techni-cal champions who can set up devices, protect privacy and switch to in-person care when needed. These hubs should ensure no one is left behind by the digital divide: offer telephone options, clear booking lines, and simple user guides.

- Co-located community hubs for seamless care: A single, well-equipped local hub that brings together primary care, district nursing, mental health professionals and social care, plus VCSE partners, would transform how care is coordinated. If a patient with multiple conditions has a care plan, it could be shared across services, with a single access point and joint appointments when appropriate. In practice, this means fewer repeat forms, faster referrals and more consistent messages about how to manage medicine, diet, mobility and social needs. A hub could also host a voluntary sector hub for carers and family members, which often makes the day-to-day management of care much smoother.

- Longer appointments for complex needs and better continuity: For many of us with chronic conditions or vulnerable mental health histories, a short 10-minute slot rarely suffices. Extending appointment times and protecting continuity—ideally seeing the same clinician when possible—would improve outcomes and cut down on repeat visits. It also supports better medication reviews, personalised care plans and fewer hospital visits due to early detection of deterioration.

- Improvements to premises and parking: Simple things matter: accessible entrances, adequate parking, clear signage, good lighting and clean waiting areas. In my town, parking is a daily hurdle and the waiting room can feel cramped. If clinics were designed with mobility in mind—from automatic doors to seating that is easy to move in and out of—patients would be less stressed before a consultation and more able to focus on their healthcare.

- Workforce incentives and sustainable funding: Rural and mobility-limited areas struggle to recruit and retain clinicians. I’d like to see targeted incentives—relocation support, flexible working patterns, and funding to create small practice networks that share staff and clinical space. These would help maintain continuity of care and reduce long wait times. Funding should also support the development of community hubs and mobile services without pulling from other essential services.

- Data sharing and governance: To make integrated care possible, safe, user-friendly data sharing across GP practices, hospital teams, social care and VCSE groups is vital. Patients should be informed and asked consent for information sharing, with clear assurances about privacy.

- Local evaluation and learning: Any new model should be piloted with clear success metrics—reductions in wait times, fewer emergency admissions, satisfaction scores from older residents, and better management of long-term conditions. Sharing what works and what doesn’t across Integrated Care Systems would help other areas adopt what suits them best.

In short, timely access will come from a blend of mobile and hub-based services, supported by calm and inclusive digital options, plus a commitment to continuity of care for those who need it most. Care should be designed around the patient journey, not the service silo, and it must be adaptable to the realities of transport, parking and premises in our communities.

From my experience here in England, and as someone aged 65+, I cannot agree that a few quick tweaks will reliably improve timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services. I’ve seen friends wait weeks for a routine GP appointment, and when a family member needed support for anxiety we faced slow access to talking therapies and crisis help. In rural areas, outreach nursing feels stretched and online booking often excludes older folk who struggle with digital systems. 

What would help most is a longer‑term, sustainable expansion of the workforce. Increase training places, support return‑to‑practice for experienced clinicians, and widen apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Also expand community mental health teams, with strong early intervention, responsive crisis care and a robust path for talking therapies, so mental health care is treated with the same urgency as physical health. If these steps aren’t accelerated, waits will persist and inequities will grow, leaving us older residents at a clear disadvantage.

I welcome the proposed steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. In rural and smaller communities, transport and parking are real barriers, especially for older residents such as my neighbours who struggle with infrequent buses and long walks to clinics in bad weather. Mobile clinics visiting village halls, care homes and outreach teams would bring care closer to people and cut missed appointments. Telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, supported by friendly staff, would help when mobility is limited or storms prevent travel. An easy-to-access referral route and modest incentives for practices to offer extended hours or weekend slots would also make a practical difference for those balancing care with other commitments. 

To reach deprived and minority groups, it is essential to provide interpreters and train staff in cultural competence, plus targeted outreach through faith groups, community associations and local venues. Multilingual information, translation of forms, and community health workers drawn from local communities would help reduce barriers and build trust. Taken together, these measures would improve timely, respectful care for all residents, including my fellow older neighbours who rely on reliable access to services.

I disagree that expanding mental health teams alone will fix access; without improved GP slots, crisis care and faster funding, waits will persist and mental health won't achieve parity with physical health.

I live in England and, at my age, I’ve seen how waits for GP and mental health appointments can stretch. My local practice often has only a small number of GP slots each day and same‑day urgent access can be hard to secure. Mental health services in particular sometimes run into multi‑week delays, and community physiotherapy feels inconsistent. To improve timely access, the biggest impact would come from expanding capacity: hire more GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists; offer longer sessions where needed; and tune scheduling so urgent slots are easier to book without long waits or constant reshuffles. It’s also essential this is matched with sustainable staffing and predictable hours to prevent burnout and longer backlogs later on.

I’m supportive of expanding online booking and e‑consultations, but I don’t want to leave anyone behind. Non‑digital options must remain strong—call‑back triage, telephone bookings, and in‑person appointments at convenient local hubs for those less comfortable with technology or without reliable internet.

Evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would help working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs. A mix of digital and non‑digital access, complemented by robust funding and local monitoring, would best improve timely care without compromising quality or safety.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. In Wales, timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services remains a reality for many people, particularly in rural and mobility‑limited areas where transport, parking and premises deficits compound delays. We do not think the current framework goes far enough to address the underlying, long‑term capacity problems. The changes that would most improve access are those that sustainably grow the workforce, bring care closer to people’s homes, and ensure mental health services are integrated and responsive as a core part of physical health care.

Key priorities we would press for are:

- Expand the workforce in a sustainable way: significantly increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, with a clear pathway from training through to retention in Wales. We need robust return‑to‑practice support, expanded apprenticeships and protected CPD funding. In several communities we visit, the main bottleneck is not a lack of appointments per se but the lack of trained staff willing to stay local. A 5–10 year plan that funds locally anchored training hubs (including in rural clusters) and creates clear career ladders would reduce reliance on short‑term locums and improve continuity of care.

- Build capacity through long‑term workforce strategies, not piecemeal fixes: better remuneration where pressures are highest, formal supervision for clinicians in training and better working conditions. We need a Wales‑wide workforce plan that sets measurable targets for GP, district nurse and mental health professional numbers, with regional catchments designed to maintain service quality in smaller communities.

- Tackle transport, parking and premises deficits with locally accessible care and flexible delivery models: mobile clinics and outreach teams should be a staple, not a pilot. We have seen rural patients miss appointments due to travel barriers and parking limitations at a single town centre clinic. Mobile GP slots, co‑located mobile diagnostics, and outreach clinics in schools, community halls or GP hubs can substantially reduce no‑show rates. Telehealth must be a genuine supplement, not a substitute for in‑person care where it is clinically necessary; invest in telehealth hubs with digital inclusion measures (training, devices for patients without home access, and robust data privacy). Incentives to encourage practitioners to work in rural settings, including housing support and travel subsidies, are essential to stabilise the workforce.

- Expand community mental health teams and ensure timely access to early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies: parity with physical health is essential. We need expanded CAMHS capacity, stronger early‑intervention teams, and around‑the‑clock crisis response where possible. Waiting times for talking therapies remain unacceptably long in many areas; scaling evidence‑based therapies (CBT‑I, IPT, ACT, etc.) and embedding them in primary care and schools will prevent more acute crises and reduce long‑term dependence on statutory services.

- Integrate services to shorten pathways and improve outcomes: more integrated care pathways between GPs, community health services and mental health teams. In practice, this means shared community hubs where a patient can access a GP, nurse, social worker and talk therapies in a single visit, rather than being shuffled between isolated services with long waits.

Evidence from our experience in rural Wales shows how critical these elements are. A weekly mobile clinic visiting six villages cut average travel times for primary care by half and reduced no‑shows in those communities. In another area, CAMHS waiting lists stretched to several months, leading to crises that could have been averted with earlier intervention and better community support. A dedicated crisis response team, available within a few hours of referral, could have prevented ambulance conveyances and hospital admissions. These examples illustrate how much difference well‑planned investment can make when it is sustained and regionally tailored.

We recognise the importance of digital tools, but we also see the risk of widening inequality if digital access or literacy is uneven. Any expansion of telehealth must be paired with practical steps to ensure everyone can participate. We also caution against treating “more online” as a substitute for real‑world access, particularly for mental health support where face‑to‑face contact and early engagement are often crucial.

In summary, the most impactful changes are a long‑term, funded plan to grow and retain the workforce; provision of mobile and outreach services to reach rural and mobility‑limited communities; and a strengthened, faster, more integrated mental health offer that achieves parity with physical health. We urge policymakers to commit to these core priorities and to monitor outcomes with transparent, locally disaggregated data to ensure improvements reach the communities most in need.

it's outrageous that i welcome the direction of this question and believe the most transformative changes to improve timely access would centre on expanding community mental health teams, expanding early intervention, strengthening crisis response, and widening access to talking therapies. When mental health services are better integrated with GP practices and community care, people get the right help faster and we can avoid unnecessary crises and hospital admissions.

- Expand community mental health teams (CMHTs). In my experience, waiting times for referral to mental health support can feel like a barrier to getting on with life. A larger CMHT with a full range of professionals—nurses, social workers, occupational therapists, psychiatrists—working in a local hub that GPs can quickly contact would make a tangible difference. I’d like to see 24/7 triage and same-day initial assessments where possible, with rapid home visits for those who cannot travel. Crucially, these teams should be co-located with primary care so a warm handover from a GP to a mental health professional is routine, not exceptional.

- Invest in early intervention and prevention. Early intervention for emerging issues should be a standard pathway, not a battle to access. This means faster access to low- and high-intensity therapies for anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and first-episode psychosis, with clearly defined targets (for example, initial contact within two weeks for routine referrals and within days for urgent concerns). Schools, workplaces, and voluntary sector partners should be supported to identify issues early, with a direct line into local CMHTs. I’ve seen friends benefit when early symptoms were addressed quickly with stepped-care options, including digital/face-to-face therapy, before problems escalated.

- Strengthen crisis response and crisis pathways. When someone tips into crisis, delay can be life-changing. A robust crisis response should include a 24/7 helpline, rapid crisis assessments, and mobile crisis teams that can support people at home or in the community. The option of crisis houses or short-term intensive home treatment can help people stabilise without unnecessary hospital admission. A well-structured crisis pathway also means A&E liaises closely with mental health services so people aren’t bounced around between services.

- Widen access to talking therapies and ensure parity with physical health. Access to Evidence-Based Talking Therapies (EBTT) like CBT, ACT, and interpersonal therapy should be timely and housed within the same framework as physical health services. This means increasing numbers of qualified therapists, reducing wait times, and offering a mix of in-person and digital options. It’s important that therapies are available in languages commonly spoken in the community and that support is culturally sensitive. Where appropriate, guided self-help and asynchronous digital programs can be offered alongside traditional therapies to reduce waiting lists while still providing clinical oversight.

- Improve GP access and care coordination. For many people, the first step is a GP appointment. Expanding same-day or next-day slots for mental health concerns, with GP-level triage that can route patients to the most appropriate service quickly, would relieve bottlenecks. Co-locating mental health staff in GP practices or deploying dedicated care coordinators who can navigate patients through CMHTs, THERAPY services, and social care would reduce delays and ensure people aren’t slipping through gaps.

- Measure, report, and review wait times transparently. Clear, publicly available targets for wait times—e.g., urgent mental health referrals assessed within 2 weeks, standard care within 6 weeks—can drive improvements. Regular local audits and patient feedback should inform service changes. In my area, transparency about wait times and outcomes has been limited; stronger oversight would help communities understand progress and hold providers to account.

From personal experience, when a family member faced rising anxiety and sleep disruption, timely access to a local CMHT and an initial talking-therapy plan within a couple of weeks made a real difference. A crisis occurred, and a well-staffed crisis team was able to step in quickly, offering home-based support that prevented escalation and hospital admission. These are not exceptional cases; they illustrate what a properly funded and well-coordinated system can deliver. If the proposed changes are implemented with sufficient staffing, appropriate training, and clear coordination across GP, community and mental health services, we will see fewer avoidable crises, shorter waits, and far better parity between mental and physical healthcare.

In short, the changes that would most improve timely access are a bigger, better-integrated CMHT network, stronger early intervention, responsive crisis services, wider availability of talking therapies, and a GP/mental health care-coordination model that keeps people out of waiting rooms longer than necessary. That is how we create a system that treats mental health with the same urgency and respect as physical health, in practical and measurable ways!

Disagree that merely more slots will fix delays. Prioritise continuity and longer consultations for complex patients, and expand multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, mental health) to handle routine cases, freeing GPs for high-need patients.

Expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and talking therapies could cut waits and help parity with physical health, but needs funding and clear integration with GPs. Multidisciplinary teams could handle routine cases, yet must ensure consistent quality, training, and rapid crisis support.

As a student with a part-time job in England, I often can’t get GP appointments during the week because of shifts and timetables. Extending hours into evenings and weekends with guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help working people and those with urgent non-emergency needs. It could reduce last-minute A&E trips and make care fairer for people who cannot attend in normal hours. But it would need proper funding, enough GPs and support staff, protected slots, and a limit to avoid overburdening practices or compromising quality. 

I also back improving NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and streamline patient flow. A better digital booking system with real-time triage notes and clear routes to the right service would cut duplication and confusion; I’ve experienced trying to book a GP for a fever and being bounced between NHS111 and triage, then visiting A&E earlier than necessary. That must be avoided through robust protocols and data sharing, with privacy safeguarded. 

Overall, a combined approach—better access hours plus smarter triage and navigation—could improve timely care, provided it is funded, well-coordinated and safe.

From where I’m standing in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services isn’t consistent for people my age. When I or friends need a GP quickly, it’s often a struggle to get an appointment that fits around study and part-time work. I recently waited about two weeks for a GP slot after a cold, and a mental health referral process I know took months to yield a first meeting. These delays aren’t just frustrating; they can let conditions worsen and pile up other pressures on urgent care. I think the biggest win would be increasing appointment slots and overall session capacity by expanding staffing, extending session lengths where needed, and making scheduling genuinely smarter so people aren’t waiting weeks for a check-in or follow-up.

There are real, practical ways to do this Obviously.... Hiring more GPs, practice nurses and therapists is essential, but it has to be paired with smarter scheduling. For example, longer appointment blocks for chronic conditions or for mental health follow-ups can reduce back-and-forth and improve care quality. A few practices in my area have started nurse-led same-day slots for minor concerns, which has helped ease GP demand and got people advice faster. Expanding to more flexible hours—early mornings, evenings and some weekend clinics—would also help students and those with irregular work patterns. And we should explore group sessions or group therapy for suitable mental health issues where appropriate, to reach more people without sacrificing quality of care.

On the NHS111 and care-navigation side, I see real potential but also important caveats. A well-designed triage and booking system could prioritise urgent cases, cut out duplication, and steer people to the right service first time. I’d like to see NHS111 equipped with better clinical triage, so someone with a mental health crisis or a high-risk symptom can be escalated promptly, with a clear, visible pathway to urgent slots if needed. A more integrated booking system that surfaces available urgent slots across nearby practices would save people from trying multiple numbers or apps. Care navigators or “flow coordinators” could help people understand what service they actually need and book the right appointment, rather than ending up in a loop of referrals and re-referrals.

That said, there are risks we must guard against. Recruiting more staff is essential, but it isn’t a quick fix; it requires sustainable funding, retention strategies, and support to prevent burnout. We must ensure triage doesn’t delay care for genuinely urgent cases or rely on less experienced staff without proper supervision. Digital booking and NHS111 tools must be accessible to everyone, including those who aren’t online or who have limited digital literacy, so non-digital phone pathways remain robust. Data sharing between services should be secure but efficient to avoid asking people for repeated information and to prevent duplicated tests or assessments.

My concrete ask would be: fund and pilot an expansion of multi-disciplinary teams in primary care (GPs, nurse practitioners, therapists) with extended hours and longer follow-up blocks; roll out smarter, centralized booking that can reserve urgent slots and quickly route people to the right service; and bolster NHS111 with clinical triage that can safely escalate genuine emergencies while improving navigation to timely care. Access to GP, community health and mental health services in rural Wales is hampered by transport, parking and premises limitations, so I’d support a package of changes that bring care closer to people while keeping them connected to their usual clinicians. From my vantage as an older resident in England, the most effective changes to improve timely access would be to protect continuity of care and to lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic and vulnerable needs. When a patient has several long‑standing conditions, brief 10‑minute slots and seeing a different clinician each time makes it hard to build a full picture of health, adjust treatment safely, or spot deteriorations early. A system that prioritises continuity—where possible seeing the same GP, or at least a stable care team—would cut down on repeated histories, missed signals, and the frustrating cycle of follow‑ups that never quite resolve the issue. Longer appointments for these patients would, I believe, improve outcomes and reduce the need for repeat visits in the longer run.

Some practical changes could make a real difference. First, guarantee longer slots for complex cases—think 20 to 30 minutes for patients with two or more chronic conditions or significant frailty—so clinicians can review medications, assess interactions, and set up coordinated care plans in one sitting. In my area, I’ve seen how a single, well‑timed review could have prevented a hospital admission; in contrast, multiple short visits often miss the big picture and leave the patient anxious about what was discussed or changed.

Second, strengthen continuity with a named GP or a stable multidisciplinary team within the practice. A care navigator or key worker who co‑ordinates between GP, district nurses, pharmacists, and social care would be invaluable—especially for those of us caring for vulnerable relatives. I’ve witnessed neighbours who have felt abandoned when a crisis hits and they can’t quickly contact someone who knows their history. A named clinician plus a nearby team would reduce that risk.

Third, expand the local workforce and integrate services more closely. More GPs and practice nurses, plus allied roles such as pharmacists in primary care for medication reviews, and mental health practitioners embedded in primary care to offer timely talking therapies or brief interventions, would address delays before they escalate. In practice, this could look like a weekly nurse‑led clinic within the GP building for chronic disease review, with an on‑site pharmacist to check prescriptions, deprescribe where appropriate, and manage polypharmacy with the patient’s consent.

Fourth, improve access pathways for mental health and community health services. Timely access to talking therapies, especially for older adults, is critical. A fast‑track or same‑week pathway within primary care, with options for home or community visits when mobility is an issue, would help avoid crises. I’ve seen situations where someone waited months for therapy, only to deteriorate in the interim; a quicker route could have stabilized them more effectively.

Fifth, strengthen home and community support. For frail residents, regular home visits by district nurses or a rapid response physiotherapist can prevent deterioration and unnecessary hospital visits. A robust home‑visit system, coordinated by a care navigator and linked to the patient’s care plan, would be especially valuable for those with mobility problems or cognitive impairment.

Sixth, improve the use of digital tools without leaving older people behind. Online booking and secure messages should be available, but with real support for those who struggle with technology. A simple telephone triage option, plus an in‑person fallback, ensures nobody is excluded. Where online data sharing exists, it must be accompanied by clear information and consent so patients and carers can follow their care plan across GP, community services and hospital.

Finally, clear accountability and local leadership are essential. Local services should publish wait‑time targets, ensure urgent same‑day access for high‑risk patients, and regularly review outcomes—such as avoidable hospital admissions, patient satisfaction, and the effectiveness of care plans. Investment now in longer appointment times, continuity of care, and integrated community support will likely reduce demand on emergency services later and improve quality of life for many older residents.

Thank you for considering these perspectives. The goal is to keep people well at home where possible, with timely, coordinated care when they need it, so they don’t drift into a crisis before help is received.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains inconsistent. With proper funding and workforce planning, we could substantially cut waiting times and improve outcomes.

We represent a coalition of patient and community groups working across England to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From our on‑the‑ground experience, the most reliable way to shorten waits and improve continuity of care is to invest in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health teams, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners. When people can access multiple services in a single building or closely linked network, triage is faster, referrals are clearer, and patients experience less confusion navigating the system.

Co‑located hubs and integrated care
- A hub model enables a single intake and shared care plans. In places where practices, district nursing, mental health outreach and social workers operate under one umbrella, patients report quicker appointment access, better management of long‑term conditions and fewer gaps between services. This is especially important for people with complex needs who currently bounce between organisations.
- We advocate for ring‑fenced funding to establish and maintain these hubs, plus a governance framework that brings GP practices, local authorities, CCGs/ICSs and VCSE partners into joint decision‑making. A pooled budget with aligned incentives would make it easier to co‑commission services, share staffing where appropriate, and standardise referral pathways.
- The plan must include interoperable IT systems and a shared patient record with consent controls. Staff should be able to see a patient’s full history across primary, community and mental health services to avoid repetitive assessments and conflicting advice. Data sharing must be secure, transparent and patient‑driven.

Workforce: recruitment, retention and wellbeing
- To deliver timely access, we need to grow and retain primary care and related staff. This means targeted recruitment, smarter international hiring, clearer career progression and incentives to join and stay in practice. Practical steps include visa facilitation and relocation packages for international GPs and nurses, loan forgiveness or return‑to‑practice incentives, and streamlined registration pathways where appropriate.
- Pay, workload and flexible working are critical. Competitive salaries, reasonable hours, more predictable rostering, and strong wellbeing support reduce burnout and turnover. We also need robust training pipelines—upskilling nurses, physician associates, mental health support workers and social care staff—so teams can function effectively in hub environments.
- We should pilot workforce models that enable staff to move between primary and community roles where needed, with clear governance to maintain quality and patient safety.

Evening and weekend access, with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots
- Providing evening and weekend clinics can dramatically improve access for working people and those with urgent but non‑emergency needs. A balanced approach would start with a limited number of after‑hours slots in high‑demand areas, with protected time for urgent same‑day assessments.
- Any expansion must be designed to protect continuity of care. After‑hours access should be integrated with daytime teams so that information flows smoothly, not limited to a separate service that fragments care. Telemedicine can complement in‑person access, but cannot replace the value of face‑to‑face urgent assessment when risk is uncertain.
- Implementation should be phased: begin in urban hubs with higher volumes, measure impact on wait times and hospital demand, and adjust schedules based on patient need and staff capacity. Clear metrics are essential: same‑day appointment availability, average waiting times, no‑show rates, patient satisfaction and outcomes.

Equity, access and sustainability
- Access improvements must be equitable. Rural areas, minority communities and people with language or mobility barriers should not be left behind. Co‑located hubs should be designed with accessible transport options, interpreters, and culturally competent staff.
- Sustainability will rely on stable long‑term funding, not just short‑term pilots. We need transparent evaluation, with findings feeding into policy and funding decisions so successful models can be scaled without eroding other critical services.

In short, timely access will improve if we combine strategically located, well‑governed co‑located hubs with a robust workforce plan and a careful expansion of evening/weekend/urgent same‑day slots. The approach must be people‑centred, data‑driven and financially sustainable, with strong linkages to social care and VCSE organisations to address non‑medical determinants of health. We urge the government to back this package with multi‑year funding, clear governance, and a rigorous evaluation framework so successful models can spread to all communities that need them.

A safety net would help—automatic check‑backs if symptoms worsen within 24–48 hours, easy re‑routing to urgent care, and visible timelines so patients aren’t left guessing what happens next.
  - A robust care navigation role could guide people through options (pharmacy check, nurse‑led clinics, physiotherapy, or mental health drop‑in) and coordinate referrals so you don’t end up making multiple calls to different services.   - Cost and training are real considerations. We must ensure these team members are appropriately supervised, with ongoing professional development and clear lines of accountability. The goal isn’t to replace GPs but to expand capacity and improve access for routine care.

Providing two weeknight clinics (e.g., Mon/Wed until 8pm) and a guaranteed same‑day urgent appointment across networks would reduce delays, spare patients long waits, and alleviate pressure on A&E. Secondly, address transport, parking and premises deficits. Our rural and mobility‑impaired patients lose days to travel. Mobile clinics, outreach teams in libraries or community hubs, telehealth hubs with dedicated transport incentives, and co‑funded premises improvements would bring services closer to people.

Thirdly, expand online booking and e‑consultations while keeping non‑digital options. Alongside user‑friendly online booking, we must offer telephone triage and home visits for those lacking digital access, with digital literacy support and patient champions.

In short, timely access requires flexible hours, mobile and remote options, and inclusive digital pathways.

Three practical changes would most improve timely access in my area. First, protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Seeing the same GP or a small team, with longer slots (around 20 minutes for general practice and longer mental health assessments), would improve outcomes and cut repeat visits. I’ve seen relatives with diabetes and anxiety have to repeat their story at every appointment, which wastes time and risks missing signals. Second, improve NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and simplify the patient flow. A clearer, more predictable process—trained triage staff, better digital booking, and a single portal for status and reminders—would reduce duplication and get urgent cases seen sooner. Third, expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and achieve parity with physical health. Quick access to talking therapies, crisis support and home-based care would prevent deterioration and cut downstream hospital attendances. If these changes are funded and coordinated, they would help people get the right help when they need it, and relieve pressure across GP services and mental health care.

i strongly believe from where I sit in England, dealing with the everyday realities of trying to get timely care for myself and for family members, I can see why the idea of co‑located hubs and broader multidisciplinary teams sounds appealing. In theory, pooling primary care with community and mental health services, social care and VCSE partners could smooth out the bumps. In practice, though, I’m not convinced this alone will deliver the prompt access people deserve, unless there are strict guardrails, realistic funding and a workable workforce plan to back it up.

First, co‑located hubs. The concept is good on paper: one building, one reception, shared appointment slots, and a single care plan that spans health and social support. But in our area, the reality is often different. Hubs can become a kind of administrative umbrella rather than a truly integrated service. Different organisations still manage their own budgets, priority lists and IT systems, which means patients repeatedly retell their history, referrals get stuck in queue, and urgent needs become treated as if they’re separate problems again. I’ve seen a mental health referral that should have been quick turn into a two‑month wait because the social care team couldn’t share information fast enough with the NHS side, and there was no clear governance to drive cross‑organ sign‑offs. 

Another practical obstacle is capacity. Co‑locating services does not automatically create more clinicians. If you don’t have enough GPs, nurses, and allied health professionals, the hub ends up shuttling patients between services, not streamlining them. We’ve had days when the same person is triaged by three different clinicians in one morning because of siloed pathways, and by the afternoon they’re back to square one with the GP anyway. That is not timely access; that is a detour through bureaucracy.

I also worry about the social care and VCSE elements. When social care slots are scarce, or when voluntary partners are funded only for short bursts, the promise of seamless local care collapses into a patchwork that suits budgets rather than patient need. If the hub exists but the social care team can’t respond promptly to home visits, equipment needs, or falls prevention, the whole thing becomes a nice façade that doesn’t serve the people relying on it most, including older residents who can’t travel easily and must depend on timely in‑home support.

To make co‑located hubs work, you’d need a clear, enforceable governance framework: a single point of accountability, common IT systems with real‑time data sharing, joint triage criteria, agreed staffing levels, and protected funding that follows patients across services. There would also need to be patient choice built in—people should be able to opt for a traditional GP appointment if that’s what they prefer—and transparent performance metrics focused on actual wait times, not process milestones.

Second, expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs for more complex care also sounds sensible. In principle, having pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates within primary care can reduce GP workload and speed up treatment for common conditions. In practice, though, this hinges on three things: (1) robust training and supervision to ensure high‑quality care; (2) access to shared patient records so, for example, a pharmacist can adjust medications with full visibility of the patient’s history; and (3) a clear, efficient referral and escalation route if a case is outside the team’s scope.

I’ve seen both good and not‑so‑good examples. A pharmacist‑led chronic condition clinic helped some patients with stable diabetes stay on track without waiting weeks for a GP appointment, but it worked best where there was a well‑established shared electronic record and daily contact with a supervising GP. In other places, pharmacists are stretched thin, with too many competing duties, so their ability to take on new consults is limited. Paramedics and physician associates can be valuable, but if the system isn’t designed to hand back information quickly and isn’t integrated with the practice’s appointment book, you end up with duplication and delays rather than speed.

What I would prioritise, if changes are to deliver timely access, are not just the structural shifts but the logistics and people who make them work: invest in recruiting and retaining more GPs and practice nurses, reduce administrative burdens that eat into clinical time, and expand flexible, same‑day triage with clearly defined pathways for urgent mental health support. Improve access to mental health services by strengthening community‑based teams, ensuring timely referrals into IAPT where appropriate, and providing crisis support that can be accessed without delay. And crucially, any move toward co‑located hubs or MDTs must come with a measurable plan to avoid tipping patients from one waiting list into another and to ensure they experience real continuity of care.

In summary, I’m not opposed to the aims of co‑located hubs or expanded multidisciplinary teams, but I am opposed to rushing them in without the necessary staffing, technology, governance and funding to back them up. If you want timely access, you need to fix the basics first—enough skilled staff, real shared systems, and clear, accountable pathways—then build the integration around those foundations so patients actually experience faster, more seamless care rather than longer queues and more handoffs.

From my experience living in England and juggling work, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services often feels like a lottery. Expanding multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases sounds efficient in theory, but in practice it can fragment care and leave patients unsure who’s responsible for their ongoing health. When a simple issue is handed to a pharmacist, physiotherapist or nurse, I end up repeating history and chasing referrals, which makes things slower rather than quicker.

Longer‑term moves like expanding training places and return‑to‑practice support are welcome in principle, but they don’t solve today’s shortages. My area already has backlogs, and apprenticeships or CPD take years to translate into extra GPs or mental health professionals on the ground. That timeline simply doesn’t help this winter when demand is high.

Evening and weekend clinics could help some workers, yet staffing them sustainably would stretch already stretched teams and could erode continuity of care. Barriers such as transport, childcare and safety would still limit who can actually use them.

What would help more in the near term is reliable same‑day urgent slots with clear triage, more GP appointment capacity with flexible hours, and enhanced digital booking and information sharing so people don’t have to chase multiple contacts. Stronger, well‑coordinated access to mental health support within primary care would also reduce avoidable calls and referrals to specialised services.
