I welcome the direction to improve timely access to GP services, community health and mental health provisions. Getting the right help quickly makes a real difference, especially for people like me who are older and rely on a steady thread of primary care to stay well at home. Two things in particular give me confidence: expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care, and sharpening the NHS111, triage and booking systems so people aren’t left looping from one service to another.

First, expanding multidisciplinary teams in everyday practice is a practical way to free GPs to focus on the more complex cases while routine issues are handled by capable colleagues. In my area, I’ve seen how a pharmacist-led medication review and a physiotherapist-led musculoskeletal clinic within the same practice can catch problems early and sort out simple issues without waiting weeks for a GP appointment. A pharmacist can check medicines, review potential interactions, and give timely advice on minor illnesses, which is especially useful for those of us on multiple prescriptions. A physiotherapist can guide back, knee or shoulder pain with exercises and self-management, reducing the need for a GP visit for every ache. Paramedics or physician associates working in surgeries or home visits can triage and treat minor emergencies at the outset or arrange home visits when travelling to the surgery is difficult. All of this keeps hospital referrals down and frees GPs to devote time to complex cases—frail patients with multiple chronic conditions, or someone dealing with a new, worrying symptom.

I’d like to see more of this in practice, with clear lines of responsibility and robust supervision so patients always feel safe. It’s important that these team members have access to the patient’s record and to communicate clearly with the GP about what was done and what needs watching. This isn’t just about convenience; it’s about better, continuous care. In the long run, it can improve outcomes and give our aging population more confidence to manage day-to-day health without waiting endlessly for appointments.

Second, the improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation matter a great deal. People get lost in the system when appointments are scattered across different portals and hotlines. A streamlined approach—one reliable triage path that prioritises urgent cases, clear guidance on the appropriate service, and a single, user-friendly booking system—would cut down on duplication and confusion. In practice, this could look like an expanded NHS111 online triage that is able to direct someone with a suspected infection, a new mental health concern, or a sudden fall to the right professional first time, with a guaranteed pathway to a same-day appointment if needed.

Care navigation teams could play a crucial role, especially for older patients who find it hard to navigate multiple services. A trained navigator could help me book a GP slot, a community nurse visit, or a mental health same-day slot, and could remind me of follow-up care. This would be particularly valuable for those with mobility issues or limited digital skills. And there must be a personal touch—phone support or in-person help at the local hub—so people who don’t use digital tools aren’t left behind.

Mental health access, in particular, needs to be timely and integrated with primary care. If someone is in distress, waiting weeks for an appointment is unacceptable. A fast-tracked pathway to counselling or community mental health teams, with proactive check-ins and crisis support, would make a real difference. What helps me is knowing that if a concern arises, a navigator or triage nurse can prioritise it and keep me informed about what comes next, rather than sending me on a loop between different services.

I appreciate that these changes require investment and careful planning. Effective roll-out would depend on training, appropriate staffing, and safeguarding measures so that patient records are accessible to the right professionals while respecting privacy. There should also be performance targets that reflect the realities of older patients—shorter waiting times for urgent cases, prompt same-day access when needed, and reliable follow-up. With these improvements, I believe more of us can stay independent at home, manage minor health concerns promptly, and experience truly coordinated care.

In short, strengthening multidisciplinary teams and tightening the triage and booking pathways would make timely access a reality rather than a hopeful aim. It’s sensible, practical and, most importantly, it aligns with what patients need in their everyday lives: quick help, clear guidance, and care that is coordinated across GP, community and mental health services.

From my vantage point in England, as a 65+ resident, I welcome the aim to speed up access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I’m uneasy about relying mainly on online booking and remote consultations. For many older people, including myself at times, internet reliability, digital skills, and even simply reaching a phone line can be a barrier. In my practice, online bookings often fail to show same-day slots; I’ve waited on a queue for 20 minutes on the phone, only to be told there were none. A remote chat is fine for minor issues, but it misses warning signs in mental health or complex medication reviews. Therefore, I urge a mixed approach with strong non-digital options: a robust, well-staffed telephone line, clear in-person booking, and home visits where needed; plus dedicated assistance in local libraries or community hubs to help people navigate online systems.

I also support investment in co-located hubs that bring together GP care, district nursing, mental health and social care with input from VCSE partners. If funded and designed accessibly—ground-floor entry, accessible transport, and data sharing with consent—these hubs could trim travel, speed up referrals, and provide a one-stop route to care. But digital-only changes risk widening gaps unless safeguards are in place.

From my experience living in England and speaking as someone in the 65-plus age group, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a daily concern that affects my ability to stay independent and well. I am cautious about quick fixes, but I do think two things could work well if they are well planned and properly funded: investing in co-located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health, social care and voluntary sector partners, and expanding appointment capacity across the board with sensible staffing and scheduling reforms. 

On the co-located hubs, I can see real benefits if done properly. In many towns the GP practice, district nursing and mental health teams operate in separate buildings with separate booking lines, which means multiple trips and repeated telling of the same information. A single, well-designed hub in a convenient location—ideally near public transport and with good parking—could act as a one-stop access point. It would be easier to coordinate care for someone with multiple long-term conditions, and it would help avoid unnecessary trips to the hospital for initial assessments. A hub that includes social care support and links to VCSE partners could help with practical needs, such as transport to appointments, nutrition advice, or home safety checks, which in turn reduces the risk of crises and hospital admissions. 

For this to work, the hub must be genuinely integrated. That means a shared front desk, common scheduling, and access to a single patient record (with clear consent and robust privacy safeguards). It should offer a mix of appointment types: same-day triage for urgent concerns, routine GP and nurse appointments, and mental health slots with therapists, plus flexible slots in the evenings or Saturdays for those who still work or have caregiving duties. We also need easy access to social care advice, practical support, and voluntary sector services in the same place or via a linked network. In my neighbourhood, a pilot hub co-locating with a community centre and the local VCSE hub, with staff cross-trained to understand the whole care picture, would make a real difference to how quickly people can get help and feel supported. Importantly, the building must be accessible: step-free entrances, clear signage, hearing loops, and simple, quiet spaces for sensitive conversations. 

On increasing appointment slots, I support expanding capacity through targeted recruitment of GPs, nurses and therapists, plus better use of the existing workforce through extended hours and smarter scheduling. For example, having more nurse-led clinics for chronic conditions could free up GP time for more complex cases. Offering same-day or next-day slots for urgent issues would prevent issues from escalating. For mental health, more consistent access to talking therapies, even if in the form of short, structured sessions with clear pathways, would greatly help many of us who are managing anxiety, depression or grief. It would also be helpful to combine brief motivational support with practical navigation through social care and community resources. 

However, there are caveats. Any expansion must be adequately funded and staffed; without that, we risk longer waits or poorer quality care. The IT systems must be interoperable across services and respect patient privacy. Co-located hubs must not become a bottleneck themselves if there is insufficient space or staff; and they should be designed with local realities in mind—urban centres, smaller towns, and rural communities all have different transport and workforce challenges. A one-size-fits-all model could fail the very people it is meant to help. 

In short, I would welcome a staged approach: establish pilot co-located hubs in a few localities with strong governance, patient and carer involvement, and clear measures of success; ensure expanded appointment capacity is coupled with flexible, accessible access points (phone, in-person, and some simple digital options); and evaluate outcomes by changes in wait times, patient satisfaction, and rates of acute crises. If done with real collaboration between GPs, nurses, mental health teams, social care, and VCSE partners, this could make timely access a realistic expectation rather than a hopeful aspiration.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. We represent a coalition of patient and community organisations across England, and we see timely access to GP, community health and mental health services as essential to people’s health, dignity and independence. Any changes should simplify the path to care, reduce duplication and ensure that those facing language, income or housing barriers are not left waiting at the bottom of the queue.

What would help most, in our view, is a balanced mix of triage improvements, smarter booking systems, and proactive care navigation, paired with targeted investment in interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach so access gaps for deprived and marginalised communities shrink.

NHS111 and clinical triage
- Implement a standardised clinical triage pathway within NHS111 that escalates clearly and promptly to a GP or urgent care practitioner when red flags are present. Too often, patients report repeated calls and mixed messages, with precious hours wasted before someone who can assess risk reviews the case.
- Ensure triage decisions are auditable and linked to real-time appointment availability, so callers are not bounced between services. Clinicians should have the authority to authorise same-day GP or urgent care slots where appropriate, with clear handovers to the receiving service.
- Create a single, monitored feedback loop so patients can see what happened after a triage call and understand the next steps if symptoms change.

Booking systems and care navigation
- Move toward a unified booking system across GP practices that supports same-day urgent slots, longer opening hours and easier access for those who work irregular hours or rely on public transport. A patient should be able to book an appropriate appointment through a single gateway—phone, online and in-person—without recounting the same information multiple times.
- Invest in “care navigation” roles within primary care and community services. Navigators would help patients understand options (GP, pharmacy, community nurse, social care, mental health services), arrange appointments, coordinate follow-up, and reduce unnecessary duplication of tests and admin.
- Require interoperability between GP records, community services and hospital systems so a patient’s information follows them seamlessly, reducing repeat questionnaires and duplicated blood tests.

Reducing duplication and smoothing patient flow
- Standardise referral and information-sharing processes so a referral to mental health, social care or physiotherapy is not re-entered in multiple systems. Streamlined pathways should also connect with community services to prevent unnecessary hospital attendance where appropriate.
- Publish local access standards and publish quarterly dashboards showing wait times by service, including by deprivation index and ethnicity, so gaps can be addressed quickly and publicly.

Interpretation, cultural competence and outreach
- Ensure funded, on-demand interpreter and translation services across GP practices, urgent care, and mental health teams, with quick-access digital interpretation where in-person staff are unavailable. Language support should be available for pre-visit planning, appointment reminders and follow-up care.
- Prioritise recruitment and retention of culturally competent staff, including bilingual clinicians and trained liaison workers who understand local communities’ needs, beliefs and concerns.
- Deliver proactive outreach in deprived and migrant communities—community hubs, faith organisations and schools can host health information sessions, signpost to services, and help people navigate the system. This outreach should be co-designed with community representatives to ensure it meets local barriers.

Mental health and community services
- Increase capacity in community and primary care mental health services with shorter waiting times, including early intervention teams and crisis support with rapid access pathways. Where appropriate, offer drop-in or extended-hours slots to reduce avoidable crises.
- Integrate mental health triage into NHS111 and GP booking systems so people with urgent mental health needs get a timely response and appropriate care, rather than being shunted between services.

What I have seen in practice and why these changes matter
- In our area, a family member with chest discomfort tried NHS111 twice over a weekend. The calls were lengthy, but the clinical input was inconsistent, and the next steps were unclear. By the time they reached urgent care, the wait felt intolerable and anxiety grew. A unified triage approach with direct escalation to urgent care could have shortened this path and improved safety.
- A patient with limited English faced delayed access because appointment letters and reminders were not consistently translated, and interpreters were not always available for the initial contact. We know language barriers disproportionately affect marginalised groups and can lead to late presentations and worse outcomes.
- In practice, GP booking portals vary between practices; some offer online access only during business hours, others require multiple logins for different services. This duplication creates confusion and discourages people with limited time or low digital literacy from seeking care promptly.

In short, timely access will improve where there is clarity about who to contact, a simple and unified way to book, staff who understand diverse communities, and a system that keeps patients moving through the right services without repetition or delay. We welcome these changes, but only if they are implemented with rigorous delivery standards, transparent reporting and meaningful involvement from local communities to ensure equity of access across England.

We would be happy to provide further detail or participate in local pilots to test these approaches and share learning across regions.

Agree. In our area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we focus on growing the workforce through targeted recruitment, including international hires, with clear incentives, better pay and flexible working, plus strong wellbeing support so staff stay. When GP practices can recruit and retain clinicians, patients get shorter waits and more stable care teams.

Protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients to improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. A longer appointment already helped my neighbour with multi‑morbid conditions to avoid repeated trips.

Target resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to reduce access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In our local clinic, interpreters for Polish and Urdu speakers and outreach to migrant communities increased registrations and trust. We saw fewer missed appointments after carers and community health workers visited homes and spoke in people’s language.

Specific examples: a practice recruited two GPs from abroad, offered relocation assistance and flexible morning/evening clinics; extended chronic care slots from 10 to 20 minutes; mental health service hubs with one-stop triage reduced waiting times.

Overall, these steps would help older residents manage chronic conditions, improve outcomes and ease pressure on urgent care.

Agree. In our area, delays for routine GP appointments and mental health support are a real barrier. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to manage everyday cases would free GPs to focus on complex care. I've seen pharmacy staff already do medication reviews efficiently; extending their remit to triage minor concerns and ensure patients are on the right meds would cut wasted GP time and reduce wait times. A physiotherapist-led triage for back and joint pain could start treatment quickly, with GPs reserved for persistent or red-flag issues. Paramedics and home-visits by allied professionals could prevent hospital trips and support older neighbours at home. 

Expanding community mental health teams, investing in early intervention and crisis response, and increasing talking therapies would tackle waits and improve parity with physical health. When mental health services are in reach, people seek help earlier—IAPT services, for instance, should be able to offer same-week access for those in crisis. Finally, more GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots, plus better scheduling—extended daytime slots, longer sessions where needed, and digital triage—would make timely care a reality instead of a wish.

I strongly support changes that would bring timely GP, community health and mentall health care closer to home. Expanding multidisciplinary teams would make a real difference. In practice, a pharmacist-led triage and medicines review could handle routine issues, repeat prescriptions and minor infections, freeing GPs to focus on more complex cases. A physiotherapist-led clinic for back pain, sports injuries and rehab would cut waiting times and reduce unnecessary referrals to specialists. Paramedics and physician associates could carry out hom visits or quick in-person assessments for non-urgent concerns, helping familie with children and older or mobility‑challenged residents access care sooner. I’d welcome a regular, nurse/clinician‑led mobile clinic visiting our town, including evenings, plus a telehealth hub at hteee local library where people can book quick video appointments or access mental health support. I live in England and timely access to GP, community and mental health services often feels fragmented. I support expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle routine cases, freeing GPs for complex care. A recent back strain was managed by physio and a pharmacist quick review, which avoided a GP visit and helped me move on quickly.

Investing in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners together could make care more seamless and reduce repeated trips. In my town a small hub is already cutting travel for older residents. My worry is funding stability and robust governance: data sharing must work, but consent and privacy must be protected, and staff need protected time to collaborate.

NHS111, triage and booking systems should prioritise urgent cases and cut duplication. I’ve faced confusing routing and slow bookings online. A well-resourced triage with phone or video options, plus straightforward same-day slots, would help people who struggle with digital tools.

In short, a targeted, well-funded rollout of integrated hubs and MDTs, with clear governance and patient involvement, could improve access without compromising care quality.

I welcome the focus on improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. Too many people still face long waits for mental health support, and that isn’t acceptable when physical health gets treated with far more immediacy. I think a real shift towards expanding community mental health teams, strengthening early intervention, bolstering crisis response and widening the availability of talking therapies will help close the parity gap and prevent crises from developing in the first place.

First, expanding community mental health teams across the age spectrum is essential. In practice, that means more full-time mental health nurses, clinical psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers and peer-support workers co-located with GPs and in community hubs. If CMHTs can be more responsive—offering same-day triage, home visits where appropriate and a dependable rapid assessment pathway—people won’t have to wait weeks for a plan or a referral to the right specialist. I’d like to see clearer target times for initial CMHT assessment, with dedicated on-call slots for urgent cases similar to physical health pathways.

Second, early intervention must be a core pillar. When younger people, or those experiencing the early signs of psychosis or debilitating anxiety, can access specialist assessment quickly, outcomes improve dramatically. That means expanding Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) teams so caseloads are manageable and referrals are fast-tracked, ideally with a same- or next-day response for suspected cases. For other conditions, robust early-intervention pathways within CMHTs and primary care would shorten the duration of distress and reduce the progression to crisis.

Third, crisis response needs to be strengthened. Crisis Resolution and Home Treatment Teams should be available 24/7, with clear paths to escalate to inpatient care only when necessary. We should also pilot community-based crisis hubs or crisis cafés in neighbourhoods as a alternative to A&E for people in acute distress. If someone in our family experiences a mental health crisis, a rapid and compassionate response that prioritises home-based care or immediate short-stay options can be life-changing and can prevent deterioration.

Fourth, talking therapies must be more accessible and appropriately funded. IAPT services have transformed access to evidence-based therapies like CBT, but waiting times still vary and some groups have less access than others. Expanding IAPT capacity with longer hours, more flexible delivery channels (in GP practices, community venues and digitally), and a broader range of therapies—including trauma-focused and person-centred approaches—would mean people can get help when they need it. It’s also important that therapies are culturally appropriate, available in multiple languages, and actively staffed by clinicians who understand local communities.

Fifth, GP access and integration with mental health services must improve. People report difficulty getting timely GP appointments, and a mental health professional embedded in primary care can triage, provide early support, and guide patients to the right specialist quickly. I’d support extended GP hours, more same-day appointments for urgent mental health concerns, and clear, streamlined referral pathways to CMHTs and IAPT without unnecessary bureaucracy.

Finally, these changes should be designed with patients and carers at the centre. Co-designing services with people who have lived experience, and publicly reporting waiting times and outcomes, will help us stay on track. It’s also vital that we invest in workforce development and retention—training more psychologists, nurses and social workers, offering competitive pay and career development—so these teams can deliver meaningful, sustainable improvements.

From my own experience, I’ve seen how delays in accessing talking therapies and crisis support can lead to escalating distress for family or friends. When a rapid, well-coordinated response is available—someone who can assess, refer and begin treatment quickly—the difference in people’s ability to cope and recover is night and day. In practice, if a local CMHT could offer same-day triage, reduce waiting times for CBT or counselling, and ensure a 24/7 crisis line with rapid access to a clinician, it would transform lives and reduce pressure on GPs and hospitals.

I urge the government to push these changes forward with adequate funding, clear targets and strong involvement from patients and communities. Timely access to mental health care is not a luxury—it’s part of delivering parity with physical health and ensuring people stay well enough to participate in work, family life and their communities.

As an organisation aiming to support communities across England, we hear regularly from people in the 55-64 age range about access to GP, community health and mental health services. Timely access isn’t just about booking slots; it’s about practical barriers that sit around daytime appointments—transport options, carers’ duties, and the need to take time off work. For many, even when a call-back or a slot is offered, getting to the clinic is the hard part due to late buses, parking pressures, or lack of flexible hours. In our area, our helpline fielded numerous calls last year from individuals seeking mental health support who found daytime sessions incompatible with work or caring responsibilities, sometimes leading them to delay help or reach crisis services later. We operate a small volunteer driver scheme to help with attendance, but that can’t substitute a system-wide change.

A more integrated approach—stronger links between GP practices, community health teams and social care; extended flexible access (evenings/weekends); simpler, clearer digital booking; and accessible information on local mental health options—would better reflect the realities of mid-life work and caregiving and avoid unnecessary delays. These considerations matter as much as increasing capacity in clinics.

Agree. In our area, strengthening multidisciplinary teams would free GPs to handle complex cases and get people seen sooner. Pharmacists could manage minor conditions, review medicines, and flag red flags early; physiotherapists could triage and treat common musculoskeletal issues, and physician associates or paramedics could cover routine checks and home visits. This would reduce GP workload and speed up access for worried patients.

NHS111 and care navigation should be integrated with live booking systems so urgent cases are prioritized and patients aren’t bounced between services. A more straightforward path—triage, then a same-day urgent slot or direct transfer to a clinician—would cut duplication and confusion. For my family, a crisp, well-structured triage route would have shaved days off waiting.

We also need more slots: recruit and train more GPs, practice nurses and therapists, and extend hours or offer group clinics for chronic conditions. With better scheduling and expanded capacity, waits can drop and people stay healthier—especially in winter when demand spikes.
